﴿And He created everything﴾ is general, encompassing the creation of essences and their actions. It was said that there is an ellipsis in the statement, its implied meaning being "and He created everything [that may be created]," so that His essence and His eternal attributes are excluded. This ellipsis is not needed, because one who says "I honored every man" does not include himself in the generality. Likewise, His essence and His eternal attributes are not included in the generality of ﴿and He created everything﴾.

(So He determined it with precise determination): if creation means determination, how then does (fa-qaddarahu, "so He determined it") come in? The meaning would become "and He determined everything, determining it with determination." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that He brought every thing into being in a way that takes proportion and balance into account, so He determined it and prepared it for what suits it. Or the bringing into being by Allah is called creation, because He does not bring anything into being for His wisdom except in a manner of proportion without disparity. So when it is said "Allah created such-and-such," it is like Allah bringing it into existence and originating it, without regard to the derivational sense, as if it were said: "He originated everything, and determined it in its origination to be varied." It was said: He gave it a limit and an end, and the meaning of (faqaddarahu) is that He determined it to endure until a known term. Ibn ‘Atiyyah said: the determination of things is their delimitation by places, times, quantities, benefit, and perfection.

﴿And they took, besides Him, gods﴾: the pronoun in (wa-ittakhadhu, "and they took") refers to what is understood from the context, because His saying ﴿and has not taken a son, and has no partner﴾ implies it; nothing is negated unless someone has claimed it. Al-Karmani said: the (waw) is a pronoun for the disbelievers, who are included in His saying "to the worlds." It was said: the word (nadhiran, "warner") indicates them, for they are the ones warned, and everyone who claims a god other than Allah is included in (wa-ittakhadhu). This is not restricted to idol-worshippers or star-worshippers. Al-Qadi said: it is unlikely that Christians are included, because they did not take gods besides Allah in the plural. The closer view is that it refers to worshippers of idols, though it may include those who worship angels, since their worshippers are numerous. This is not necessarily what he said, because (wa-ittakhadhu) is plural and (ālihah, "gods") is plural; when plural is matched with plural, singular is matched with singular, and it is not necessary that plural be matched with plural so that the object of Christian worship is included in the word (ālihah).

Then He described the gods by the negation of their creating anything of things, indicating the complete absence of power; then by the fact that they are themselves created by Allah in essence, or are fashioned by carving and shaping into a particular form. This is more emphatic in lowliness. Attributing creation to humans is permissible, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

*"Indeed you do determine what you have made, while some people make and do not determine."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: (khalq, "creation") here means (ifti‘al, "fashioning"), as in His saying ﴿and you fashion a lie﴾ (Al-‘Ankabut: 17). The meaning is that they preferred, over His worship, the worship of gods who are the most evident form of incapacity: they cannot control anything of Allah's acts or the acts of servants, since they do not fashion anything, while they themselves are fashioned, because their worshippers make them by carving and shaping.

﴿And they do not control for themselves﴾ the repelling of harm from themselves or the bringing of benefit to themselves, while they are capable of such. If they are incapable of fashioning, repelling harm, and bringing benefit, which servants are able to do, then they are even more incapable of death, life, and resurrection, which none can control except Allah.

(And those who disbelieve say): Ibn ‘Abbas said: this refers to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his followers. (Ifk, "falsehood") is the worst of lies.

﴿And other people helped him with it﴾. Mujahid said: a people of the Jews who conveyed the reports of past nations to him. It was also said: ‘Addas, the client (mawla) of Huwaytib ibn ‘Abd al-‘Uzza, and Yasar, the client of al-‘Ala' ibn al-Hadrami, and Jabr, the client of ‘Amir. They were People of the Book who read the Torah and had become Muslims, and the Messenger used to look after them. Ibn ‘Abbas said: they pointed to a group of slaves of the Arabs from Persia: Abu Fukayhah, the client of the Hadramis, and Jabr, Yasar, ‘Addas, and others. Al-Dahhak said: they meant Abu Fukayhah, the Roman. Al-Mubarrad said: by "other people" they meant the believers, because (akhar, "other") can only be of the same kind as the first. This is not necessarily so, because it is not required that they share a category of humanity, nor is it required that they share a description. Do you not see His saying ﴿a company fighting in the way of Allah and another company disbelieving﴾ (Al ‘Imran: 13)? Both share the general category of "company" but differ in description.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (faqad ja'u, "they have indeed come") refers back to (alladhina kafaru, "those who disbelieved"). The meaning is that these disbelievers have arrived at injustice, as you say "I came to the place," so that (ja'a, "came") is transitive by itself; this was said by al-Kisa'i. It is also permissible that the preposition be elided, meaning "with injustice and falsehood," so the verb is connected directly to its object. Al-Zajjaj said: when (ja'a) is used, it has both of these usages. Their injustice was that they made the Arab learn from the non-Arab a speech in Arabic whose eloquence overcame all the eloquent Arabs. The falsehood (zur) was that they slandered him by attributing to him what he was innocent of. It was also said: the pronoun refers back to "other people," and this is from the speech of the disbelievers. The pronoun in (waqalu, "and they said") refers to the disbelievers.

The discussion of ﴿tales of the ancients﴾ has already been given. (Iktatabaha, "he had it written down") means he gathered them, from the expression "kataba al-shay'," meaning he gathered it. Or it is from writing (kitabah), meaning he wrote them with his own hand. In that case, it is part of their lie against him, while they know that he does not write. It is like (istakabba al-ma') and (is-tabbahu), meaning he poured it and spilled it. The form (iftaʿala) may indicate effort and exertion, or it may mean he ordered it to be written, as in their saying "he had himself cupped" (ihtajama) or "he had himself bled" (iftasada) when he ordered that done.

﴿So they are dictated to him﴾: that is, they are cast upon him so that he may memorize them, because the image of casting upon one who memorizes is like the image of dictation to a scribe.

"And [they said:] 'Tales of the ancients' (asatir al-awwalin)" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is" or "this is" (asatir), and "ikhtatabahā" (he had it written down) is a second predicate. It is also permissible for "asatir" to be the subject and "ikhtatabahā" the predicate. The majority of readers read "ikhtatabahā" in the active voice. The reading of Talha is in the passive voice, and the meaning is "a scribe wrote it for him," because he was unlettered and did not write with his own hand, and that is part of the completeness of his miracle. Then the preposition (lām) was dropped, so the verb reached the pronoun, and "ikhtatabahā" became "iyyāhu kātib" (a scribe wrote it for him). This is like His saying: "And Musa chose his people" (al-A'raf: 155). Then the verb was made passive with the pronoun which is "iyyāhu," so it changed into a hidden nominative after having been an exposed accusative, and the pronoun of "asatir" remained in its state, so "ikhtatabahā" became as you see. End of quotation. This is from al-Zamakhshari, and it is not valid according to the school of the Basran majority, because "ikhtatabahā" in the sense of "he had it written" takes two objects: one of them is "musarrah" (explicit), which is the pronoun of "asatir," and the other is "muqayyad" (implicit), which is his pronoun, peace be upon him. Then the verb was extended, and the preposition was dropped, so "ikhtatabahā" became "iyyāhu kātib." When this verb is made passive, only the object that is explicit both in wording and in estimation may stand in for the subject, not the object that is explicit in wording but implicit in estimation. Accordingly, the construction would be "ukhtutibat-hu" and not "ikhtatabahā." Upon what we have stated, the Arabic usage has come down for this type, in which one of the two objects is explicit both in wording and in estimation, and the other is explicit in wording but not in estimation. The poet, who is al-Farazdaq, said:

"And among us is the one chosen for men, for generosity and bounty, when the violent winds blow."

Had it come according to what al-Zamakhshari established, the construction would be: "wa-minnā alladhī ukhtīra-hu al-rijāl," because "ikhtāra" reached "al-rijāl" by dropping the preposition, since its estimate is "ukhtīra min al-rijāl." The apparent meaning is that His saying: "He had it written, and it is dictated to him morning and evening" (al-Furqan: 5) is part of the speech of the disbelievers. It is related from al-Hasan that it is the speech of Allah, glorified is He, refuting them. It would only be correct if you read the hamza in "ikhtatabahā" as an interrogative of the sort that carries the sense of denial, and its meaning would be like His saying:

"I rejoice if the noble are struck, and if I take a herd of camels, short-haired and bare."

Al-Hasan is entitled to stop at "al-awwalin." The apparent meaning is that the dictation is restricted to the time when people disperse and the time when they retire to their dwellings, namely the morning (bukra) and the evening (asil), or they may be an expression for continuity. Talha and Isa read "fahiya tutla" with a taa in place of the meem.

"Say: He who knows the secret has sent it down" (al-Furqan: 6), i.e., every hidden secret. He answered them with this, namely by describing Him, exalted is He, with knowledge, because this Qur'an could only proceed from one who knows all knowables, given what it contains of the inimitability of its composition, which cannot be produced by anyone, even if he sought help from the whole world, and given its inclusion of the interests of the world and of kinds of sciences. He was satisfied with knowledge of the secret because whatever is other than it is more fitting for His knowledge to encompass. Or "He knows" refers to what you conceal of scheming against His Messenger while you know the falsehood of what you say, so He will repay you. "Indeed He is ever Forgiving and Merciful" (al-Furqan: 6): an encouragement that if they repent He will forgive them what passed of their disbelief and show mercy to them. Or "Forgiving and Merciful" concerns His giving them respite and not hastening punishment upon them for what they deserved of punishment because of their obstinacy (p-483). Or, when something indicating punishment preceded, He followed it with something indicating power over it, because one characterized by forgiveness and mercy is able to punish.

"And they said" (al-Furqan: 7): the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they had gathered with the Messenger in a well-known assembly, which Ibn Ishaq mentioned in the Sira. 'Utba and others said: "If you love leadership, we will make you our chief; or if wealth, we will gather wealth for you." When he refused them, they gathered against him and said: "What is wrong with you? You are a messenger from Allah, eating food and walking in the markets seeking provision. Ask your Lord to send down with you an angel to warn with you, or to cast to you a treasure from which you spend, or to turn for you the mountains of Makkah into gold, and the mountains be removed, and in their place be gardens through which water flows." They spread this argument, and the verse was revealed. The particle of the genitive (lam) was written in the Mushaf separated from "hadha," and this is an interrogative accompanied by mockery, meaning: "What is wrong with this one who claims to be a messenger?" They objected to him for what is the custom of messengers, as He said: "And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets" (al-Furqan: 20), i.e., his condition is like our condition, meaning he ought to be independent of eating and of seeking a living. Then they said: "Suppose he is a human; why is he not supported with an angel to warn with him, or a treasure cast down to him from heaven, by which he might be strengthened and not need to seek a livelihood?" Then they were content that he should have a garden from which he eats and gains provision, like the wealthy.

It is read "fatakūnu" with the raf', related by Abu Mu'adh, as a coordination with "unzila," because "unzila" is in the place of a nominative and is a past verb standing in the position of the present, i.e., "why is an angel not sent down to him?" Or it is the answer to the exhortation with the omission of "huwa," i.e., "then he [it] will be." The reading of the majority is with the naṣb as an answer to the exhortation. As for His saying "aw yulqā" (or a treasure be cast), the "aw" may be coordinated with "unzila," meaning "why is not...," so the sought object is one of these matters or all of them together according to the difference of the speakers. It is not permissible to read with naṣb "aw yulqā" or "aw takūnu" as coordinated with "fayakūna," because they are in the ruling of what is sought by the exhortation, not in the ruling of the answer, since His saying is "law lā unzila." Qatada and al-A'mash read "aw yakūnu" with yaa from below. And he read "ya'kulu" with the third-person yaa, i.e., the Messenger, and Zayd ibn 'Ali, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit, Talha and al-A'mash read it with the nun of the plural, i.e., they themselves eat from that garden, so they benefit from it in their worldly life and livelihood.

"And the wrongdoers said" (al-Furqan: 8), i.e., to the believers. Al-Zamakhshari said: "By 'the wrongdoers' he meant them themselves, by their very persons; the apparent noun was placed in the place of the pronoun so that they would be recorded as wrongdoers for what they said," end of quotation. His construction "wa-aradā bi-l-zālimīna iyyāhum bi-a'yānihim" is not a sound Arabic construction; rather the Arabic construction would be "wa-aradahum bi-a'yānihim bi-l-zālimīn." "You follow only a man affected by magic" (al-Furqan: 8): "masḥūran" means one whose mind has been overcome by magic, and this is more apparent; or one having a "sihr" (windpipe/lungs); or he is fed with food and drink, i.e., nourished; or his "sahr" (lung) was struck, as you say "ra'istuhu" meaning "I struck his head." It was said: "masḥūran" means a magician, by which they meant he is a human like them, not an angel. Its interpretation has been mentioned in al-Isra'. According to these two views it is said that those who said this were al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid and those who followed them.

"See how they struck for you examples" (al-Furqan: 9): i.e., they said those sayings about you and invented for you those attributes and conditions, rare ones, such as prophethood shared between a human and an angel, the casting of a treasure upon you, and other things. So they remained bewildered, astray, not finding a saying to settle upon; i.e., they strayed from the truth, so they find no path to it. It was said: "They struck for you examples" of the bewitched, the soothsayer, the poet and others, "so they went astray": they missed the way, so they find no path of guidance and cannot attain it, because they are entangled in its opposite, error. It was said: "So they are not able to find a way" (al-Furqan: 9) to a proof or evidence for what they say. Thus at one time they say: he is eloquent and fluent, fabricating the Qur'an from himself; at another: he is a madman; at another: he is a magician; at another: he is bewitched. Ibn 'Abbas said: these polytheists made likenesses for you by saying "he is bewitched," so by that they strayed from the right course, and so they find no path to the truth with which He sent you. Mujahid said: they do not find an exit that would take them out of the examples which they struck for you. Its meaning is that they struck these examples for you in order to reach your denial by them, but they went astray from the path of truth and from attaining what they wanted.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "See how" (p-484) the people occupied themselves with striking these examples which have no benefit, because when they went astray and wanted to disparage your prophethood, they found no way to disparage it, since criticism of it can only concern what undermines the miracles he claimed, not this kind of speech. Al-Farra' said: "They are not able to find a stratagem regarding your matter." Al-Suddi said: "a way" to criticism.

When the polytheists said what they said, it was narrated that it was said to him: If you wish, we will give you the treasures of the world and its keys, which no one has been given before you nor will anyone be given after you, and that will not diminish anything of yours in the Hereafter; or if you wish, we will gather it for you in the Hereafter. He said: "Let that be gathered for me in the Hereafter." Then "Blessed is He who..." was revealed. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, from him, peace be upon him, that he said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, presented to me the plain of Makkah as gold, and I said: "No, rather one day of satiety and three days of hunger," for that is more for my remembrance and my supplication.

Al-Zamakhshari said regarding "tabāraka": meaning it increased in good, "the One who, if He wills" (al-Furqan: 10), would grant you in this world "good" better than what they said, namely that He would make for you the like of what He promised you in the Hereafter of gardens and palaces, end of quotation.

The indication of "dhālika" (that) apparently refers to what the disbelievers mentioned of the garden and the treasure in this world; Mujahid said so. Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation that it refers to his eating food and walking in the markets is far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that this "making" would be in this world if Allah willed it. It was said: in the Hereafter. "In" was placed before the will to alert that this is not attained except by His mercy, and that it is contingent upon the pure exercise of His will; no servant has a right over Allah, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. The first is more eloquent in rebuking the disbelievers and refuting them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is refuted by His saying after that: 'Nay, they denied the Hour'" (al-Furqan: 11). Not so; for the meaning with it is firmly established, and it is a coordination upon what was related from them: he says, "Nay, He brought something more marvelous than all that," which is their denial of the Hour.

The majority read "wa-yajʿal" with the jazm, considered coordinated upon the place of "jaʿala," because the estimate is "in yashaʾ yajʿal." It is also permissible that it be marfu', its lam assimilated into the lam of "laka," but that is known only from the school of Abu 'Amr. Among the Seven, Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read with the jazm. The school of the three does not include assimilation of identical letters when the first is vowelled; it is from the school of Abu 'Amr as we mentioned. Mujahid, Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Humayd, Abu Bakr and Mahbub, from Abu 'Amr, read with the raf'. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The resumption, and its basis is coordination upon the meaning in His saying 'jaʿala,' because the answer to the condition is the place of resumption. Do you not see that sentences of beginning and predicate may stand in the place of the answer to the condition?" Al-Hawfi said: "Whoever reads with raf' makes it a resumed sentence, cut off from what precedes it," end of quotation. Abu al-Baqa' said: "And with raf' by way of resumption." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is read 'wa-yajʿalu' with raf' as coordination upon 'jaʿala,' because when the condition is in the past form it is permissible for its answer to be jazm or raf', like his saying:

"And if a friend comes to him on a day of asking, he says: 'Neither is my property absent nor is my sanctuary,'" end of quotation.

What Al-Zamakhshari held, that when the verb of the condition is past the answer may be raf', is not the school of Sibawayh, for Sibawayh's school is that the answer is omitted, and that this present verb in the raf' is intended to be preposed; and because the answer is omitted, the verb of the condition can only be in the past form.

The Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that it is the apodosis (jawab) itself, and that it is elided with the fa' (the particle "fa'") omitted. Others held that it is the apodosis without any elision of the fa' and without any inversion (taqdim). Since the particle of condition (adat al-shart) has no visible effect on the protasis (fi'l al-shart) because the latter is in the past form (madi al-lafz), it is too weak to govern the apodosis verb, so the apodosis verb is not governed by it and remains in the nominative (marfu'an). The majority (al-Jumhur) held that this construction is eloquent (fasih) and permissible in speech. Some of our companions said: it is a poetic necessity (darura), since it occurs only in poetry, and it is with the fa' understood. The discussion of these positions is mentioned in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw).

ʿUbayd Allah ibn Musa and Talha ibn Sulayman read (wa-yajʿala) with the accusative (bil-nasb), on the basis of the implied "an" (idmar an). Abu al-Fath said: it is in the apodosis with the waw, and this is a weak reading, end of quote. The parallel to these three readings is the verse of al-Nabigha:

*"If Abu Qabus dies, the spring of the people will die, and the sacred month,*
*and we will take after him the tail-ends of a life, a humped back that has no hump."*

It is narrated with the jussive (jazm) of "na'khudh," with its nominative (raf'), and with its accusative (nasb).

﴿Rather, they denied the Hour﴾. Al-Karmani said: the meaning is that what prevented them from belief was not your eating food or your walking in the marketplace, but rather their denial of the Hour prevented them. It was also said: what they clung to is not a doubt, but rather the driving force behind their denial of you is their denial of the Hour, finding it burdensome to prepare for it. It was also said: it is possible that it is connected to what follows it, as if he said: "Rather, they denied the Hour," so how would they turn to this answer, and how would they believe in the hastening of the like of what He promised you in the Hereafter, when they do not believe in the Hereafter? End of quote. "Bal" (rather) is used to leave aside the preceding expression without negating its meaning and to take up another expression.

(Wa-aʿtadna) means: we made it prepared. (Saʿiran) means: a fire of great kindling. From al-Hasan: it is a name of Jahannam.

(Idha ra'athum): it was said: this is literal, and that Jahannam has two eyes; a report has been transmitted on this. If it is authentic, it is the correct view; otherwise it is a metaphor (majaz), meaning that it became from them at the distance a viewer sees from afar, like their saying: "their houses see each other (tatarra'a)," meaning they face and oppose one another, and from this: "their two fires do not see each other (la tatarra'a naraha)."

Some people said: "fire" is the name of a fiery animal that speaks, sees, hears, changes, and exhales; this was related by al-Karmani. It was also said: it is by elision of a noun (hadhf mudaf), meaning: its guardians saw them from a far place. It was said: a distance of five hundred years. It was said: a hundred years. It was said: one year.

(Sami'u laha): a sound of rage, because rage is not heard. When it is by elision of the noun, the meaning is: they became enraged and exhaled in anger at the disbelievers and with a desire for vengeance upon them. It was also said: (sami'u) means the sound of its blazing and its flaring. It was also said: it is like the verse of the poet:

*"So would that your husband had become one who girds on a sword and a spear."*

This is explained in two ways: the first is elision, meaning: "and one who holds a spear." The second is ta'min (implicit meaning): the verb "mutaqallidan" (girding on) is made to carry the meaning of "mutasallihan" (armed), and so it is with the verse, meaning: (they heard it) and they saw ﴿a raging and a roaring﴾, and each one returns to what suits it. Or (sami'u) is made to carry the meaning of "adraku" (perceived), so that it includes the raging and the roaring.

(Makanan) is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning: in a narrow place. From Ibn Abbas: it narrows upon them like the narrowing of the spear's butt into the shaft, while they are bound together (muqarranin): their hands are tied to their necks with chains. It was said: with each disbeliever is bound his devil in one chain, and upon their feet are shackles.

Ibn Kathir and Ubayd, from Abu Amr, read (dayyiqan). Ibn Atiyya said: Abu Shayba, the companion of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, read (muqarranun) with a waw, and it is an anomalous reading (shadha). The correct reading is the reading of the people. Ibn Khalawayh attributed it to Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Its grammatical point is that it is raised (yartafi'a) as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (ulqu), a substitution of an indefinite for a definite, and it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

The apparent meaning is the call for destruction (du'a' al-thubur), which is ruin, so they say: "Woe, our destruction!" meaning, it is said: "O destruction! This is your time." It was also said: the one called upon is omitted; its estimation is: they called upon one who would not answer them, saying: "Let us be destroyed, a destruction." Thubur, Ibn Abbas said, is woe (wayl); al-Dahhak said it is ruin (halak). From it is the verse of Ibn al-Zibaʿra:

*"When he runs alongside the devil in the paths of error, and whoever inclines to its inclination is destroyed (mathbur)."*

(La tad'u al-yawm) it is said to them: "Do not call (la tad'u)," or they are more entitled to be told this even if there is no speech there, meaning: do not restrict yourselves to one sorrow, but rather grieve a great deal of grief. Its abundance is either because the torment is perpetual, so it is constantly renewed, or because it consists of kinds, and each kind is a cause of ruin (thubur) due to its severity and horror.

ʿAmr ibn Muhammad read (thabura) with a fatha on the tha' in all three instances. The form fa'ul with a fatha on the fa' among verbal nouns is rare, like "batul." Ali ibn Isa related: "ma thabaraka 'an hadha al-amr," meaning: what turned you away from this matter. It is as if they called out for what they had done and said: "Woe, what turned us from obedience to God!" as you say: "Woe, our regret!" It is narrated that the first to cry out with that is Iblis, who says: "Woe, my destruction!" until he is clothed in a garment of Jahannam, which he places on his forehead and drags from behind him; then his followers follow him in speech, and the guardians of Jahannam say to them: ﴿Do not call out today...﴾ the verse.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Khatal and his companions.

The apparent meaning is that the demonstrative (al-ishara) (p-486) with "dhalika" refers to the Fire and the states of its people. It was said: it refers to the Garden and the treasure in their statement. It was said: it refers to the Garden and the palaces made in this world on condition of God's will. "Khayr" here does not indicate superiority; rather, it follows the usage of the Arabs in explaining the excellence of a thing and its specificity in excellence to the exclusion of its opposite, as in His saying:

*"So your evil is for your good, the ransom."*

And as in the saying of the Arabs: "Is misery more beloved to you or happiness?" And as in His saying: ﴿The prison is more beloved to me than what they call me to﴾ (Yusuf 33). This interrogation is by way of reproach and rebuke.

Ibn Atiyya said: Since the speech is an interrogation, it is permissible for its wording to come in the comparative form between the Garden and the Fire in goodness, because the one who addresses may test his interlocutor with whatever he wishes, to see whether he answers correctly or incorrectly. Sibawayh and others prohibited the comparative when the speech is a declarative statement, because there is in it a contradiction; but when it is an interrogation, that is permissible, end of quote.

What he mentioned is contradicted by his saying: "So your evil is for your good," and his saying: ﴿The prison is more beloved to me﴾, since this is a declarative statement. Likewise the saying: "Honey is sweeter than vinegar," unless the declarative is restricted by the condition that the judgment is clear to the hearer, such that nothing stirs in his mind and he does not hesitate as to which of the two is better, in which case it is permissible.

The pronoun in (allati) is elided, meaning: "which He promised," and the pronoun in (ma yashaʾun) is likewise, meaning: "what they wish for." In His saying "what they wish for" there is evidence that the attainment of all desires does not occur except in the Garden. His saying (jaza'an wa-masiran) encompasses the reward and its abode, as He said: ﴿How excellent is the reward and how good a resting place﴾ (al-Kahf 31), and in its opposite: ﴿How evil is the drink and how bad a resting place﴾ (al-Kahf 29), because by the goodness of the place the bliss is multiplied, just as by its badness the torment is multiplied.

(Wa'dan), meaning: promised. (Mas'ula), meaning: asked for. The angels asked for it in their saying: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the gardens of Eden which You promised them﴾ (Ghafir 8). This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. And the people in their saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ (Al 'Imran 194), ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾ (al-Baqara 201). Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd said its meaning is the same.

Al-Farra' said: ﴿a promise to be asked﴾ means: obligatory, as one says: "I will certainly give you a thousand, a promise to be asked," meaning: obligatory, even if it is not asked. It was said: what al-Farra' said is absurd, end of quote. It is not absurd; the meaning is that it ought to be asked, this promise which You made, or it is about to be asked, meaning: it is its right to be something asked for. And (upon your Lord), meaning: by reason of the promise it has become something that must be. Al-Zamakhshari said: that was a promised thing, obligatory upon your Lord to fulfil, genuinely deserving to be asked and sought, because it is a recompense and a due that is merited; and this is according to the doctrine of the al-Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds God is bound by justice and reward).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verses 1–16 (part 1 of 3)**

Surat al-Furqan

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful

[p. 479] ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He has not taken a son, and He has no partner in the dominion. He created everything and determined it with precise measure.﴾ ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods that create nothing, and they are themselves created. They control not harm nor benefit for themselves, and they control neither death nor life nor resurrection.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say: "This is nothing but a fabrication which he has invented, and other people have helped him with it." Indeed they have committed injustice and falsehood.﴾ ﴿And they say: "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ ﴿Say: "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed He is ever Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿And they say: "What is this Messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets? Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner with him?"﴾ ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden from which he eats?" And the wrongdoers say: "You follow only a man under enchantment."﴾ ﴿Look how they strike similitudes for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ ﴿Blessed is He who, if He willed, would give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He would give you palaces.﴾ ﴿Rather, they deny the Hour, and We have prepared a blazing fire for whoever denies the Hour.﴾ ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they will hear its raging and its roaring.﴾ ﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place of it, bound together, they will call out there for destruction.﴾ ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.﴾ ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the righteous? It is their reward and final destination."﴾ ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever. It is a promise incumbent upon your Lord, to be asked of Him.﴾

[p. 480] This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Ibn ‘Abbas and Qatadah said: except for three verses, which were revealed in Medina, namely ﴿And those who do not call upon another god with Allah﴾ (Al-Furqan: 68) up to His saying ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (Al-Furqan: 70). Al-Dahhak said it is Medinan, except from its beginning up to His saying "and resurrection," so that part is Meccan.

The connection (munasabah) between the beginning of this surah and the end of what precedes it is that when Allah mentioned the obligation of the believers’ pledge of allegiance to the Messenger, and that when they were with him in an important matter, none of them could depart without his permission, and He warned against whoever opposes his command, and mentioned that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that He, exalted is He, knows what they are upon and will recompense them for it, this constituted the utmost in warning and admonition. It was therefore appropriate to open this surah by stating that He, exalted is He, is far removed in His attributes from deficiencies, abundant in good, and that among His goodness is that He ﴿sent down the Criterion﴾ upon His Messenger as a warner to them. Thus there is in this both encouragement to seek His goodness and a warning against His punishment.

(Tabaraka) is a form of (tafa‘ala), the intransitive reflexive (mutawi‘) of (barraka). It is a verb that is not conjugated in the usual way and is not used for anyone other than Allah, so no present tense, active participle, or verbal noun is derived from it. Al-Tirimmah said:

*You are Blessed; none gives what You have withheld, and none withholds what You have given, O Lord.*

Ibn ‘Abbas said: He has always been and will never cease. Al-Khalil said: He is glorified (tamajjada). Al-Dahhak said: He is magnified (ta‘azzama). Al-Asma‘i related "tabarakta ‘alaykum" from an Arab who climbed a hill and said this to his companions, meaning: I have exalted myself and risen high. According to these interpretations, the word is an attribute of essence (sifat dhat). Ibn ‘Abbas also said, as did al-Hasan and al-Nakha‘i: it derives from blessing (barakah), which is the increase of good from Him. The meaning is that His goodness and His giving have increased and become abundant. According to this, it is an attribute of action (sifat fi‘l), and the verb is attributed to (alladhi, "He who"). Although they do not acknowledge that He is the One who sent down the Criterion, the proof of its miraculous nature is established, so the relative clause becomes known through the evidence, even though they deny it. It has already been explained in Al ‘Imran why the Qur'an was called al-Furqan.

The majority read (upon His servant), meaning the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn al-Zubayr read (upon His servants), meaning the Messenger and his community, as in His saying ﴿We have sent down to you﴾ and ﴿what was sent down to us﴾. It is unlikely that "the Criterion" refers to the previous scriptures, and that "His servant" refers to those to whom they were sent, making it a collective noun, like His saying ﴿And if you count the favor of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ (Ibrahim: 34). The pronoun in (liyakuna, "that he may be") — Ibn Zayd said it refers back to (His servant). This is preferred because it is the principal subject to which the verb is attributed, and it is from the description of Him, exalted is He, as in His saying ﴿Indeed We were warners﴾ (Al-Dukhan: 3). Apparently (nadhiran, "warner") means (mundhir, one who warns). It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun meaning warning (inadh), like (nakir) meaning denial (inkar). Among this usage is ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ (Al-Qamar: 16). (Lil-‘alamin, "to the worlds") is general, encompassing humans and jinn, whether contemporaries of his or those who came after him. This is known from the mass-transmitted hadith and the apparent meaning of the verses. Ibn al-Zubayr read (lil-‘alamin) as "to the jinn and humans," which is an explanation of (lil-‘alamin).

Since at the end of the surah (Al-Nur: 64) there was ﴿Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, which was a statement that what is in them is His possession, He here states that the dominion over them belongs to Him, that is, His subjugation of them and of what is in them. Thus possession and dominion over them and what is in them are combined for Him. The relative pronoun (alladhi) here is either a cut-off apposition (maqtu‘) for praise, in the nominative or accusative, or an adjective, or a substitute (badal) for (alladhi nazzala). What follows (nazzala) is part of the relative clause (silah) and is connected to it, so it is not considered a separation between the adjective or substitute and its head.

(He has not taken a son): the apparent meaning is the negation of taking, that is, He has not made anyone into the position of a son. It was said the meaning is: He has not had a son, in the sense of His saying "He has not begotten," because procreation is impossible for Him. This is a refutation of the polytheists of Quraysh and of the Christians and Jews who attribute a son to Allah.

﴿And He has no partner in the dominion﴾ is an emphasis on His saying ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and a refutation of whoever makes a partner for Allah.

﴿And He created everything﴾ is general, encompassing the creation of essences and their actions. It was said that there is an ellipsis in the statement, its implied meaning being "and He created everything [that may be created]," so that His essence and His eternal attributes are excluded. This ellipsis is not needed, because one who says "I honored every man" does not include himself in the generality. Likewise, His essence and His eternal attributes are not included in the generality of ﴿and He created everything﴾.

(So He determined it with precise determination): if creation means determination, how then does (fa-qaddarahu, "so He determined it") come in? The meaning would become "and He determined everything, determining it with determination." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that He brought every thing into being in a way that takes proportion and balance into account, so He determined it and prepared it for what suits it. Or the bringing into being by Allah is called creation, because He does not bring anything into being for His wisdom except in a manner of proportion without disparity. So when it is said "Allah created such-and-such," it is like Allah bringing it into existence and originating it, without regard to the derivational sense, as if it were said: "He originated everything, and determined it in its origination to be varied." It was said: He gave it a limit and an end, and the meaning of (faqaddarahu) is that He determined it to endure until a known term. Ibn ‘Atiyyah said: the determination of things is their delimitation by places, times, quantities, benefit, and perfection.

﴿And they took, besides Him, gods﴾: the pronoun in (wa-ittakhadhu, "and they took") refers to what is understood from the context, because His saying ﴿and has not taken a son, and has no partner﴾ implies it; nothing is negated unless someone has claimed it. Al-Karmani said: the (waw) is a pronoun for the disbelievers, who are included in His saying "to the worlds." It was said: the word (nadhiran, "warner") indicates them, for they are the ones warned, and everyone who claims a god other than Allah is included in (wa-ittakhadhu). This is not restricted to idol-worshippers or star-worshippers. Al-Qadi said: it is unlikely that Christians are included, because they did not take gods besides Allah in the plural. The closer view is that it refers to worshippers of idols, though it may include those who worship angels, since their worshippers are numerous. This is not necessarily what he said, because (wa-ittakhadhu) is plural and (ālihah, "gods") is plural; when plural is matched with plural, singular is matched with singular, and it is not necessary that plural be matched with plural so that the object of Christian worship is included in the word (ālihah).

Then He described the gods by the negation of their creating anything of things, indicating the complete absence of power; then by the fact that they are themselves created by Allah in essence, or are fashioned by carving and shaping into a particular form. This is more emphatic in lowliness. Attributing creation to humans is permissible, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

*"Indeed you do determine what you have made, while some people make and do not determine."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: (khalq, "creation") here means (ifti‘al, "fashioning"), as in His saying ﴿and you fashion a lie﴾ (Al-‘Ankabut: 17). The meaning is that they preferred, over His worship, the worship of gods who are the most evident form of incapacity: they cannot control anything of Allah's acts or the acts of servants, since they do not fashion anything, while they themselves are fashioned, because their worshippers make them by carving and shaping.

﴿And they do not control for themselves﴾ the repelling of harm from themselves or the bringing of benefit to themselves, while they are capable of such. If they are incapable of fashioning, repelling harm, and bringing benefit, which servants are able to do, then they are even more incapable of death, life, and resurrection, which none can control except Allah.

(And those who disbelieve say): Ibn ‘Abbas said: this refers to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his followers. (Ifk, "falsehood") is the worst of lies.

﴿And other people helped him with it﴾. Mujahid said: a people of the Jews who conveyed the reports of past nations to him. It was also said: ‘Addas, the client (mawla) of Huwaytib ibn ‘Abd al-‘Uzza, and Yasar, the client of al-‘Ala' ibn al-Hadrami, and Jabr, the client of ‘Amir. They were People of the Book who read the Torah and had become Muslims, and the Messenger used to look after them. Ibn ‘Abbas said: they pointed to a group of slaves of the Arabs from Persia: Abu Fukayhah, the client of the Hadramis, and Jabr, Yasar, ‘Addas, and others. Al-Dahhak said: they meant Abu Fukayhah, the Roman. Al-Mubarrad said: by "other people" they meant the believers, because (akhar, "other") can only be of the same kind as the first. This is not necessarily so, because it is not required that they share a category of humanity, nor is it required that they share a description. Do you not see His saying ﴿a company fighting in the way of Allah and another company disbelieving﴾ (Al ‘Imran: 13)? Both share the general category of "company" but differ in description.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (faqad ja'u, "they have indeed come") refers back to (alladhina kafaru, "those who disbelieved"). The meaning is that these disbelievers have arrived at injustice, as you say "I came to the place," so that (ja'a, "came") is transitive by itself; this was said by al-Kisa'i. It is also permissible that the preposition be elided, meaning "with injustice and falsehood," so the verb is connected directly to its object. Al-Zajjaj said: when (ja'a) is used, it has both of these usages. Their injustice was that they made the Arab learn from the non-Arab a speech in Arabic whose eloquence overcame all the eloquent Arabs. The falsehood (zur) was that they slandered him by attributing to him what he was innocent of. It was also said: the pronoun refers back to "other people," and this is from the speech of the disbelievers. The pronoun in (waqalu, "and they said") refers to the disbelievers.

The discussion of ﴿tales of the ancients﴾ has already been given. (Iktatabaha, "he had it written down") means he gathered them, from the expression "kataba al-shay'," meaning he gathered it. Or it is from writing (kitabah), meaning he wrote them with his own hand. In that case, it is part of their lie against him, while they know that he does not write. It is like (istakabba al-ma') and (is-tabbahu), meaning he poured it and spilled it. The form (iftaʿala) may indicate effort and exertion, or it may mean he ordered it to be written, as in their saying "he had himself cupped" (ihtajama) or "he had himself bled" (iftasada) when he ordered that done.

﴿So they are dictated to him﴾: that is, they are cast upon him so that he may memorize them, because the image of casting upon one who memorizes is like the image of dictation to a scribe.

"And [they said:] 'Tales of the ancients' (asatir al-awwalin)" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is" or "this is" (asatir), and "ikhtatabahā" (he had it written down) is a second predicate. It is also permissible for "asatir" to be the subject and "ikhtatabahā" the predicate. The majority of readers read "ikhtatabahā" in the active voice. The reading of Talha is in the passive voice, and the meaning is "a scribe wrote it for him," because he was unlettered and did not write with his own hand, and that is part of the completeness of his miracle. Then the preposition (lām) was dropped, so the verb reached the pronoun, and "ikhtatabahā" became "iyyāhu kātib" (a scribe wrote it for him). This is like His saying: "And Musa chose his people" (al-A'raf: 155). Then the verb was made passive with the pronoun which is "iyyāhu," so it changed into a hidden nominative after having been an exposed accusative, and the pronoun of "asatir" remained in its state, so "ikhtatabahā" became as you see. End of quotation. This is from al-Zamakhshari, and it is not valid according to the school of the Basran majority, because "ikhtatabahā" in the sense of "he had it written" takes two objects: one of them is "musarrah" (explicit), which is the pronoun of "asatir," and the other is "muqayyad" (implicit), which is his pronoun, peace be upon him. Then the verb was extended, and the preposition was dropped, so "ikhtatabahā" became "iyyāhu kātib." When this verb is made passive, only the object that is explicit both in wording and in estimation may stand in for the subject, not the object that is explicit in wording but implicit in estimation. Accordingly, the construction would be "ukhtutibat-hu" and not "ikhtatabahā." Upon what we have stated, the Arabic usage has come down for this type, in which one of the two objects is explicit both in wording and in estimation, and the other is explicit in wording but not in estimation. The poet, who is al-Farazdaq, said:

"And among us is the one chosen for men, for generosity and bounty, when the violent winds blow."

Had it come according to what al-Zamakhshari established, the construction would be: "wa-minnā alladhī ukhtīra-hu al-rijāl," because "ikhtāra" reached "al-rijāl" by dropping the preposition, since its estimate is "ukhtīra min al-rijāl." The apparent meaning is that His saying: "He had it written, and it is dictated to him morning and evening" (al-Furqan: 5) is part of the speech of the disbelievers. It is related from al-Hasan that it is the speech of Allah, glorified is He, refuting them. It would only be correct if you read the hamza in "ikhtatabahā" as an interrogative of the sort that carries the sense of denial, and its meaning would be like His saying:

"I rejoice if the noble are struck, and if I take a herd of camels, short-haired and bare."

Al-Hasan is entitled to stop at "al-awwalin." The apparent meaning is that the dictation is restricted to the time when people disperse and the time when they retire to their dwellings, namely the morning (bukra) and the evening (asil), or they may be an expression for continuity. Talha and Isa read "fahiya tutla" with a taa in place of the meem.

"Say: He who knows the secret has sent it down" (al-Furqan: 6), i.e., every hidden secret. He answered them with this, namely by describing Him, exalted is He, with knowledge, because this Qur'an could only proceed from one who knows all knowables, given what it contains of the inimitability of its composition, which cannot be produced by anyone, even if he sought help from the whole world, and given its inclusion of the interests of the world and of kinds of sciences. He was satisfied with knowledge of the secret because whatever is other than it is more fitting for His knowledge to encompass. Or "He knows" refers to what you conceal of scheming against His Messenger while you know the falsehood of what you say, so He will repay you. "Indeed He is ever Forgiving and Merciful" (al-Furqan: 6): an encouragement that if they repent He will forgive them what passed of their disbelief and show mercy to them. Or "Forgiving and Merciful" concerns His giving them respite and not hastening punishment upon them for what they deserved of punishment because of their obstinacy (p-483). Or, when something indicating punishment preceded, He followed it with something indicating power over it, because one characterized by forgiveness and mercy is able to punish.

"And they said" (al-Furqan: 7): the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they had gathered with the Messenger in a well-known assembly, which Ibn Ishaq mentioned in the Sira. 'Utba and others said: "If you love leadership, we will make you our chief; or if wealth, we will gather wealth for you." When he refused them, they gathered against him and said: "What is wrong with you? You are a messenger from Allah, eating food and walking in the markets seeking provision. Ask your Lord to send down with you an angel to warn with you, or to cast to you a treasure from which you spend, or to turn for you the mountains of Makkah into gold, and the mountains be removed, and in their place be gardens through which water flows." They spread this argument, and the verse was revealed. The particle of the genitive (lam) was written in the Mushaf separated from "hadha," and this is an interrogative accompanied by mockery, meaning: "What is wrong with this one who claims to be a messenger?" They objected to him for what is the custom of messengers, as He said: "And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets" (al-Furqan: 20), i.e., his condition is like our condition, meaning he ought to be independent of eating and of seeking a living. Then they said: "Suppose he is a human; why is he not supported with an angel to warn with him, or a treasure cast down to him from heaven, by which he might be strengthened and not need to seek a livelihood?" Then they were content that he should have a garden from which he eats and gains provision, like the wealthy.

It is read "fatakūnu" with the raf', related by Abu Mu'adh, as a coordination with "unzila," because "unzila" is in the place of a nominative and is a past verb standing in the position of the present, i.e., "why is an angel not sent down to him?" Or it is the answer to the exhortation with the omission of "huwa," i.e., "then he [it] will be." The reading of the majority is with the naṣb as an answer to the exhortation. As for His saying "aw yulqā" (or a treasure be cast), the "aw" may be coordinated with "unzila," meaning "why is not...," so the sought object is one of these matters or all of them together according to the difference of the speakers. It is not permissible to read with naṣb "aw yulqā" or "aw takūnu" as coordinated with "fayakūna," because they are in the ruling of what is sought by the exhortation, not in the ruling of the answer, since His saying is "law lā unzila." Qatada and al-A'mash read "aw yakūnu" with yaa from below. And he read "ya'kulu" with the third-person yaa, i.e., the Messenger, and Zayd ibn 'Ali, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit, Talha and al-A'mash read it with the nun of the plural, i.e., they themselves eat from that garden, so they benefit from it in their worldly life and livelihood.

"And the wrongdoers said" (al-Furqan: 8), i.e., to the believers. Al-Zamakhshari said: "By 'the wrongdoers' he meant them themselves, by their very persons; the apparent noun was placed in the place of the pronoun so that they would be recorded as wrongdoers for what they said," end of quotation. His construction "wa-aradā bi-l-zālimīna iyyāhum bi-a'yānihim" is not a sound Arabic construction; rather the Arabic construction would be "wa-aradahum bi-a'yānihim bi-l-zālimīn." "You follow only a man affected by magic" (al-Furqan: 8): "masḥūran" means one whose mind has been overcome by magic, and this is more apparent; or one having a "sihr" (windpipe/lungs); or he is fed with food and drink, i.e., nourished; or his "sahr" (lung) was struck, as you say "ra'istuhu" meaning "I struck his head." It was said: "masḥūran" means a magician, by which they meant he is a human like them, not an angel. Its interpretation has been mentioned in al-Isra'. According to these two views it is said that those who said this were al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid and those who followed them.

"See how they struck for you examples" (al-Furqan: 9): i.e., they said those sayings about you and invented for you those attributes and conditions, rare ones, such as prophethood shared between a human and an angel, the casting of a treasure upon you, and other things. So they remained bewildered, astray, not finding a saying to settle upon; i.e., they strayed from the truth, so they find no path to it. It was said: "They struck for you examples" of the bewitched, the soothsayer, the poet and others, "so they went astray": they missed the way, so they find no path of guidance and cannot attain it, because they are entangled in its opposite, error. It was said: "So they are not able to find a way" (al-Furqan: 9) to a proof or evidence for what they say. Thus at one time they say: he is eloquent and fluent, fabricating the Qur'an from himself; at another: he is a madman; at another: he is a magician; at another: he is bewitched. Ibn 'Abbas said: these polytheists made likenesses for you by saying "he is bewitched," so by that they strayed from the right course, and so they find no path to the truth with which He sent you. Mujahid said: they do not find an exit that would take them out of the examples which they struck for you. Its meaning is that they struck these examples for you in order to reach your denial by them, but they went astray from the path of truth and from attaining what they wanted.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "See how" (p-484) the people occupied themselves with striking these examples which have no benefit, because when they went astray and wanted to disparage your prophethood, they found no way to disparage it, since criticism of it can only concern what undermines the miracles he claimed, not this kind of speech. Al-Farra' said: "They are not able to find a stratagem regarding your matter." Al-Suddi said: "a way" to criticism.

When the polytheists said what they said, it was narrated that it was said to him: If you wish, we will give you the treasures of the world and its keys, which no one has been given before you nor will anyone be given after you, and that will not diminish anything of yours in the Hereafter; or if you wish, we will gather it for you in the Hereafter. He said: "Let that be gathered for me in the Hereafter." Then "Blessed is He who..." was revealed. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, from him, peace be upon him, that he said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, presented to me the plain of Makkah as gold, and I said: "No, rather one day of satiety and three days of hunger," for that is more for my remembrance and my supplication.

Al-Zamakhshari said regarding "tabāraka": meaning it increased in good, "the One who, if He wills" (al-Furqan: 10), would grant you in this world "good" better than what they said, namely that He would make for you the like of what He promised you in the Hereafter of gardens and palaces, end of quotation.

The indication of "dhālika" (that) apparently refers to what the disbelievers mentioned of the garden and the treasure in this world; Mujahid said so. Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation that it refers to his eating food and walking in the markets is far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that this "making" would be in this world if Allah willed it. It was said: in the Hereafter. "In" was placed before the will to alert that this is not attained except by His mercy, and that it is contingent upon the pure exercise of His will; no servant has a right over Allah, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. The first is more eloquent in rebuking the disbelievers and refuting them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is refuted by His saying after that: 'Nay, they denied the Hour'" (al-Furqan: 11). Not so; for the meaning with it is firmly established, and it is a coordination upon what was related from them: he says, "Nay, He brought something more marvelous than all that," which is their denial of the Hour.

The majority read "wa-yajʿal" with the jazm, considered coordinated upon the place of "jaʿala," because the estimate is "in yashaʾ yajʿal." It is also permissible that it be marfu', its lam assimilated into the lam of "laka," but that is known only from the school of Abu 'Amr. Among the Seven, Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read with the jazm. The school of the three does not include assimilation of identical letters when the first is vowelled; it is from the school of Abu 'Amr as we mentioned. Mujahid, Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Humayd, Abu Bakr and Mahbub, from Abu 'Amr, read with the raf'. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The resumption, and its basis is coordination upon the meaning in His saying 'jaʿala,' because the answer to the condition is the place of resumption. Do you not see that sentences of beginning and predicate may stand in the place of the answer to the condition?" Al-Hawfi said: "Whoever reads with raf' makes it a resumed sentence, cut off from what precedes it," end of quotation. Abu al-Baqa' said: "And with raf' by way of resumption." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is read 'wa-yajʿalu' with raf' as coordination upon 'jaʿala,' because when the condition is in the past form it is permissible for its answer to be jazm or raf', like his saying:

"And if a friend comes to him on a day of asking, he says: 'Neither is my property absent nor is my sanctuary,'" end of quotation.

What Al-Zamakhshari held, that when the verb of the condition is past the answer may be raf', is not the school of Sibawayh, for Sibawayh's school is that the answer is omitted, and that this present verb in the raf' is intended to be preposed; and because the answer is omitted, the verb of the condition can only be in the past form.

The Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that it is the apodosis (jawab) itself, and that it is elided with the fa' (the particle "fa'") omitted. Others held that it is the apodosis without any elision of the fa' and without any inversion (taqdim). Since the particle of condition (adat al-shart) has no visible effect on the protasis (fi'l al-shart) because the latter is in the past form (madi al-lafz), it is too weak to govern the apodosis verb, so the apodosis verb is not governed by it and remains in the nominative (marfu'an). The majority (al-Jumhur) held that this construction is eloquent (fasih) and permissible in speech. Some of our companions said: it is a poetic necessity (darura), since it occurs only in poetry, and it is with the fa' understood. The discussion of these positions is mentioned in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw).

ʿUbayd Allah ibn Musa and Talha ibn Sulayman read (wa-yajʿala) with the accusative (bil-nasb), on the basis of the implied "an" (idmar an). Abu al-Fath said: it is in the apodosis with the waw, and this is a weak reading, end of quote. The parallel to these three readings is the verse of al-Nabigha:

*"If Abu Qabus dies, the spring of the people will die, and the sacred month,*
*and we will take after him the tail-ends of a life, a humped back that has no hump."*

It is narrated with the jussive (jazm) of "na'khudh," with its nominative (raf'), and with its accusative (nasb).

﴿Rather, they denied the Hour﴾. Al-Karmani said: the meaning is that what prevented them from belief was not your eating food or your walking in the marketplace, but rather their denial of the Hour prevented them. It was also said: what they clung to is not a doubt, but rather the driving force behind their denial of you is their denial of the Hour, finding it burdensome to prepare for it. It was also said: it is possible that it is connected to what follows it, as if he said: "Rather, they denied the Hour," so how would they turn to this answer, and how would they believe in the hastening of the like of what He promised you in the Hereafter, when they do not believe in the Hereafter? End of quote. "Bal" (rather) is used to leave aside the preceding expression without negating its meaning and to take up another expression.

(Wa-aʿtadna) means: we made it prepared. (Saʿiran) means: a fire of great kindling. From al-Hasan: it is a name of Jahannam.

(Idha ra'athum): it was said: this is literal, and that Jahannam has two eyes; a report has been transmitted on this. If it is authentic, it is the correct view; otherwise it is a metaphor (majaz), meaning that it became from them at the distance a viewer sees from afar, like their saying: "their houses see each other (tatarra'a)," meaning they face and oppose one another, and from this: "their two fires do not see each other (la tatarra'a naraha)."

Some people said: "fire" is the name of a fiery animal that speaks, sees, hears, changes, and exhales; this was related by al-Karmani. It was also said: it is by elision of a noun (hadhf mudaf), meaning: its guardians saw them from a far place. It was said: a distance of five hundred years. It was said: a hundred years. It was said: one year.

(Sami'u laha): a sound of rage, because rage is not heard. When it is by elision of the noun, the meaning is: they became enraged and exhaled in anger at the disbelievers and with a desire for vengeance upon them. It was also said: (sami'u) means the sound of its blazing and its flaring. It was also said: it is like the verse of the poet:

*"So would that your husband had become one who girds on a sword and a spear."*

This is explained in two ways: the first is elision, meaning: "and one who holds a spear." The second is ta'min (implicit meaning): the verb "mutaqallidan" (girding on) is made to carry the meaning of "mutasallihan" (armed), and so it is with the verse, meaning: (they heard it) and they saw ﴿a raging and a roaring﴾, and each one returns to what suits it. Or (sami'u) is made to carry the meaning of "adraku" (perceived), so that it includes the raging and the roaring.

(Makanan) is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning: in a narrow place. From Ibn Abbas: it narrows upon them like the narrowing of the spear's butt into the shaft, while they are bound together (muqarranin): their hands are tied to their necks with chains. It was said: with each disbeliever is bound his devil in one chain, and upon their feet are shackles.

Ibn Kathir and Ubayd, from Abu Amr, read (dayyiqan). Ibn Atiyya said: Abu Shayba, the companion of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, read (muqarranun) with a waw, and it is an anomalous reading (shadha). The correct reading is the reading of the people. Ibn Khalawayh attributed it to Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Its grammatical point is that it is raised (yartafi'a) as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (ulqu), a substitution of an indefinite for a definite, and it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

The apparent meaning is the call for destruction (du'a' al-thubur), which is ruin, so they say: "Woe, our destruction!" meaning, it is said: "O destruction! This is your time." It was also said: the one called upon is omitted; its estimation is: they called upon one who would not answer them, saying: "Let us be destroyed, a destruction." Thubur, Ibn Abbas said, is woe (wayl); al-Dahhak said it is ruin (halak). From it is the verse of Ibn al-Zibaʿra:

*"When he runs alongside the devil in the paths of error, and whoever inclines to its inclination is destroyed (mathbur)."*

(La tad'u al-yawm) it is said to them: "Do not call (la tad'u)," or they are more entitled to be told this even if there is no speech there, meaning: do not restrict yourselves to one sorrow, but rather grieve a great deal of grief. Its abundance is either because the torment is perpetual, so it is constantly renewed, or because it consists of kinds, and each kind is a cause of ruin (thubur) due to its severity and horror.

ʿAmr ibn Muhammad read (thabura) with a fatha on the tha' in all three instances. The form fa'ul with a fatha on the fa' among verbal nouns is rare, like "batul." Ali ibn Isa related: "ma thabaraka 'an hadha al-amr," meaning: what turned you away from this matter. It is as if they called out for what they had done and said: "Woe, what turned us from obedience to God!" as you say: "Woe, our regret!" It is narrated that the first to cry out with that is Iblis, who says: "Woe, my destruction!" until he is clothed in a garment of Jahannam, which he places on his forehead and drags from behind him; then his followers follow him in speech, and the guardians of Jahannam say to them: ﴿Do not call out today...﴾ the verse.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Khatal and his companions.

The apparent meaning is that the demonstrative (al-ishara) (p-486) with "dhalika" refers to the Fire and the states of its people. It was said: it refers to the Garden and the treasure in their statement. It was said: it refers to the Garden and the palaces made in this world on condition of God's will. "Khayr" here does not indicate superiority; rather, it follows the usage of the Arabs in explaining the excellence of a thing and its specificity in excellence to the exclusion of its opposite, as in His saying:

*"So your evil is for your good, the ransom."*

And as in the saying of the Arabs: "Is misery more beloved to you or happiness?" And as in His saying: ﴿The prison is more beloved to me than what they call me to﴾ (Yusuf 33). This interrogation is by way of reproach and rebuke.

Ibn Atiyya said: Since the speech is an interrogation, it is permissible for its wording to come in the comparative form between the Garden and the Fire in goodness, because the one who addresses may test his interlocutor with whatever he wishes, to see whether he answers correctly or incorrectly. Sibawayh and others prohibited the comparative when the speech is a declarative statement, because there is in it a contradiction; but when it is an interrogation, that is permissible, end of quote.

What he mentioned is contradicted by his saying: "So your evil is for your good," and his saying: ﴿The prison is more beloved to me﴾, since this is a declarative statement. Likewise the saying: "Honey is sweeter than vinegar," unless the declarative is restricted by the condition that the judgment is clear to the hearer, such that nothing stirs in his mind and he does not hesitate as to which of the two is better, in which case it is permissible.

The pronoun in (allati) is elided, meaning: "which He promised," and the pronoun in (ma yashaʾun) is likewise, meaning: "what they wish for." In His saying "what they wish for" there is evidence that the attainment of all desires does not occur except in the Garden. His saying (jaza'an wa-masiran) encompasses the reward and its abode, as He said: ﴿How excellent is the reward and how good a resting place﴾ (al-Kahf 31), and in its opposite: ﴿How evil is the drink and how bad a resting place﴾ (al-Kahf 29), because by the goodness of the place the bliss is multiplied, just as by its badness the torment is multiplied.

(Wa'dan), meaning: promised. (Mas'ula), meaning: asked for. The angels asked for it in their saying: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the gardens of Eden which You promised them﴾ (Ghafir 8). This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. And the people in their saying: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ (Al 'Imran 194), ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾ (al-Baqara 201). Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd said its meaning is the same.

Al-Farra' said: ﴿a promise to be asked﴾ means: obligatory, as one says: "I will certainly give you a thousand, a promise to be asked," meaning: obligatory, even if it is not asked. It was said: what al-Farra' said is absurd, end of quote. It is not absurd; the meaning is that it ought to be asked, this promise which You made, or it is about to be asked, meaning: it is its right to be something asked for. And (upon your Lord), meaning: by reason of the promise it has become something that must be. Al-Zamakhshari said: that was a promised thing, obligatory upon your Lord to fulfil, genuinely deserving to be asked and sought, because it is a recompense and a due that is merited; and this is according to the doctrine of the al-Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds God is bound by justice and reward).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verses 1–16 (part 1 of 3)**

Surat al-Furqan

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful

[p. 479] ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He has not taken a son, and He has no partner in the dominion. He created everything and determined it with precise measure.﴾ ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, gods that create nothing, and they are themselves created. They control not harm nor benefit for themselves, and they control neither death nor life nor resurrection.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say: "This is nothing but a fabrication which he has invented, and other people have helped him with it." Indeed they have committed injustice and falsehood.﴾ ﴿And they say: "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ ﴿Say: "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed He is ever Forgiving, Merciful."﴾ ﴿And they say: "What is this Messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets? Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner with him?"﴾ ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden from which he eats?" And the wrongdoers say: "You follow only a man under enchantment."﴾ ﴿Look how they strike similitudes for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ ﴿Blessed is He who, if He willed, would give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He would give you palaces.﴾ ﴿Rather, they deny the Hour, and We have prepared a blazing fire for whoever denies the Hour.﴾ ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they will hear its raging and its roaring.﴾ ﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place of it, bound together, they will call out there for destruction.﴾ ﴿Do not call out today for one destruction, but call out for many destructions.﴾ ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which has been promised to the righteous? It is their reward and final destination."﴾ ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever. It is a promise incumbent upon your Lord, to be asked of Him.﴾

[p. 480] This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars. Ibn ‘Abbas and Qatadah said: except for three verses, which were revealed in Medina, namely ﴿And those who do not call upon another god with Allah﴾ (Al-Furqan: 68) up to His saying ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (Al-Furqan: 70). Al-Dahhak said it is Medinan, except from its beginning up to His saying "and resurrection," so that part is Meccan.

The connection (munasabah) between the beginning of this surah and the end of what precedes it is that when Allah mentioned the obligation of the believers’ pledge of allegiance to the Messenger, and that when they were with him in an important matter, none of them could depart without his permission, and He warned against whoever opposes his command, and mentioned that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that He, exalted is He, knows what they are upon and will recompense them for it, this constituted the utmost in warning and admonition. It was therefore appropriate to open this surah by stating that He, exalted is He, is far removed in His attributes from deficiencies, abundant in good, and that among His goodness is that He ﴿sent down the Criterion﴾ upon His Messenger as a warner to them. Thus there is in this both encouragement to seek His goodness and a warning against His punishment.

(Tabaraka) is a form of (tafa‘ala), the intransitive reflexive (mutawi‘) of (barraka). It is a verb that is not conjugated in the usual way and is not used for anyone other than Allah, so no present tense, active participle, or verbal noun is derived from it. Al-Tirimmah said:

*You are Blessed; none gives what You have withheld, and none withholds what You have given, O Lord.*

Ibn ‘Abbas said: He has always been and will never cease. Al-Khalil said: He is glorified (tamajjada). Al-Dahhak said: He is magnified (ta‘azzama). Al-Asma‘i related "tabarakta ‘alaykum" from an Arab who climbed a hill and said this to his companions, meaning: I have exalted myself and risen high. According to these interpretations, the word is an attribute of essence (sifat dhat). Ibn ‘Abbas also said, as did al-Hasan and al-Nakha‘i: it derives from blessing (barakah), which is the increase of good from Him. The meaning is that His goodness and His giving have increased and become abundant. According to this, it is an attribute of action (sifat fi‘l), and the verb is attributed to (alladhi, "He who"). Although they do not acknowledge that He is the One who sent down the Criterion, the proof of its miraculous nature is established, so the relative clause becomes known through the evidence, even though they deny it. It has already been explained in Al ‘Imran why the Qur'an was called al-Furqan.

The majority read (upon His servant), meaning the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn al-Zubayr read (upon His servants), meaning the Messenger and his community, as in His saying ﴿We have sent down to you﴾ and ﴿what was sent down to us﴾. It is unlikely that "the Criterion" refers to the previous scriptures, and that "His servant" refers to those to whom they were sent, making it a collective noun, like His saying ﴿And if you count the favor of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ (Ibrahim: 34). The pronoun in (liyakuna, "that he may be") — Ibn Zayd said it refers back to (His servant). This is preferred because it is the principal subject to which the verb is attributed, and it is from the description of Him, exalted is He, as in His saying ﴿Indeed We were warners﴾ (Al-Dukhan: 3). Apparently (nadhiran, "warner") means (mundhir, one who warns). It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun meaning warning (inadh), like (nakir) meaning denial (inkar). Among this usage is ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ (Al-Qamar: 16). (Lil-‘alamin, "to the worlds") is general, encompassing humans and jinn, whether contemporaries of his or those who came after him. This is known from the mass-transmitted hadith and the apparent meaning of the verses. Ibn al-Zubayr read (lil-‘alamin) as "to the jinn and humans," which is an explanation of (lil-‘alamin).

Since at the end of the surah (Al-Nur: 64) there was ﴿Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, which was a statement that what is in them is His possession, He here states that the dominion over them belongs to Him, that is, His subjugation of them and of what is in them. Thus possession and dominion over them and what is in them are combined for Him. The relative pronoun (alladhi) here is either a cut-off apposition (maqtu‘) for praise, in the nominative or accusative, or an adjective, or a substitute (badal) for (alladhi nazzala). What follows (nazzala) is part of the relative clause (silah) and is connected to it, so it is not considered a separation between the adjective or substitute and its head.

(He has not taken a son): the apparent meaning is the negation of taking, that is, He has not made anyone into the position of a son. It was said the meaning is: He has not had a son, in the sense of His saying "He has not begotten," because procreation is impossible for Him. This is a refutation of the polytheists of Quraysh and of the Christians and Jews who attribute a son to Allah.

﴿And He has no partner in the dominion﴾ is an emphasis on His saying ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and a refutation of whoever makes a partner for Allah.

﴿And He created everything﴾ is general, encompassing the creation of essences and their actions. It was said that there is an ellipsis in the statement, its implied meaning being "and He created everything [that may be created]," so that His essence and His eternal attributes are excluded. This ellipsis is not needed, because one who says "I honored every man" does not include himself in the generality. Likewise, His essence and His eternal attributes are not included in the generality of ﴿and He created everything﴾.

(So He determined it with precise determination): if creation means determination, how then does (fa-qaddarahu, "so He determined it") come in? The meaning would become "and He determined everything, determining it with determination." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that He brought every thing into being in a way that takes proportion and balance into account, so He determined it and prepared it for what suits it. Or the bringing into being by Allah is called creation, because He does not bring anything into being for His wisdom except in a manner of proportion without disparity. So when it is said "Allah created such-and-such," it is like Allah bringing it into existence and originating it, without regard to the derivational sense, as if it were said: "He originated everything, and determined it in its origination to be varied."
