Whoever interprets *lam yarju lasʿaha* (he does not hope for its sting) as meaning he does not hope to repel it or to be freed from it, this interpretation is possible, and he is thereby prepared for patience and works hard at his affairs. But al-Farra' and others transmitted this as the Hudhayl usage in negation, and the poet is a Hudhali. So one should not strain for interpretation, and it should be understood according to his dialect.

﴿Why have not the angels been sent down to us﴾ so that You tell us that you are truly a messenger? (*aw naraa rabbana*) or we see our Lord, so that He informs us of that. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and others. This is like what the Jews said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God plainly﴾ [al-Baqara: 55], and like their saying, meaning the polytheists: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels before us as a group﴾ [al-Isra: 92]. All of this is for the sake of obstinacy. Otherwise, the miracles he brought them would suffice if they had been granted success. (*laqadi istakbaru*) meaning they became proud, (*fi anfusihim*) meaning they magnified themselves by asking to see God, though they were not worthy of it. The meaning is that asking for this is only because of what they concealed in their souls of arrogance toward the truth, which is disbelief and stubbornness hidden in their hearts, the outward appearance of which does not show what they have, as He said: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but greatness, which they will never attain﴾ [Ghafir: 56]. The *lam* in *laqad* is the answer to an omitted oath. *ʿAtaw* means they went beyond the limit in wrongdoing, and He described it as *kabir* (great), emphasizing its extremity, meaning they dared to say this great statement only because they had reached the utmost of arrogance and the highest point of insolence. Here (ʿutuwwan) occurs in its original form, while in Maryam (ʿitiyyan) occurs because the joining of two *waws* is disliked, and there is a change for the sake of matching the endings. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *ʿataw* means they disbelieved with the utmost disbelief and were gravely indecent. ʿIkrima said: they tyrannized. Ibn Salam said: they disobeyed. Ibn ʿIsa said: they transgressed. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This sentence, in its excellence of completion, is extreme in its style. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*And the neighbor of Jassas, we consented with her fang to Kulayb, ... the fang of Kulayb is high, its gift.*

In this kind of verb there is a sign of wonder without a word of wonder. Do you not see that the meaning is: how great their arrogance is, how much their insolence is, and how high-priced is the fang whose price is Kulayb?"

(*yawma yarawna al-malaʾika*) (*yawma*) is in the accusative governed by (*udhkur*, remember), which is the closer option, or by a verb indicated by (*la bushra*, there is no good news), meaning they are denied good news. *La bushra* does not govern it, because it is a verbal noun, and because it is negated by *la* of generic negation, since what follows that *la* does not work on what precedes it. Likewise the particle that enters on nouns works like *laysa* (is not). The entry of *la* on *bushra* is for negating all kinds of good news. The apparent meaning of this day is the Day of Resurrection, due to His later words: (*wa-qadimna ila ma ʿamilu*, and We will turn to what they did). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is at death. The meaning is that those who demanded the descent of the angels do not know what evil will be theirs when they see them, and the absence of good news, and the occurrence of loss and the disliked.

(*bushra*) may be built with *la*, or it may be in the accusative with the intention of tanwin (nunation), prevented from taking tanwin because of its necessary feminine form. If it is built with *la*, the predicate may be (*yawma'idhin*), and (*lil-mujrimin*) is a predicate after a predicate, or a qualifier of *bushra*, or a complement connected to what the predicate is connected to. (*yawma'idhin*) may be a qualifier of *bushra* and the predicate (*lil-mujrimin*). There is a dispute between Sibawayh and al-Akhfash over whether the predicate belongs to *la* itself or to the subject that is the whole of *la* and what is built with it. If it has the intention of nunation and is declinable, (*yawma'idhin*) may be governed by *bushra*, and it may be a qualifier, and the predicate is from the predicate. He allowed that (*yawma'idhin*) and (*lil-mujrimin*) be the predicate, and he allowed that (*yawma'idhin*) be the predicate and (*lil-mujrimin*) a qualifier. A predicate, when the subject is not built for *la* itself, is by consensus.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (*yawma'idhin*) is for repetition, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him. It cannot be a repetition, whether it is meant as verbal emphasis or as apposition, because (*yawm*) is in the accusative governed by what was previously mentioned, namely *udhkur* or "they are denied good news." What follows *la* that governs a noun does not get governed by what precedes it. On his estimate, the governing element would be what precedes *illa*. The apparent meaning is the generality of *al-mujrimin* (the guilty), so these speakers are included among them. It was said that it may be placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (*wa-yaqulun*, and they say) refers back to those who spoke, because those spoken of were asking for the descent of the angels, and then when they saw them they disliked meeting them and were frightened of them, because they meet them only with what they hate. So when they saw them they said what they used to say at the meeting of the enemy and the onset of hardship. Mujahid said the same, saying: (*hijran*) is a protection they seek from the angels. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: when the Arabs disliked something they said *hijran*. Abu ʿUbayda said: these two words are a protective formula for the Arabs, which someone says when he fears another in the sacred precinct or in a sacred month, when he meets him and there is a blood-feud between them. End of quotation. From this is the saying of al-Mutallamis:

*She yearned for the far palm, so I said to her: forbidden barrier, is it not the date-palm groves?*

meaning: what you yearn for is forbidden. Sibawayh mentioned (*hijran*) among the accusative verbal nouns that are not inflected. Some of the rajaz poets said:

*She said, and in it there is bewilderment and terror: a protection, which is seen from you, and a barrier.*

Moreover, it is obligatory to supply its governing verb. Sibawayh said: a man says to another, "Will you do such-and-such?" and he replies, "Ḥijran" (a prohibition, a barrier). It derives from "ḥajara-hu," meaning he prevented him, because the one who seeks refuge is asking Allah to prevent the disliked thing from reaching him. Abu Raja', al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "ḥujran" with a damma on the ḥa'.

It was said: the pronoun in "wa-yaqūlūna" (they say) refers to the angels, meaning the angels say to the criminals, "Ḥijran maḥjūran" (a barrier, a forbidden barrier), "upon you is good news." "Maḥjūran" is an adjective that emphasizes the meaning of "ḥijran," as they said: "mawt māʾit" (a dying death) and "dhayl dhāʾil" (a trailing train). The literal "arrival" (qudūm ḥaqīqī) is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted, so it is a metaphor for His judgment and its execution. It was also said: or it is by omitting a modifier, meaning "our angels arrived," and this was attributed to Him because it is by His command. The expression "we arrived" (qadimnā) is apt, because one who arrives at a disliked matter, which he neither approves nor commanded, is one who changes and removes it. So He likened the condition of these people and their deeds that they performed in their disbelief, such as maintaining ties of kinship, relieving the distressed, hospitality to guests, bestowing favour upon a captive, and other noble deeds, to the condition of a people who opposed their ruler, so he went to what was under their authority and tore it apart such that no trace of it remained. Among their proverbs: "Less than dust." And "havaan manthūran" (scattered dust) is an adjective of "al-habāʾ" (dust). He likened them to dust for its insignificance and because it is not benefited from; then He described it as "manthūran," because one sees dust arranged along with the light, and when the wind stirs it, you see it scattered and gone.

Al-Zamakhshari said: or He made it, meaning "manthūran," a third object of "jaʿalnāhu" (We made it), that is, "fa-jaʿalnāhu" (so We made it) combining the worthlessness of dust and its scattering, like His saying: "Be apes, despised" (al-Baqara 65), meaning combining transformation and abasement. End of quote.

Ibn Durustawayh dissented, opposing the grammarians in forbidding that kāna have two predicates and more. The analogy of his view on jaʿala would be to forbid it from having a third predicate.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-habāʾ al-manthūr" is what the winds blow away and scatter. Also from him: "al-habāʾ" is poured-out water. "Al-mustaqarr" is the place of settling, in most times. "Al-maqīl" is the place to which they retreat for rest with the spouses and enjoyment; there is no sleep in Paradise, so the place of their resting with the houris is called "maqīl" by way of comparison, since the place chosen for a midday rest is the most pleasant of places. In the word "aḥsan" there is an allusion to what their resting place is adorned with: the beauty of faces, the comeliness of forms, and other embellishments.

As for "khayr" (better): it was said that it is not used in its basic sense of indicating superiority, otherwise it would imply good in the resting place of the people of the Fire. It can be retained in its basic sense, with the comparison made between those who settle and those who rest, in terms of the time in which this occurs. So the meaning is: "better as a place of settling" in the Hereafter than the affluent disbelievers in this world, and "better as a place of rest" in the Hereafter than those in this world. It was also said: "better as a place of settling" than them, if they had a place of settling; the estimate is then that the existence of a settling place for them would be good.

From Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil: the reckoning will be completed in the span of half a day of the days of this world, and the people of Paradise will take their midday rest in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 3):**

(p-487) ﴿On the Day He gathers them and what they worshipped besides Allah, He will say, "Did you lead these, My servants, astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?" They will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for us to take any protectors other than You, but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance, and they were a people doomed to ruin."﴾ ﴿Indeed, they have denied you in what you say, so you cannot avert [the punishment] or find help. And whoever among you does wrong, We will make him taste a great punishment.﴾ ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets. And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾ ﴿Those who do not expect the meeting with Us say, "Why were the angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great insolence.﴾ ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good tidings that Day for the criminals, and they will say, "A forbidding, forbidden [barrier]!"﴾ ﴿And We will turn to the work they did and make it scattered dust.﴾ ﴿The companions of the Garden, that Day, are better in their resting place and finer in their place of repose.﴾

They recited (yahshuruhum) and (fayaqulu) with the ya' in both places: Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Ibn Kathir and Hafs. Al-Hasan, Talha and Ibn 'Amir recited both with the nun. The rest of the seven recited (nahshuruhum) with the nun, (p-488) and (fayaqulu) with the ya'. Al-A'raj recited (yahshiruhum) with a kasra on the shin. The author of al-Lawami' said: "This is the analogical form throughout the Qur'an for transitive triliteral verbs, since yaf'ulu with a damma on the 'ayn may come from the intransitive fa'ula (with a damma in the past tense)." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is rare in usage but strong in analogy, since yaf'ilu with a kasra on the 'ayn is more analogical than yaf'ulu with a damma on the 'ayn in transitive verbs, end quote." This is not as they both stated. Rather, the transitive verb fa'ula, whose letters are all sound, when it is not for intensification and has no guttural 'ayn or lam, comes in the forms yaf'ulu and yaf'ilu frequently. If one of the two usages is well known, it is followed; otherwise the choice is open. Some of our companions even gave the choice between them, whether they heard the word or not.

(And what they worshipped): al-Dahhak and 'Ikrima said: these are the idols that do not understand, and Allah empowers them to utter this reply. Al-Kalbi said: Allah will bring the idols back to life on that Day to rebuke their worshippers. The majority said: it refers to those among rational beings who were worshipped without commanding worship of themselves, such as the angels, 'Isa and 'Uzayr. This is the most apparent view, as in His saying, (Did you lead these astray?) and what follows of the dialogue, whose apparent sense is that it does not come except from rational beings. Something similar is stated explicitly in His saying, ﴿Then He will say to the angels, "Did these used to worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40] and ﴿"O 'Isa, son of Maryam, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. His questioning, although He knows the one questioned about, is so that they will answer with what they answered, whereupon He rebukes their worshippers by their denial of them. This increases their grief, gladdens the believers at their situation and their salvation from the disgrace of those people, and makes the recounting of that in the Qur'an a kindness to those who are responsible. The interrogative came with the noun preceding the verb, and the construction (a-dalaltum) or (a-dallu) did not come; because both misguiding (al-idlal) and going astray (al-dalal) occur, and the question is only from the one who performs it. A parallel to this was mentioned in ﴿"Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 62]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it is a clear refutation of the view of those who claim that Allah actually misguides His servants, since He says to those worshipped besides Him, (Did you lead them astray?) or did they go astray by themselves, so that they disown their error and seek refuge in Him from being misguiders, and say, 'Rather, You bestowed favor without precedent upon these and their fathers, the favor of a generous and bountiful one.' They made the mercy, whose due is to be the cause of thanks, the cause of disbelief and the forgetting of the remembrance, and that was the cause of their ruin. When the angels and the messengers themselves disown the attribution of misguidance, which is the work of the devils, to them, and seek refuge from them, they are far more free from it and more exalted above it with respect to their Lord, who is Self-Sufficient and Just. They have indeed exalted Him when they attributed to Him the bestowing of favor by blessing and enjoyment of it. They ascribed the forgetting of the remembrance and the causing of ruin to the disbelievers, thereby explaining the metaphorical misguidance that Allah attributed to His Essence in His saying, ﴿He misguides whom He wills﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27]. Had He been the Misguider in the literal sense, the ready answer would have been, 'Rather, You misguided them,' end quote." This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school).

The meaning: (Did you) cause these people to fall into misguidance and be attributed to them, in their going astray from the truth? Or (did they stray) by themselves from it? (Dalla) originally takes (ʿan) after it, as in His saying, ﴿"Who strays from His way"﴾ [al-An'am: 117]; then it was extended and the preposition was dropped, so one says (adallahu 'an al-sabil). Just as (hada) takes (ila) and then it is dropped, and (yadillu) is the intransitive counterpart of (adalla), as you say, "I made him sit and he sat."

(Subhanaka) is a declaration of Allah's transcendence above having anyone associated with Him in worship or singled out for worship. How could it be that any of them would misguide anyone, when they are the purified and sanctified, that any of them should be a rival, while He is the One exalted above rivals and equals?

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(Subhanaka) is an expression of their amazement at what was said, since they are angels and prophets, infallible, so how far they are from misguiding, which is specific to Iblis and his party," end quote.

'Alqama recited (ma yanbaghi) without (kana). The recitation of the majority with it is more apt in meaning, because they were reporting a state that existed in the world, and the time of reporting is not subject to governing action. Abu 'Isa al-Aswad al-Qari recited (yunbagha lana) in the passive. Ibn Khalawayh said: "Sibawayh claimed that yunbagha is a dialect."

The majority recited (an nattakhidha) in the active voice, and (min awliya') is the object with an added (min). Its addition was made acceptable by the negation extending over (nattakhidha), because it is governed by (yanbaghi). When seeking is negated, its object is necessarily negated, which is taking a protector besides Allah. A parallel is ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not wish that any good be sent down upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], (p-489) meaning: any good. The meaning is: it would not be correct or proper for us, and we being infallible, to take anyone as a protector besides You. So how could it be correct for us to make others take us as protectors besides You?! Abu Muslim said: "(It was not for us) to become like the devils, desiring disbelief and so taking the disbelievers as protectors." He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257].

Abu al-Darda', Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Raja', Nasr ibn 'Alqama, Zayd ibn 'Ali and his brother al-Baqir, Makhul, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Hafs ibn 'Ubayd, al-Nakha'i, al-Sulami, Shayba, Abu Bishr and al-Za'farani recited (an yuttakhadha) in the passive. (Ittakhadha) is used sometimes with one object, as in ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 21], and the majority's recitation is upon this; and sometimes with two objects, as in ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23]. It was said that this recitation is from the second usage: the first object is the pronoun in (nattakhidha), and the second is (min awliya'), with (min) being partitive, meaning: none of the protectors is taken. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This recitation is weakened by the entry of (min) in (min awliya')." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others objected with this. Abu al-Fath said: "(min awliya') is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and (min) entered as an addition because of the preceding negation, as you say, 'I did not take Zayd as any agent (min wakil).'" It was also said: (min awliya') is the second object with an added (min). This is not permitted according to most grammarians, for it is only permitted that (min) enters as an addition upon the first object, under its condition.

al-Hajjaj recited (an nattakhidha min dunika awliya'), and it reached 'Asim, who said: "The one born prematurely is hated! Does he not know that it contains (min)?"

Since their statement, (It was not for us to take any protectors other than You), implied that we did not misguide them and did not compel them to refrain from belief, it was apt to be followed by the adversative (bal-kin), and the meaning: "But You bestowed abundance of blessings upon them and their fathers, and prolonged their lives, and it was obligatory upon them to thank You for them and to believe in what the messengers brought. So that became a cause of turning away from the remembrance of Allah." It was said: (But You gave them enjoyment) is like an allusion to what Musa stated explicitly in His saying, ﴿It is none but Your trial﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. That is: You are the one who gave them their desires of the world until they became drowned in the sea of appetites, so this diverted them from turning to Your obedience and occupying themselves with serving You. (The remembrance) is what people are reminded of through the tongues of the prophets, or the revealed books, or the Qur'an.

(Bur): it was said to be a verbal noun used as a description of the singular and the plural. It was also said to be the plural of (ba'ir), like (a'idh) and ('uudh). It was said to mean "ruined." It was said to mean "corrupt," and this is the dialect of the Azd, who say, "amrun ba'ir," meaning corrupt; and "bara al-bida'a," meaning it became corrupt. al-Hasan said: "There is no good in them," from their saying, "ardun bur," meaning a land left uncultivated with no vegetation. It was said: (bura) means "blind to the truth."

(They have denied you): this is from the speech of Allah without any disagreement, and it is a sudden turn. The argument and the binding are a fourth fine feature, especially when the turn of address (iltifat) is combined with it. It is by implying a saying, like His saying, (O People of the Book) to His saying (there has come to you), meaning: We said, "There has come to you." And like the poet's words:

They said: "The farthest we are asked to reach is Khurasan, then the return." So we came to Khurasan.

meaning: we said, "We have come." Similarly here, meaning: We said, "They have denied you." If the one who answers is the idols, then the address is to the disbelievers, meaning: the idols you worship have denied you by their saying, (It was not for us), and if the address is to the rational beings worshipped, such as 'Isa, the angels and 'Uzayr, peace be upon them, which is the apparent view, then it is in harmony with the address in (Did you lead them astray?), meaning: those worshipped denied you (in what you say), that is, in your saying that you misled them and in your claim that you are their protectors besides Allah. Whoever recited (bima taqulun) with the ta' of address, the meaning is "in what you say," that is: (Exalted are You! It was not for us to take any protectors besides You). It was also said: the address is to the disbelieving worshippers, meaning: those worshipped denied you in what you say of the answer.

(Exalted are You! It was not for us), or "in what you say, you yourselves, of slander against them," they were addressed in a manner of rebuke and reproach. It was also said: it is an address to the believers in the world, meaning: the disbelievers have denied you, O believers, in what you say of monotheism and the law. The majority recited (bima taqulun) with the ta' from above. Abu Haywa and Ibn al-Salt, on the authority of Qunbul, recited it with the ya' from below.

Hafs, Abu Haywa, al-A'mash and Talha recited (fa-ma tastaTi'un) with the ta' of address, and this recitation is supported by the fact that the address in (kadhdhabukum) is to the disbelieving worshippers. It is mentioned that Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr recited (bima yaqulun fama yasti'un) with the ya' in both, meaning: they. (Sarfan) means: averting the punishment, or repentance, or a stratagem, from their saying, "innahu la-yatasarraf," meaning: he schemes. If the address in (kadhdhabukum) is to the disbelievers, then the ta' runs in accordance with it, and the ya' is a turn of address. If the address is to the worshipped, then the ta' is a turn of address and the ya' runs in accordance with the pronoun of (kadhdhabukum), which is nominative. If the address is to the believers, the community of the Messenger, peace be upon him, in His saying (They have denied you), then the meaning is that they are severe in their obstinacy in denial. (Fama tastaTi'un) means: you are not able to turn them away from what they are upon of that. With the ya', (fama yasti'un sarfan) means: they cannot avert [the punishment] for themselves from what they are upon, or they cannot avert you from the truth you are upon. (Wa-la nasran): they cannot help themselves against the affliction they incurred by their denial.

(ومَن يَظْلِمْ مِنكم) The apparent meaning is that it is general. It has also been said that it is addressed to the believers, and it has been said that it is addressed to the disbelievers. Here *al-zulm* (wrongdoing) means *al-shirk* (association of partners with God). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jurayj. It is possible that sins other than *shirk* are included in *al-zulm*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The great punishment applies to everyone who does wrong. The disbeliever is a wrongdoer, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13], and the defiant sinner (*fasiq*) is a wrongdoer, as in His words: ﴿And whoever does not repent, then it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]." End of quotation. There is a hidden Mu'tazilite tendency (*dasisat al-i'tizal*; the Mu'tazila being the rationalist school that holds that the grave sinner is in an intermediate position) in this. It was read as *yudhiqhu* with the *ya* of the third person, meaning God, who is the apparent subject. It has also been said that the subject is *huwa*, i.e., *al-zulm*, which is the verbal noun understood from *bi-zulmin* (with wrongdoing), meaning: wrongdoing makes him taste it.

When criticism of the Messenger for eating food and walking in the markets had preceded, God informed that this is a constant practice in every messenger. The object of *arsalna* (We sent) is, according to al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari, and those who followed them, omitted; its estimated form is *aḥadan* (anyone). Ibn ʿAtiyya estimated it as *rijalan aw rusulan* (men or messengers). The pronoun in *innahum* refers to that omitted object, as in His words: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: "there is none of us who is not..." According to these scholars the clause is a qualifier, namely His words *illa innahum* (except that they), as if He had said: "except eating and walking." According to al-Farra' the object is omitted and it is a relative pronoun estimated after *illa*, meaning *illa man* (except whoever), and the pronoun *innahum* refers back to *man* according to its meaning, so it is an exceptive construction with missing complement (*istithna' mufarrigh*). It has also been said that before *innahum* there is an omitted saying, meaning *illa* [qila] *innahum* (except it was said that they...). These two opinions are weak in Arabic. Ibn al-Anbari said: the estimate is *illa wa-innahum* (except and they...), meaning the clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and this is the preferred view. He answered those who said that what follows *illa* may come as a qualifier; as for omitting the relative pronoun, it is weak. Abu al-Baqa' also went to the view that it is a circumstantial clause, saying: "It was said that if the *lam* were not there it would be in the genitive, because the clause is circumstantial, the meaning being *illa wa-hum yaʾkulun* (except while they eat)." It was read *annahum* with a *fatha*, on the basis that the *lam* is an added particle and *anna* is verbal (*masdariyya*), with the estimate *illa annahum yaʾkulun* (except that they eat), meaning: We did not make them messengers to the people except because they are like them.

The majority read *wa-yamshun* (and walk), the present tense of *mashā* in the simple form. ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAbd Allah read *yumashsha'un*, with doubling and in the passive voice, meaning: their needs and people carry them along. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If *yumashsha'un* were read, it would be more appropriate, were it not for the transmission." Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami also read it doubled but in the active voice, and it has the same meaning as the majority reading *yamshun*. A poet said:

*And he walked among the camel-pens of the watering place, seeking from them young she-camels, difficult and rideable.*

(وجَعَلْنا بَعْضَكم) Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is general for the believer and the disbeliever. So the healthy person is a trial for the sick, the rich is a trial for the poor, the grateful poor is a trial for the rich, the messenger specially honored with prophethood is a trial for the noble disbelievers of his time, and likewise the scholars and the just rulers. Ibn al-Qasim recited this verse when he saw Ashhab. End of quotation. Something similar was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the questioning with *ataṣbirun* (will you be patient?) is specific to the sincere believers, so it belongs to the community of Muhammad. It is as if he made the respite given to the disbelievers a trial for the believers, meaning a test, and then questioned them: "Will you be patient or not?" Then he explained His words ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾ as a promise to the patient and a threat to the disobedient.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *fitna* means a trial and affliction. This is a consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning what they said and found strange: his eating food and walking in the markets, after he had argued against them with the example of all the other messengers. He says: "My practice and the requirement of My wisdom is to test some of you, people, with others." The meaning is that He tested the messengers with those they were sent to, with their hostility toward them, their sayings that go beyond fairness, and various kinds of harm, and He asked them for good patience. A similar verse is ﴿You will certainly hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with God much harm﴾ [Al ʿImran: 186], and so on. The position of *ataṣbirun* after mention of the trial is like the position of *ayyukum* (which of you) after the test in His words: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

(بَصِيرًا) knowing what is right in what He tests with and in other matters. So let your chest not tighten, and do not let their sayings move you, for in your patience toward them is happiness and your success in both abodes. It has been said that it is a consolation for what they reproached him for, namely poverty, when they said: ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden﴾ [al-Furqan: 8]. It is also said that He made the rich a trial for the poor so that He may see whether you will be patient, and that this is His wisdom and His will: He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills. It has also been said: We made you a trial for them, because if you had been rich, possessor of treasures and gardens, their inclination toward you and their obedience to you would have been for the world or mixed with the world. We sent you poor so that the obedience of whoever obeys you among them would be purely for God's sake, without worldly greed. It has been said: Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, and those of their rank used to say: "If we accept Islam after ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Bilal, so-and-so, and so-and-so have accepted it before us, they will be raised above us," relying on their precedence. So it is the temptation of some of them by others. End of quotation. In this there is some exaggeration. This last view is the view of al-Kalbi, al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj. The better view is that His words *wa-jaʿalna baʿḍakum li-baʿḍin fitna* (We made some of you a trial for others) include all the meanings of these expressions, because there is a shared common element among all of them.

It has been said that in His words *ataṣbirun* the question has the meaning of a command, meaning: "be patient." The apparent meaning is to take *al-rajaʾ* (hope) in its well-known usage, and the meaning is: they do not hope to meet Us with good, nor to receive Our reward for obedience, because they deny the resurrection in their disbelief in what I brought. Abu ʿUbayda and a group said: its meaning is "they do not fear." al-Farra' said: "(they do not hope for resurrection) means they do not fear." This word is Tihami (a dialect of Hijaz), and it is also from the dialect of Hudhayl. When negation is combined with *rajaʾ* they take it to mean fear. So you say: "So-and-so does not hope for his Lord," meaning he does not fear his Lord. From this is His words: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾ [Nuh: 13], meaning you do not fear the greatness of God. When they say: "So-and-so hopes for his Lord," this is the meaning of hope, not of fear. A poet said:

*When the bees sting him, he does not hope for their sting, and he swears alliance with them in a house of woven, ... wall.*

Another said:

*Do not expect when you meet the defender, whether they have met seven or one.*

End of quotation. Hope for reward necessarily involves fear of punishment. Whoever denies the resurrection hopes for no reward and fears no punishment. Whoever interprets *lam yarju lasʿaha* (he does not hope for its sting) as meaning he does not hope to repel it or to be freed from it, this interpretation is possible, and he is thereby prepared for patience and works hard at his affairs. But al-Farra' and others transmitted this as the Hudhayl usage in negation, and the poet is a Hudhali. So one should not strain for interpretation, and it should be understood according to his dialect.

﴿Why have not the angels been sent down to us﴾ so that You tell us that you are truly a messenger? (*aw naraa rabbana*) or we see our Lord, so that He informs us of that. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and others. This is like what the Jews said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God plainly﴾ [al-Baqara: 55], and like their saying, meaning the polytheists: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels before us as a group﴾ [al-Isra: 92]. All of this is for the sake of obstinacy. Otherwise, the miracles he brought them would suffice if they had been granted success. (*laqadi istakbaru*) meaning they became proud, (*fi anfusihim*) meaning they magnified themselves by asking to see God, though they were not worthy of it. The meaning is that asking for this is only because of what they concealed in their souls of arrogance toward the truth, which is disbelief and stubbornness hidden in their hearts, the outward appearance of which does not show what they have, as He said: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but greatness, which they will never attain﴾ [Ghafir: 56]. The *lam* in *laqad* is the answer to an omitted oath. *ʿAtaw* means they went beyond the limit in wrongdoing, and He described it as *kabir* (great), emphasizing its extremity, meaning they dared to say this great statement only because they had reached the utmost of arrogance and the highest point of insolence. Here (ʿutuwwan) occurs in its original form, while in Maryam (ʿitiyyan) occurs because the joining of two *waws* is disliked, and there is a change for the sake of matching the endings. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *ʿataw* means they disbelieved with the utmost disbelief and were gravely indecent. ʿIkrima said: they tyrannized. Ibn Salam said: they disobeyed. Ibn ʿIsa said: they transgressed. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This sentence, in its excellence of completion, is extreme in its style. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*And the neighbor of Jassas, we consented with her fang to Kulayb, ... the fang of Kulayb is high, its gift.*

In this kind of verb there is a sign of wonder without a word of wonder. Do you not see that the meaning is: how great their arrogance is, how much their insolence is, and how high-priced is the fang whose price is Kulayb?"

(*yawma yarawna al-malaʾika*) (*yawma*) is in the accusative governed by (*udhkur*, remember), which is the closer option, or by a verb indicated by (*la bushra*, there is no good news), meaning they are denied good news. *La bushra* does not govern it, because it is a verbal noun, and because it is negated by *la* of generic negation, since what follows that *la* does not work on what precedes it. Likewise the particle that enters on nouns works like *laysa* (is not). The entry of *la* on *bushra* is for negating all kinds of good news. The apparent meaning of this day is the Day of Resurrection, due to His later words: (*wa-qadimna ila ma ʿamilu*, and We will turn to what they did). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is at death. The meaning is that those who demanded the descent of the angels do not know what evil will be theirs when they see them, and the absence of good news, and the occurrence of loss and the disliked.

(*bushra*) may be built with *la*, or it may be in the accusative with the intention of tanwin (nunation), prevented from taking tanwin because of its necessary feminine form. If it is built with *la*, the predicate may be (*yawma'idhin*), and (*lil-mujrimin*) is a predicate after a predicate, or a qualifier of *bushra*, or a complement connected to what the predicate is connected to. (*yawma'idhin*) may be a qualifier of *bushra* and the predicate (*lil-mujrimin*). There is a dispute between Sibawayh and al-Akhfash over whether the predicate belongs to *la* itself or to the subject that is the whole of *la* and what is built with it. If it has the intention of nunation and is declinable, (*yawma'idhin*) may be governed by *bushra*, and it may be a qualifier, and the predicate is from the predicate. He allowed that (*yawma'idhin*) and (*lil-mujrimin*) be the predicate, and he allowed that (*yawma'idhin*) be the predicate and (*lil-mujrimin*) a qualifier. A predicate, when the subject is not built for *la* itself, is by consensus.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (*yawma'idhin*) is for repetition, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him. It cannot be a repetition, whether it is meant as verbal emphasis or as apposition, because (*yawm*) is in the accusative governed by what was previously mentioned, namely *udhkur* or "they are denied good news." What follows *la* that governs a noun does not get governed by what precedes it. On his estimate, the governing element would be what precedes *illa*. The apparent meaning is the generality of *al-mujrimin* (the guilty), so these speakers are included among them. It was said that it may be placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (*wa-yaqulun*, and they say) refers back to those who spoke, because those spoken of were asking for the descent of the angels, and then when they saw them they disliked meeting them and were frightened of them, because they meet them only with what they hate. So when they saw them they said what they used to say at the meeting of the enemy and the onset of hardship. Mujahid said the same, saying: (*hijran*) is a protection they seek from the angels. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: when the Arabs disliked something they said *hijran*. Abu ʿUbayda said: these two words are a protective formula for the Arabs, which someone says when he fears another in the sacred precinct or in a sacred month, when he meets him and there is a blood-feud between them. End of quotation. From this is the saying of al-Mutallamis:

*She yearned for the far palm, so I said to her: forbidden barrier, is it not the date-palm groves?*

meaning: what you yearn for is forbidden. Sibawayh mentioned (*hijran*) among the accusative verbal nouns that are not inflected. Some of the rajaz poets said:

*She said, and in it there is bewilderment and terror: a protection, which is seen from you, and a barrier.*

Moreover, it is obligatory to supply its governing verb. Sibawayh said: a man says to another, "Will you do such-and-such?" and he replies, "Ḥijran" (a prohibition, a barrier). It derives from "ḥajara-hu," meaning he prevented him, because the one who seeks refuge is asking Allah to prevent the disliked thing from reaching him. Abu Raja', al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "ḥujran" with a damma on the ḥa'.

It was said: the pronoun in "wa-yaqūlūna" (they say) refers to the angels, meaning the angels say to the criminals, "Ḥijran maḥjūran" (a barrier, a forbidden barrier), "upon you is good news." "Maḥjūran" is an adjective that emphasizes the meaning of "ḥijran," as they said: "mawt māʾit" (a dying death) and "dhayl dhāʾil" (a trailing train). The literal "arrival" (qudūm ḥaqīqī) is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted, so it is a metaphor for His judgment and its execution. It was also said: or it is by omitting a modifier, meaning "our angels arrived," and this was attributed to Him because it is by His command. The expression "we arrived" (qadimnā) is apt, because one who arrives at a disliked matter, which he neither approves nor commanded, is one who changes and removes it. So He likened the condition of these people and their deeds that they performed in their disbelief, such as maintaining ties of kinship, relieving the distressed, hospitality to guests, bestowing favour upon a captive, and other noble deeds, to the condition of a people who opposed their ruler, so he went to what was under their authority and tore it apart such that no trace of it remained. Among their proverbs: "Less than dust." And "havaan manthūran" (scattered dust) is an adjective of "al-habāʾ" (dust). He likened them to dust for its insignificance and because it is not benefited from; then He described it as "manthūran," because one sees dust arranged along with the light, and when the wind stirs it, you see it scattered and gone.

Al-Zamakhshari said: or He made it, meaning "manthūran," a third object of "jaʿalnāhu" (We made it), that is, "fa-jaʿalnāhu" (so We made it) combining the worthlessness of dust and its scattering, like His saying: "Be apes, despised" (al-Baqara 65), meaning combining transformation and abasement. End of quote.

Ibn Durustawayh dissented, opposing the grammarians in forbidding that kāna have two predicates and more. The analogy of his view on jaʿala would be to forbid it from having a third predicate.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-habāʾ al-manthūr" is what the winds blow away and scatter. Also from him: "al-habāʾ" is poured-out water. "Al-mustaqarr" is the place of settling, in most times. "Al-maqīl" is the place to which they retreat for rest with the spouses and enjoyment; there is no sleep in Paradise, so the place of their resting with the houris is called "maqīl" by way of comparison, since the place chosen for a midday rest is the most pleasant of places. In the word "aḥsan" there is an allusion to what their resting place is adorned with: the beauty of faces, the comeliness of forms, and other embellishments.

As for "khayr" (better): it was said that it is not used in its basic sense of indicating superiority, otherwise it would imply good in the resting place of the people of the Fire. It can be retained in its basic sense, with the comparison made between those who settle and those who rest, in terms of the time in which this occurs. So the meaning is: "better as a place of settling" in the Hereafter than the affluent disbelievers in this world, and "better as a place of rest" in the Hereafter than those in this world. It was also said: "better as a place of settling" than them, if they had a place of settling; the estimate is then that the existence of a settling place for them would be good.

From Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil: the reckoning will be completed in the span of half a day of the days of this world, and the people of Paradise will take their midday rest in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 3):**

(p-487) ﴿On the Day He gathers them and what they worshipped besides Allah, He will say, "Did you lead these, My servants, astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?" They will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for us to take any protectors other than You, but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance, and they were a people doomed to ruin."﴾ ﴿Indeed, they have denied you in what you say, so you cannot avert [the punishment] or find help. And whoever among you does wrong, We will make him taste a great punishment.﴾ ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets. And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾ ﴿Those who do not expect the meeting with Us say, "Why were the angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great insolence.﴾ ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good tidings that Day for the criminals, and they will say, "A forbidding, forbidden [barrier]!"﴾ ﴿And We will turn to the work they did and make it scattered dust.﴾ ﴿The companions of the Garden, that Day, are better in their resting place and finer in their place of repose.﴾

They recited (yahshuruhum) and (fayaqulu) with the ya' in both places: Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Ibn Kathir and Hafs. Al-Hasan, Talha and Ibn 'Amir recited both with the nun. The rest of the seven recited (nahshuruhum) with the nun, (p-488) and (fayaqulu) with the ya'. Al-A'raj recited (yahshiruhum) with a kasra on the shin. The author of al-Lawami' said: "This is the analogical form throughout the Qur'an for transitive triliteral verbs, since yaf'ulu with a damma on the 'ayn may come from the intransitive fa'ula (with a damma in the past tense)." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is rare in usage but strong in analogy, since yaf'ilu with a kasra on the 'ayn is more analogical than yaf'ulu with a damma on the 'ayn in transitive verbs, end quote." This is not as they both stated. Rather, the transitive verb fa'ula, whose letters are all sound, when it is not for intensification and has no guttural 'ayn or lam, comes in the forms yaf'ulu and yaf'ilu frequently. If one of the two usages is well known, it is followed; otherwise the choice is open. Some of our companions even gave the choice between them, whether they heard the word or not.

(And what they worshipped): al-Dahhak and 'Ikrima said: these are the idols that do not understand, and Allah empowers them to utter this reply. Al-Kalbi said: Allah will bring the idols back to life on that Day to rebuke their worshippers. The majority said: it refers to those among rational beings who were worshipped without commanding worship of themselves, such as the angels, 'Isa and 'Uzayr. This is the most apparent view, as in His saying, (Did you lead these astray?) and what follows of the dialogue, whose apparent sense is that it does not come except from rational beings. Something similar is stated explicitly in His saying, ﴿Then He will say to the angels, "Did these used to worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40] and ﴿"O 'Isa, son of Maryam, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. His questioning, although He knows the one questioned about, is so that they will answer with what they answered, whereupon He rebukes their worshippers by their denial of them. This increases their grief, gladdens the believers at their situation and their salvation from the disgrace of those people, and makes the recounting of that in the Qur'an a kindness to those who are responsible. The interrogative came with the noun preceding the verb, and the construction (a-dalaltum) or (a-dallu) did not come; because both misguiding (al-idlal) and going astray (al-dalal) occur, and the question is only from the one who performs it. A parallel to this was mentioned in ﴿"Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 62]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it is a clear refutation of the view of those who claim that Allah actually misguides His servants, since He says to those worshipped besides Him, (Did you lead them astray?) or did they go astray by themselves, so that they disown their error and seek refuge in Him from being misguiders, and say, 'Rather, You bestowed favor without precedent upon these and their fathers, the favor of a generous and bountiful one.' They made the mercy, whose due is to be the cause of thanks, the cause of disbelief and the forgetting of the remembrance, and that was the cause of their ruin. When the angels and the messengers themselves disown the attribution of misguidance, which is the work of the devils, to them, and seek refuge from them, they are far more free from it and more exalted above it with respect to their Lord, who is Self-Sufficient and Just. They have indeed exalted Him when they attributed to Him the bestowing of favor by blessing and enjoyment of it. They ascribed the forgetting of the remembrance and the causing of ruin to the disbelievers, thereby explaining the metaphorical misguidance that Allah attributed to His Essence in His saying, ﴿He misguides whom He wills﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27]. Had He been the Misguider in the literal sense, the ready answer would have been, 'Rather, You misguided them,' end quote." This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school).

The meaning: (Did you) cause these people to fall into misguidance and be attributed to them, in their going astray from the truth? Or (did they stray) by themselves from it? (Dalla) originally takes (ʿan) after it, as in His saying, ﴿"Who strays from His way"﴾ [al-An'am: 117]; then it was extended and the preposition was dropped, so one says (adallahu 'an al-sabil). Just as (hada) takes (ila) and then it is dropped, and (yadillu) is the intransitive counterpart of (adalla), as you say, "I made him sit and he sat."

(Subhanaka) is a declaration of Allah's transcendence above having anyone associated with Him in worship or singled out for worship. How could it be that any of them would misguide anyone, when they are the purified and sanctified, that any of them should be a rival, while He is the One exalted above rivals and equals?

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(Subhanaka) is an expression of their amazement at what was said, since they are angels and prophets, infallible, so how far they are from misguiding, which is specific to Iblis and his party," end quote.

'Alqama recited (ma yanbaghi) without (kana). The recitation of the majority with it is more apt in meaning, because they were reporting a state that existed in the world, and the time of reporting is not subject to governing action. Abu 'Isa al-Aswad al-Qari recited (yunbagha lana) in the passive. Ibn Khalawayh said: "Sibawayh claimed that yunbagha is a dialect."

The majority recited (an nattakhidha) in the active voice, and (min awliya') is the object with an added (min). Its addition was made acceptable by the negation extending over (nattakhidha), because it is governed by (yanbaghi). When seeking is negated, its object is necessarily negated, which is taking a protector besides Allah. A parallel is ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not wish that any good be sent down upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105], (p-489) meaning: any good. The meaning is: it would not be correct or proper for us, and we being infallible, to take anyone as a protector besides You. So how could it be correct for us to make others take us as protectors besides You?! Abu Muslim said: "(It was not for us) to become like the devils, desiring disbelief and so taking the disbelievers as protectors." He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257].

Abu al-Darda', Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Raja', Nasr ibn 'Alqama, Zayd ibn 'Ali and his brother al-Baqir, Makhul, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Hafs ibn 'Ubayd, al-Nakha'i, al-Sulami, Shayba, Abu Bishr and al-Za'farani recited (an yuttakhadha) in the passive. (Ittakhadha) is used sometimes with one object, as in ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 21], and the majority's recitation is upon this; and sometimes with two objects, as in ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23]. It was said that this recitation is from the second usage: the first object is the pronoun in (nattakhidha), and the second is (min awliya'), with (min) being partitive, meaning: none of the protectors is taken. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This recitation is weakened by the entry of (min) in (min awliya')." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others objected with this. Abu al-Fath said: "(min awliya') is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and (min) entered as an addition because of the preceding negation, as you say, 'I did not take Zayd as any agent (min wakil).'" It was also said: (min awliya') is the second object with an added (min). This is not permitted according to most grammarians, for it is only permitted that (min) enters as an addition upon the first object, under its condition.

al-Hajjaj recited (an nattakhidha min dunika awliya'), and it reached 'Asim, who said: "The one born prematurely is hated! Does he not know that it contains (min)?"

Since their statement, (It was not for us to take any protectors other than You), implied that we did not misguide them and did not compel them to refrain from belief, it was apt to be followed by the adversative (bal-kin), and the meaning: "But You bestowed abundance of blessings upon them and their fathers, and prolonged their lives, and it was obligatory upon them to thank You for them and to believe in what the messengers brought. So that became a cause of turning away from the remembrance of Allah." It was said: (But You gave them enjoyment) is like an allusion to what Musa stated explicitly in His saying, ﴿It is none but Your trial﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. That is: You are the one who gave them their desires of the world until they became drowned in the sea of appetites, so this diverted them from turning to Your obedience and occupying themselves with serving You. (The remembrance) is what people are reminded of through the tongues of the prophets, or the revealed books, or the Qur'an.

(Bur): it was said to be a verbal noun used as a description of the singular and the plural. It was also said to be the plural of (ba'ir), like (a'idh) and ('uudh). It was said to mean "ruined." It was said to mean "corrupt," and this is the dialect of the Azd, who say, "amrun ba'ir," meaning corrupt; and "bara al-bida'a," meaning it became corrupt. al-Hasan said: "There is no good in them," from their saying, "ardun bur," meaning a land left uncultivated with no vegetation. It was said: (bura) means "blind to the truth."

(They have denied you): this is from the speech of Allah without any disagreement, and it is a sudden turn. The argument and the binding are a fourth fine feature, especially when the turn of address (iltifat) is combined with it. It is by implying a saying, like His saying, (O People of the Book) to His saying (there has come to you), meaning: We said, "There has come to you." And like the poet's words:

They said: "The farthest we are asked to reach is Khurasan, then the return." So we came to Khurasan.

meaning: we said, "We have come." Similarly here, meaning: We said, "They have denied you." If the one who answers is the idols, then the address is to the disbelievers, meaning: the idols you worship have denied you by their saying, (It was not for us), and if the address is to the rational beings worshipped, such as 'Isa, the angels and 'Uzayr, peace be upon them, which is the apparent view, then it is in harmony with the address in (Did you lead them astray?), meaning: those worshipped denied you (in what you say), that is, in your saying that you misled them and in your claim that you are their protectors besides Allah. Whoever recited (bima taqulun) with the ta' of address, the meaning is "in what you say," that is: (Exalted are You! It was not for us to take any protectors besides You). It was also said: the address is to the disbelieving worshippers, meaning: those worshipped denied you in what you say of the answer.

(Exalted are You! It was not for us), or "in what you say, you yourselves, of slander against them," they were addressed in a manner of rebuke and reproach. It was also said: it is an address to the believers in the world, meaning: the disbelievers have denied you, O believers, in what you say of monotheism and the law. The majority recited (bima taqulun) with the ta' from above. Abu Haywa and Ibn al-Salt, on the authority of Qunbul, recited it with the ya' from below.

Hafs, Abu Haywa, al-A'mash and Talha recited (fa-ma tastaTi'un) with the ta' of address, and this recitation is supported by the fact that the address in (kadhdhabukum) is to the disbelieving worshippers. It is mentioned that Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr recited (bima yaqulun fama yasti'un) with the ya' in both, meaning: they. (Sarfan) means: averting the punishment, or repentance, or a stratagem, from their saying, "innahu la-yatasarraf," meaning: he schemes. If the address in (kadhdhabukum) is to the disbelievers, then the ta' runs in accordance with it, and the ya' is a turn of address. If the address is to the worshipped, then the ta' is a turn of address and the ya' runs in accordance with the pronoun of (kadhdhabukum), which is nominative. If the address is to the believers, the community of the Messenger, peace be upon him, in His saying (They have denied you), then the meaning is that they are severe in their obstinacy in denial. (Fama tastaTi'un) means: you are not able to turn them away from what they are upon of that. With the ya', (fama yasti'un sarfan) means: they cannot avert [the punishment] for themselves from what they are upon, or they cannot avert you from the truth you are upon. (Wa-la nasran): they cannot help themselves against the affliction they incurred by their denial.

(ومَن يَظْلِمْ مِنكم) The apparent meaning is that it is general. It has also been said that it is addressed to the believers, and it has been said that it is addressed to the disbelievers. Here *al-zulm* (wrongdoing) means *al-shirk* (association of partners with God). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jurayj. It is possible that sins other than *shirk* are included in *al-zulm*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The great punishment applies to everyone who does wrong. The disbeliever is a wrongdoer, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13], and the defiant sinner (*fasiq*) is a wrongdoer, as in His words: ﴿And whoever does not repent, then it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]." End of quotation. There is a hidden Mu'tazilite tendency (*dasisat al-i'tizal*; the Mu'tazila being the rationalist school that holds that the grave sinner is in an intermediate position) in this. It was read as *yudhiqhu* with the *ya* of the third person, meaning God, who is the apparent subject. It has also been said that the subject is *huwa*, i.e., *al-zulm*, which is the verbal noun understood from *bi-zulmin* (with wrongdoing), meaning: wrongdoing makes him taste it.

When criticism of the Messenger for eating food and walking in the markets had preceded, God informed that this is a constant practice in every messenger. The object of *arsalna* (We sent) is, according to al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari, and those who followed them, omitted; its estimated form is *aḥadan* (anyone). Ibn ʿAtiyya estimated it as *rijalan aw rusulan* (men or messengers). The pronoun in *innahum* refers to that omitted object, as in His words: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: "there is none of us who is not..." According to these scholars the clause is a qualifier, namely His words *illa innahum* (except that they), as if He had said: "except eating and walking." According to al-Farra' the object is omitted and it is a relative pronoun estimated after *illa*, meaning *illa man* (except whoever), and the pronoun *innahum* refers back to *man* according to its meaning, so it is an exceptive construction with missing complement (*istithna' mufarrigh*). It has also been said that before *innahum* there is an omitted saying, meaning *illa* [qila] *innahum* (except it was said that they...). These two opinions are weak in Arabic. Ibn al-Anbari said: the estimate is *illa wa-innahum* (except and they...), meaning the clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and this is the preferred view. He answered those who said that what follows *illa* may come as a qualifier; as for omitting the relative pronoun, it is weak. Abu al-Baqa' also went to the view that it is a circumstantial clause, saying: "It was said that if the *lam* were not there it would be in the genitive, because the clause is circumstantial, the meaning being *illa wa-hum yaʾkulun* (except while they eat)." It was read *annahum* with a *fatha*, on the basis that the *lam* is an added particle and *anna* is verbal (*masdariyya*), with the estimate *illa annahum yaʾkulun* (except that they eat), meaning: We did not make them messengers to the people except because they are like them.

The majority read *wa-yamshun* (and walk), the present tense of *mashā* in the simple form. ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAbd Allah read *yumashsha'un*, with doubling and in the passive voice, meaning: their needs and people carry them along. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If *yumashsha'un* were read, it would be more appropriate, were it not for the transmission." Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami also read it doubled but in the active voice, and it has the same meaning as the majority reading *yamshun*. A poet said:

*And he walked among the camel-pens of the watering place, seeking from them young she-camels, difficult and rideable.*

(وجَعَلْنا بَعْضَكم) Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is general for the believer and the disbeliever. So the healthy person is a trial for the sick, the rich is a trial for the poor, the grateful poor is a trial for the rich, the messenger specially honored with prophethood is a trial for the noble disbelievers of his time, and likewise the scholars and the just rulers. Ibn al-Qasim recited this verse when he saw Ashhab. End of quotation. Something similar was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the questioning with *ataṣbirun* (will you be patient?) is specific to the sincere believers, so it belongs to the community of Muhammad. It is as if he made the respite given to the disbelievers a trial for the believers, meaning a test, and then questioned them: "Will you be patient or not?" Then he explained His words ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾ as a promise to the patient and a threat to the disobedient.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *fitna* means a trial and affliction. This is a consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning what they said and found strange: his eating food and walking in the markets, after he had argued against them with the example of all the other messengers. He says: "My practice and the requirement of My wisdom is to test some of you, people, with others." The meaning is that He tested the messengers with those they were sent to, with their hostility toward them, their sayings that go beyond fairness, and various kinds of harm, and He asked them for good patience. A similar verse is ﴿You will certainly hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with God much harm﴾ [Al ʿImran: 186], and so on. The position of *ataṣbirun* after mention of the trial is like the position of *ayyukum* (which of you) after the test in His words: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

(بَصِيرًا) knowing what is right in what He tests with and in other matters. So let your chest not tighten, and do not let their sayings move you, for in your patience toward them is happiness and your success in both abodes. It has been said that it is a consolation for what they reproached him for, namely poverty, when they said: ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden﴾ [al-Furqan: 8]. It is also said that He made the rich a trial for the poor so that He may see whether you will be patient, and that this is His wisdom and His will: He enriches whom He wills and impoverishes whom He wills. It has also been said: We made you a trial for them, because if you had been rich, possessor of treasures and gardens, their inclination toward you and their obedience to you would have been for the world or mixed with the world. We sent you poor so that the obedience of whoever obeys you among them would be purely for God's sake, without worldly greed. It has been said: Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, and those of their rank used to say: "If we accept Islam after ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Bilal, so-and-so, and so-and-so have accepted it before us, they will be raised above us," relying on their precedence. So it is the temptation of some of them by others. End of quotation. In this there is some exaggeration. This last view is the view of al-Kalbi, al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj. The better view is that His words *wa-jaʿalna baʿḍakum li-baʿḍin fitna* (We made some of you a trial for others) include all the meanings of these expressions, because there is a shared common element among all of them.

It has been said that in His words *ataṣbirun* the question has the meaning of a command, meaning: "be patient." The apparent meaning is to take *al-rajaʾ* (hope) in its well-known usage, and the meaning is: they do not hope to meet Us with good, nor to receive Our reward for obedience, because they deny the resurrection in their disbelief in what I brought. Abu ʿUbayda and a group said: its meaning is "they do not fear." al-Farra' said: "(they do not hope for resurrection) means they do not fear." This word is Tihami (a dialect of Hijaz), and it is also from the dialect of Hudhayl. When negation is combined with *rajaʾ* they take it to mean fear. So you say: "So-and-so does not hope for his Lord," meaning he does not fear his Lord. From this is His words: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾ [Nuh: 13], meaning you do not fear the greatness of God. When they say: "So-and-so hopes for his Lord," this is the meaning of hope, not of fear. A poet said:

*When the bees sting him, he does not hope for their sting, and he swears alliance with them in a house of woven, ... wall.*

Another said:

*Do not expect when you meet the defender, whether they have met seven or one.*

End of quotation. Hope for reward necessarily involves fear of punishment. Whoever denies the resurrection hopes for no reward and fears no punishment. Whoever interprets *lam yarju lasʿaha* (he does not hope for its sting) as meaning he does not hope to repel it or to be freed from it, this interpretation is possible, and he is thereby prepared for patience and works hard at his affairs. But al-Farra' and others transmitted this as the Hudhayl usage in negation, and the poet is a Hudhali. So one should not strain for interpretation, and it should be understood according to his dialect.

﴿Why have not the angels been sent down to us﴾ so that You tell us that you are truly a messenger? (*aw naraa rabbana*) or we see our Lord, so that He informs us of that. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and others. This is like what the Jews said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God plainly﴾ [al-Baqara: 55], and like their saying, meaning the polytheists: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels before us as a group﴾ [al-Isra: 92]. All of this is for the sake of obstinacy. Otherwise, the miracles he brought them would suffice if they had been granted success. (*laqadi istakbaru*) meaning they became proud, (*fi anfusihim*) meaning they magnified themselves by asking to see God, though they were not worthy of it. The meaning is that asking for this is only because of what they concealed in their souls of arrogance toward the truth, which is disbelief and stubbornness hidden in their hearts, the outward appearance of which does not show what they have, as He said: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but greatness, which they will never attain﴾ [Ghafir: 56]. The *lam* in *laqad* is the answer to an omitted oath. *ʿAtaw* means they went beyond the limit in wrongdoing, and He described it as *kabir* (great), emphasizing its extremity, meaning they dared to say this great statement only because they had reached the utmost of arrogance and the highest point of insolence. Here (ʿutuwwan) occurs in its original form, while in Maryam (ʿitiyyan) occurs because the joining of two *waws* is disliked, and there is a change for the sake of matching the endings. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *ʿataw* means they disbelieved with the utmost disbelief and were gravely indecent. ʿIkrima said: they tyrannized. Ibn Salam said: they disobeyed. Ibn ʿIsa said: they transgressed. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This sentence, in its excellence of completion, is extreme in its style. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*And the neighbor of Jassas, we consented with her fang to Kulayb, ... the fang of Kulayb is high, its gift.*

In this kind of verb there is a sign of wonder without a word of wonder. Do you not see that the meaning is: how great their arrogance is, how much their insolence is, and how high-priced is the fang whose price is Kulayb?"

(*yawma yarawna al-malaʾika*) (*yawma*) is in the accusative governed by (*udhkur*, remember), which is the closer option, or by a verb indicated by (*la bushra*, there is no good news), meaning they are denied good news. *La bushra* does not govern it, because it is a verbal noun, and because it is negated by *la* of generic negation, since what follows that *la* does not work on what precedes it. Likewise the particle that enters on nouns works like *laysa* (is not). The entry of *la* on *bushra* is for negating all kinds of good news. The apparent meaning of this day is the Day of Resurrection, due to His later words: (*wa-qadimna ila ma ʿamilu*, and We will turn to what they did). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is at death. The meaning is that those who demanded the descent of the angels do not know what evil will be theirs when they see them, and the absence of good news, and the occurrence of loss and the disliked.

(*bushra*) may be built with *la*, or it may be in the accusative with the intention of tanwin (nunation), prevented from taking tanwin because of its necessary feminine form. If it is built with *la*, the predicate may be (*yawma'idhin*), and (*lil-mujrimin*) is a predicate after a predicate, or a qualifier of *bushra*, or a complement connected to what the predicate is connected to. (*yawma'idhin*) may be a qualifier of *bushra* and the predicate (*lil-mujrimin*). There is a dispute between Sibawayh and al-Akhfash over whether the predicate belongs to *la* itself or to the subject that is the whole of *la* and what is built with it. If it has the intention of nunation and is declinable, (*yawma'idhin*) may be governed by *bushra*, and it may be a qualifier, and the predicate is from the predicate. He allowed that (*yawma'idhin*) and (*lil-mujrimin*) be the predicate, and he allowed that (*yawma'idhin*) be the predicate and (*lil-mujrimin*) a qualifier. A predicate, when the subject is not built for *la* itself, is by consensus.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (*yawma'idhin*) is for repetition, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him. It cannot be a repetition, whether it is meant as verbal emphasis or as apposition, because (*yawm*) is in the accusative governed by what was previously mentioned, namely *udhkur* or "they are denied good news." What follows *la* that governs a noun does not get governed by what precedes it. On his estimate, the governing element would be what precedes *illa*. The apparent meaning is the generality of *al-mujrimin* (the guilty), so these speakers are included among them. It was said that it may be placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (*wa-yaqulun*, and they say) refers back to those who spoke, because those spoken of were asking for the descent of the angels, and then when they saw them they disliked meeting them and were frightened of them, because they meet them only with what they hate. So when they saw them they said what they used to say at the meeting of the enemy and the onset of hardship. Mujahid said the same, saying: (*hijran*) is a protection they seek from the angels. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: when the Arabs disliked something they said *hijran*. Abu ʿUbayda said: these two words are a protective formula for the Arabs, which someone says when he fears another in the sacred precinct or in a sacred month, when he meets him and there is a blood-feud between them. End of quotation. From this is the saying of al-Mutallamis:

*She yearned for the far palm, so I said to her: forbidden barrier, is it not the date-palm groves?*

meaning: what you yearn for is forbidden. Sibawayh mentioned (*hijran*) among the accusative verbal nouns that are not inflected. Some of the rajaz poets said:

*She said, and in it there is bewilderment and terror: a protection, which is seen from you, and a barrier.*

Moreover, it is obligatory to supply its governing verb. Sibawayh said: a man says to another, "Will you do such-and-such?" and he replies, "Ḥijran" (a prohibition, a barrier). It derives from "ḥajara-hu," meaning he prevented him, because the one who seeks refuge is asking Allah to prevent the disliked thing from reaching him. Abu Raja', al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "ḥujran" with a damma on the ḥa'.

It was said: the pronoun in "wa-yaqūlūna" (they say) refers to the angels, meaning the angels say to the criminals, "Ḥijran maḥjūran" (a barrier, a forbidden barrier), "upon you is good news." "Maḥjūran" is an adjective that emphasizes the meaning of "ḥijran," as they said: "mawt māʾit" (a dying death) and "dhayl dhāʾil" (a trailing train). The literal "arrival" (qudūm ḥaqīqī) is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted, so it is a metaphor for His judgment and its execution. It was also said: or it is by omitting a modifier, meaning "our angels arrived," and this was attributed to Him because it is by His command. The expression "we arrived" (qadimnā) is apt, because one who arrives at a disliked matter, which he neither approves nor commanded, is one who changes and removes it. So He likened the condition of these people and their deeds that they performed in their disbelief, such as maintaining ties of kinship, relieving the distressed, hospitality to guests, bestowing favour upon a captive, and other noble deeds, to the condition of a people who opposed their ruler, so he went to what was under their authority and tore it apart such that no trace of it remained. Among their proverbs: "Less than dust." And "havaan manthūran" (scattered dust) is an adjective of "al-habāʾ" (dust). He likened them to dust for its insignificance and because it is not benefited from; then He described it as "manthūran," because one sees dust arranged along with the light, and when the wind stirs it, you see it scattered and gone.

Al-Zamakhshari said: or He made it, meaning "manthūran," a third object of "jaʿalnāhu" (We made it), that is, "fa-jaʿalnāhu" (so We made it) combining the worthlessness of dust and its scattering, like His saying: "Be apes, despised" (al-Baqara 65), meaning combining transformation and abasement. End of quote.

Ibn Durustawayh dissented, opposing the grammarians in forbidding that kāna have two predicates and more. The analogy of his view on jaʿala would be to forbid it from having a third predicate.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "al-habāʾ al-manthūr" is what the winds blow away and scatter. Also from him: "al-habāʾ" is poured-out water. "Al-mustaqarr" is the place of settling, in most times. "Al-maqīl" is the place to which they retreat for rest with the spouses and enjoyment; there is no sleep in Paradise, so the place of their resting with the houris is called "maqīl" by way of comparison, since the place chosen for a midday rest is the most pleasant of places. In the word "aḥsan" there is an allusion to what their resting place is adorned with: the beauty of faces, the comeliness of forms, and other embellishments.

As for "khayr" (better): it was said that it is not used in its basic sense of indicating superiority, otherwise it would imply good in the resting place of the people of the Fire. It can be retained in its basic sense, with the comparison made between those who settle and those who rest, in terms of the time in which this occurs. So the meaning is: "better as a place of settling" in the Hereafter than the affluent disbelievers in this world, and "better as a place of rest" in the Hereafter than those in this world. It was also said: "better as a place of settling" than them, if they had a place of settling; the estimate is then that the existence of a settling place for them would be good.

From Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil: the reckoning will be completed in the span of half a day of the days of this world, and the people of Paradise will take their midday rest in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verses 17–24 (part 1 of 3):**

(p-487) ﴿On the Day He gathers them and what they worshipped besides Allah, He will say, "Did you lead these, My servants, astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?" They will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for us to take any protectors other than You, but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance, and they were a people doomed to ruin."﴾ ﴿Indeed, they have denied you in what you say, so you cannot avert [the punishment] or find help. And whoever among you does wrong, We will make him taste a great punishment.﴾ ﴿We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets. And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾ ﴿Those who do not expect the meeting with Us say, "Why were the angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great insolence.﴾ ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good tidings that Day for the criminals, and they will say, "A forbidding, forbidden [barrier]!"﴾ ﴿And We will turn to the work they did and make it scattered dust.﴾ ﴿The companions of the Garden, that Day, are better in their resting place and finer in their place of repose.﴾

They recited (yahshuruhum) and (fayaqulu) with the ya' in both places: Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Ibn Kathir and Hafs. Al-Hasan, Talha and Ibn 'Amir recited both with the nun. The rest of the seven recited (nahshuruhum) with the nun, (p-488) and (fayaqulu) with the ya'. Al-A'raj recited (yahshiruhum) with a kasra on the shin. The author of al-Lawami' said: "This is the analogical form throughout the Qur'an for transitive triliteral verbs, since yaf'ulu with a damma on the 'ayn may come from the intransitive fa'ula (with a damma in the past tense)." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is rare in usage but strong in analogy, since yaf'ilu with a kasra on the 'ayn is more analogical than yaf'ulu with a damma on the 'ayn in transitive verbs, end quote."
