And [the verb] (hādiyan) and (naṣīran) are in the accusative, either as ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) or as tamyīz (accusative of specification). "They said," that is, the disbelievers, in the manner of a demand (iqtirāḥ) and an objection (i'tirāḍ) that indicates their aversion to the truth. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Here (nuzzila) means only (unzila), like (khubbira) meaning (ukhbira). Otherwise it would be self-contradictory." End quote.

He said that (nuzzila) means (unzila) because (nuzzila), in his view, originally implies distribution (tafrīq). So if he left it with its original sense of distribution, he would contradict himself. As for His saying (jumlatan wāḥidatan), we have established that (nuzzila) does not necessarily imply distribution, because the doubling (taḍ'īf) in it, in our view, is synonymous with the hamza (of causation). We have explained this at the beginning of Āl ʿImrān. The speakers of this were the Quraysh disbelievers, who said: "If this were from Allah, it would have been sent down all at once, as the Torah and the Gospel were." It was also said that those who said this were the Jews, but this view is of no use, because the matter of the argument from it and its miraculous nature does not differ whether it is revealed all at once or in parts. Rather, its miraculous nature is more evident in its being revealed in parts, since they were challenged to produce a surah like it. Had it been revealed all at once and they were challenged to produce something like what was revealed, they would have been more incapable than when they were challenged to produce a surah of it and they failed.

The referent of "this" (al-mushār ilayhi) is not mentioned. It was said: it is from the words of the disbelievers, and they pointed to the Torah and the Gospel, meaning: a revelation like the revelation of those divine books, all at once. Then (linuthabbita bihi fu'adaka), "that We may strengthen your heart thereby," is a causal clause for an omitted element, meaning: We divided it over times, "that We may strengthen your heart thereby." It was also said: it is a new sentence from the speech of Allah, not from their speech. Since their statement implied the meaning "why was it revealed in parts?", the words "thus" (kadhālika) refer to the distribution, meaning: "thus" it was revealed in parts.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The wisdom in it is that by distributing it We strengthen your heart so that you understand it and memorise it, because the one who receives knowledge can only strengthen his heart to retain knowledge bit by bit, part after part. Had it been cast upon him all at once, he would have been unable to retain it. The Messenger (peace be upon him) differed in his condition from the condition of Dawūd, Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them), since he was unlettered and could not write, whereas they could read and write. So he had no choice but to receive and memorise, and it was revealed to him in portions over twenty years. It was also said: over twenty-three years. Also, it would descend according to events and in response to questioners, and because some of it was abrogated (mansūkh) and some of it abrogating (nāsikh), and this could only be done with what was revealed in parts. End quote.

The lām in (linuthabbita bihi) is the lām of purpose. Abū Ḥātim said: it is the lām of oath, and the implied meaning is "by Allah, He will surely strengthen," so the nūn was dropped and the lām was given a kasra. End quote. This is a view that is extremely weak. He (Abū Ḥātim) inclined toward the opinion of al-Akhfash that the answer of an oath may be introduced by the lām of kay (purpose), and he took as an example: "and that the hearts of [those who disbelieve in the Hereafter] may incline toward it" (al-Anʿām 6:113). But this is a weaker opinion. ʿAbdullah read (liyuthabbita) with the yā', meaning: that Allah may strengthen. (Wa-rattalnāhu), meaning: We made it distinct (faṣṣalnāhu). It was said: We made it clear (bayyannāhu). It was said: We explained it (fassarnāhu).

﴿And they will not bring you any example﴾ which they set forth by way of objection, as their comparison in this case with the Torah and the Gospel, except that We bring you the truth concerning it, and it is clearer in exposition and detail. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿And they will not bring you any example﴾, with a strange question among their false questions, as if it were an example of falsehood, except that We bring you the true answer, which cannot be evaded, and which is better in meaning and in what it conveys than their question. Since tafsīr (exegesis) is the disclosure of what the speech indicates, it is placed in the position of its meaning, so they say: the tafsīr of this speech is such-and-such, just as it is said: its meaning is such-and-such. Or (wa-lā yaʾtūnaka) means with a strange condition and attribute, as they say: why was not this your attribute and condition? For example, that an angel be sent with you to warn with you, or a treasure be cast to you, or that you have a garden, or that the Qur'an be sent down to you all at once. Except that We give you what befits you in Our wisdom and will to be given, and what is better in disclosing what you were sent with and in proving its soundness. End quote. It was also said: (wa-lā yaʾtūnaka) with a doubt aimed at nullifying your matter, except that We bring you the truth that refutes the doubt of the people of ignorance and nullifies the speech of the people of deviation. The comparative (muḍaḍal ʿalayhi) is omitted, meaning: ﴿and better in exposition﴾ than their example, and their example is their saying: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"

﴿Those who are gathered﴾ (alladhīna yuḥsharūn). Al-Kirmānī said: it is connected to His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day﴾ (al-Furqān 25:24), etc. It was said: it may also be connected to His saying: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy among the criminals﴾ (al-Furqān 25:31). End quote. What appears evident is that when they objected concerning the discourse of the Qur'an and its being revealed in parts, their speech implied that they were people of guidance and goodness, and that they were on the straight path. For this reason they objected, so Allah, exalted is He, informed about their state and what their affair would lead to in the Hereafter, by describing them as ﴿worse in place and further astray from the way﴾. Apparently, the disbelievers will be gathered on their faces, by being dragged upon their faces. In a ḥadīth: "He who made them walk on their feet is able to make them walk on their faces." This is the view of the majority. It was also said that it is a metaphor for extreme humiliation, disgrace and shame. It was also said that it is from the Arab saying: "So-and-so passed on his face" when he did not know where he went. It is said: "He went on his face" when he hastened, heading for his destination. And (sharr) and (aḍall) are not in their usual sense of comparison. The words (sharrun makānan), meaning "worse in station," correspond to His saying (khayrun mustaqarran), "better in abode," and it is possible that by place (makān) is meant rank and nobility, not a dwelling. They parsed (alladhīna) as the subject, and the clause (ulāʾika) as the predicate. In my view it is also permissible that (alladhīna) be the predicate of an omitted subject, since the disbelievers and what they said were previously mentioned, so He said, to humiliate them and to make them hear of what their state will lead to: "They are those who will be gathered," then He resumed with informative speech about them, saying: ﴿Those are worse in place﴾.

(p-494) The two Ḥaramiyyān (the Meccan and Medinan readers) and Ibn ʿĀmir read *tashsha'aqqu* with the *tāʾ* of *tatashaqqaqu* assimilated into the *shīn* (*idghām*, assimilation) here. The rest of the Seven read it with that *tāʾ* omitted. The meaning is the Day of Resurrection, as in His words: ﴿the sky will be split asunder by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18].

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of readers) read *wa-nuzzila* as a past tense, intensive (*mushaddad*) form in the passive voice. Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Rajāʾ read *wa-nazala* as a past tense in the active voice. Also from him (Abū Rajāʾ) is *wa-anzala* in the active voice, and its verbal noun came as *tanzīlan*, whose regular form would be *inzālan*. But since *anzala* and *nazzala* have the same meaning, it is permissible for the verbal noun of one to be used for the other, as the poet said:

> *Until I folded myself up, the folding of the fertile one (?)*

It is as if he said: "until I folded (inṭawaytu)." Al-Aʿmash and ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Masʿūd), according to Ibn ʿAṭiyya's transmission, read *wa-unzila* as a past tense, quadriliteral (*rubāʿī*), in the passive voice, whose present form is *yunazzalu*. Jannāḥ ibn Ḥubaysh and al-Khaffāf, from Abū ʿAmr, read *wa-nazala* as a triliteral, light (*mukhaffaf*) form in the active voice. Hārūn, from Abū ʿAmr, read *wa-tunazzalu* with a *tāʾ* at the beginning, as the present of the intensive *nazzala* in the active voice. Abū Muʿādh and Kharija, from Abū ʿAmr, read *wa-nuzzila al-malāʾikatu* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* and a shadda on the *zāy*, dropping the *nūn* of *wa-nunazzilu*. In some of the codices (*maṣāḥif*, plural of *muṣḥaf*) it is written *wa-nunazzilu* with a *nūn*, the present of the intensive *nazzala* in the active voice. Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributed this reading to Ibn Kathīr alone, saying: "It is the reading of the people of Mecca, and it is also related from Abū ʿAmr." Also from Ubayy (ibn Kaʿb) is *wa-tanazzalat*. Ubayy also read *wa-nuzzilat* as a past tense, intensive, in the passive voice with the feminine *tāʾ*.

The author of *al-Lawāmiʿ* said, from al-Khaffāf from Abū ʿAmr: *wa-nuzila* is light and in the passive voice, with *al-malāʾikatu* in the nominative (*raf ʿan*). If this reading is sound, then a genitive construction was omitted from it: the *muḍāf* (the head noun) was dropped and the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the genitive noun) was put in its place. The intended sense is *nazala nuzūlu al-malāʾikati*, so the verbal noun *nuzūl* was dropped and its case was transferred to *al-malāʾikatu*, meaning "the descent of the angels descended." This is because the verbal noun can have the meaning of the noun (of the agent). This is among the things that come according to the school of Sībawayh regarding the arrangement of the intransitive verb with its object, since the verb indicates its verbal noun. End of quotation.

Abū al-Fatḥ (Ibn Jinnī) said: This is not well known, because *nazala* is not transitive to an object, so that it would be made passive here with *al-malāʾikatu*. Its explanation is that it is like *zukima al-rajulu* and *junna* (both meaning "he was afflicted"), for one only says *azkamahu Allāh* and *ajannahu Allāh* (God afflicted him with them). This is a matter of transmission (*samāʿ*), not analogy (*qiyās*). End of quotation. These are eleven readings.

Apparently *al-ghamām* is the familiar cloud. It was said that it is God, in His words: ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210]. Ibn Jurayj said: "*al-ghamām* is the cloud in which God comes in Paradise, so they claim." Al-Ḥasan said: "It is a veil between the sky and the earth, in which the angels ascend to copy out the deeds of the children of Adam so that they may be reckoned." It was said: it is a white, thin cloud like mist, which the Children of Israel did not have during their wandering in the wilderness.

Apparently *al-samāʾ* is the sky that shades us. It was said: "It will split, sky after sky," as Muqātil said. The *bāʾ* (in *bi-al-ghamām*) is the *bāʾ* of circumstance (*ḥāl*), meaning "clouded over." Or it is the *bāʾ* of cause, meaning "because of the rising of the cloud from it," as if the cloud is that by which the sky is split, just as one says: "the hump was split with the knife, and it split by it." A parallel to this is His words: ﴿the sky will be split by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18]. Or it has the sense of *ʿan* (from) according to three opinions.

The difference between the causal *bāʾ* and *ʿan* is that *inshaqqa ʿan kadhā* means "it opened from that," while *inshaqqa bi-kadhā* means that thing is the one that splits it.

(p-495) *Wa-nuzzila al-malāʾikatu* means: down to the earth, because the reward and reckoning are taking place. *Al-ḥaqq* is an attribute of *al-mulk*, meaning "the established," because all sovereignty will be annulled on that day, and nothing will remain except His sovereignty, may He be exalted. The predicate of *al-mulk* is *yawmaʾidhin*. *Al-Raḥmān* is connected to *al-ḥaqq*, or it is explanatory, that is *li-al-Raḥmān*. It was said: the predicate is *li-al-Raḥmān*, and *yawmaʾidhin* is governed by *al-mulk*. It was said: the predicate is *al-ḥaqq*, and *li-al-Raḥmān* is connected to it, or it is explanatory. That day was hard for the disbelievers because of their entering the Fire and the terrors that come with it. His words *ʿalā al-kāfirīna* ("for the disbelievers") indicate that it is made easy for the believers. There is a hadith that it will be eased until it is lighter for the believer than an obligatory prayer he prayed in the world.

The general sense of *al-ẓālim* ("the wrongdoer") is apparent, since the *alif-lām* in it is generic (*li-al-jins*). This was said by Mujāhid and Abū Rajāʾ, and they said: "Fulān" is a euphemism (*kināya*) for Satan.

Ibn ʿAbbās and a group said: *al-ẓālim* here is ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, since he had inclined toward Islam, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf is the one referred to by *Fulān*. There had been a close friendship between them, and he (Ubayy) forbade him from Islam, and he (ʿUqba) obeyed him. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās the opposite of this view. It was said: the occasion of revelation was ʿUqba and Ubayy. It was said: ʿUqba was a close friend of Umayya, and ʿUqba embraced Islam. Umayya said: "My face is forbidden to your face if you pledge allegiance to Muḥammad." So he disbelieved and apostatized to please Umayya, and so it was revealed. This was said by al-Shaʿbī. He mentioned ʿUqba's offensive conduct toward the Messenger, which was the reason the Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "I will not meet you outside Mecca without striking your head with the sword." So ʿUqba was killed on the Day of Badr, in cold blood; he commanded ʿAlī, who struck his neck. Ubayy ibn Khalaf was killed on the Day of Uḥud in single combat.

The purpose is to mention the terror of the Day of Resurrection, through the regret of the wrongdoer and his wish that he had not obeyed his friend who used to command him to wrongdoing. There is no wrongdoer except that he generally has a special friend, referred to as "Fulān." The apparent meaning is that the wrongdoer (*yaʿaḍḍu ʿalā yadayhi*) does the act of one who is regretful and grieving. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "He eats his hands up to the elbows, then they grow back, and he continues like this, whenever he eats them they grow back." It was said: it is a metaphor (*majāz*) used to express bewilderment, grief, regret, and sorrow. The lexicographers reported that one who is sorrowful, grieving, and remorseful bites his thumb out of regret. The poet said:

> *She slapped her cheek with light red (wine) cups;*
> *they received from them the torment of white, torturing ones.*
>
> *The jujube complained of the daisy's blossom,*
> *and the rose complained of the jujube's freshness.*

And in the proverb: "He eats his hands in regret and sheds tears of blood." Al-Zamakhsharī said: biting the fingertips and the hands, falling into the hand, eating the fingers, grinding the teeth, and their variants, are all euphemisms (*kināyāt*) for rage and anguish, because they are among their accompaniments. So the accompaniment is mentioned and the thing accompanied is indicated by it, and the speech is elevated thereby to a level of eloquence, and the listener finds in himself an awe and admiration that he does not find in the plain statement of the thing referred to. End of quotation. The poet said about grinding the teeth:

> *He refused humiliation, while al-Nuʿmān was grinding his teeth*
> *against him, and the swords were his refuges.*

*Yaqūlu* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: saying "Oh, would that I..." If the *alif-lām* in *al-rasūl* is for a known referent (*ʿahd*), the meaning is that ʿUqba wished that he had accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ) and followed the path of truth. If the *alif-lām* is generic, the meaning is that he wished to follow the path of the Messenger, which is faith. Then *al-rasūl* is generic, because every wrongdoer has been obligated to follow what a messenger from God brought, until the Muḥammadan community came and abrogated all previous religions, so after its coming no religion is accepted other than what it brought.

Then he calls out with woe and regret, saying: *yā waylatā*, meaning "Oh, my destruction!" Like His words: ﴿Oh, my regret over what I neglected in the side of God﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Quṭayb read *yā waylatī* with a *kasra* on the *tāʾ*, and the *yāʾ* is the *yāʾ* of possession (*iḍāfa*), which is the original form, because a man calls out to his woe, which is his destruction, saying to it: "Come, this is your time." A group read it with *imāla* (inclination of the vowel). Abū ʿAlī said: leaving out the *imāla* is better, because this word originally had a *yāʾ*, and the *kasra* was changed to a *fatḥa* and the *yāʾ* to an *alif*, fleeing from the *yāʾ*. Whoever uses *imāla* returns to what he originally fled from.

*Fulān* is a euphemism for a proper name and is inflected. *Fulu* is a euphemism for an indefinite human, like "O man (*yā rajul*)," and it is restricted to vocative use. *Fulah* in the sense of "O woman" is similar. The final letter of *fulu* is a *yāʾ* or a *wāw*, and it is not a truncated form of *Fulān*, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. Ibn ʿUṣfūr, Ibn Mālik, and the author of *al-Basīṭ* erred in saying that *fulu* is a euphemism for a proper name, like *Fulān*. Sībawayh's book contains what we have said, by transmission from the Arabs.

*Al-dhikr* is the remembrance of God, or the Qur'an, or the admonition. The apparent meaning is to take Satan in his literal sense, because it is he who whispered to him in the friendship of the one who misled him, so He named him Satan, because he misleads just as Satan misleads. Then He abandoned him and did not benefit him in the end. This sentence may be part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and it may be a report from God's speech, indicating the manner of their misguidance and warning against Satan, who brought them to that point. In the authentic hadith, the good companion is likened to musk and the bad companion to the one who blows the bellows.

The apparent meaning is that the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to his Lord, and his report that his people, the Quraysh, abandoned the Qur'an, is something that happened to him in the world. This is evident from his turning to it, consoling and comforting himself with His words: ﴿Thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, and that He is sufficient as a guide and helper. So it is a promise from Him of victory. This statement by the Messenger, and his complaint in it, is a warning to his people. A group, including Abū Muslim, said that it is his (ﷺ) statement in the Hereafter, like His words: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you against these as a witness?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 41].

The apparent meaning of *mahjūran* is "abandoned," meaning abandoned from belief in it, rejected and cast away from being heard, with a *fatḥa* on the *hāʾ*. This was said by Mujāhid, al-Nakhaʿī, and their followers. It was also said: it is from *al-hujr* (abuse or incoherent speech), and the implication is that it is *mahjūran fīhi* ("abused in it"), meaning that it is false. The myths of the ancients are that when they heard it they would make senseless noise in it, like His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise over it﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 26].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also possible that *al-mahjūr* has the sense of *al-hajr* (abandonment), like *al-malḥūd* and *al-maʿqūl*, and the meaning is that they took it as abandonment. And *al-ʿadūw* may be singular or plural. End of quotation.

What appears evident is that when they objected concerning the discourse of the Qur'an and its being revealed in parts, their speech implied that they were people of guidance and goodness, and that they were on the straight path. Apparently, the disbelievers will be gathered on their faces, by being dragged upon their faces. In a ḥadīth: "He who made them walk on their feet is able to make them walk on their faces." This is the view of the majority. It was also said that it is a metaphor for extreme humiliation, disgrace and shame. It was also said that it is from the Arab saying: "So-and-so passed on his face" when he did not know where he went. It is said: "He went on his face" when he hastened, heading for his destination. And (sharr) and (aḍall) are not in their usual sense of comparison. The words (sharrun makānan), meaning "worse in station," correspond to His saying (khayrun mustaqarran), "better in abode," and it is possible that by place (makān) is meant rank and nobility, not a dwelling. They parsed (alladhīna) as the subject, and the clause (ulāʾika) as the predicate. In my view it is also permissible that (alladhīna) be the predicate of an omitted subject, since the disbelievers and what they said were previously mentioned, so He said, to humiliate them and to make them hear of what their state will lead to: "They are those who will be gathered," then He resumed with informative speech about them, saying: ﴿Those are worse in place﴾.

(p-494) The two Ḥaramiyyān (the Meccan and Medinan readers) and Ibn ʿĀmir read *tashsha'aqqu* with the *tāʾ* of *tatashaqqaqu* assimilated into the *shīn* (*idghām*, assimilation) here. The rest of the Seven read it with that *tāʾ* omitted. The meaning is the Day of Resurrection, as in His words: ﴿the sky will be split asunder by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18].

Al-Jumhūr (the majority of readers) read *wa-nuzzila* as a past tense, intensive (*mushaddad*) form in the passive voice. Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Rajāʾ read *wa-nazala* as a past tense in the active voice. Also from him (Abū Rajāʾ) is *wa-anzala* in the active voice, and its verbal noun came as *tanzīlan*, whose regular form would be *inzālan*. But since *anzala* and *nazzala* have the same meaning, it is permissible for the verbal noun of one to be used for the other, as the poet said:

> *Until I folded myself up, the folding of the fertile one (?)*

It is as if he said: "until I folded (inṭawaytu)." Al-Aʿmash and ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Masʿūd), according to Ibn ʿAṭiyya's transmission, read *wa-unzila* as a past tense, quadriliteral (*rubāʿī*), in the passive voice, whose present form is *yunazzalu*. Jannāḥ ibn Ḥubaysh and al-Khaffāf, from Abū ʿAmr, read *wa-nazala* as a triliteral, light (*mukhaffaf*) form in the active voice. Hārūn, from Abū ʿAmr, read *wa-tunazzalu* with a *tāʾ* at the beginning, as the present of the intensive *nazzala* in the active voice. Abū Muʿādh and Kharija, from Abū ʿAmr, read *wa-nuzzila al-malāʾikatu* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* and a shadda on the *zāy*, dropping the *nūn* of *wa-nunazzilu*. In some of the codices (*maṣāḥif*, plural of *muṣḥaf*) it is written *wa-nunazzilu* with a *nūn*, the present of the intensive *nazzala* in the active voice. Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributed this reading to Ibn Kathīr alone, saying: "It is the reading of the people of Mecca, and it is also related from Abū ʿAmr." Also from Ubayy (ibn Kaʿb) is *wa-tanazzalat*. Ubayy also read *wa-nuzzilat* as a past tense, intensive, in the passive voice with the feminine *tāʾ*.

The author of *al-Lawāmiʿ* said, from al-Khaffāf from Abū ʿAmr: *wa-nuzila* is light and in the passive voice, with *al-malāʾikatu* in the nominative (*raf ʿan*). If this reading is sound, then a genitive construction was omitted from it: the *muḍāf* (the head noun) was dropped and the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the genitive noun) was put in its place. The intended sense is *nazala nuzūlu al-malāʾikati*, so the verbal noun *nuzūl* was dropped and its case was transferred to *al-malāʾikatu*, meaning "the descent of the angels descended." This is because the verbal noun can have the meaning of the noun (of the agent). This is among the things that come according to the school of Sībawayh regarding the arrangement of the intransitive verb with its object, since the verb indicates its verbal noun. End of quotation.

Abū al-Fatḥ (Ibn Jinnī) said: This is not well known, because *nazala* is not transitive to an object, so that it would be made passive here with *al-malāʾikatu*. Its explanation is that it is like *zukima al-rajulu* and *junna* (both meaning "he was afflicted"), for one only says *azkamahu Allāh* and *ajannahu Allāh* (God afflicted him with them). This is a matter of transmission (*samāʿ*), not analogy (*qiyās*). End of quotation. These are eleven readings.

Apparently *al-ghamām* is the familiar cloud. It was said that it is God, in His words: ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210]. Ibn Jurayj said: "*al-ghamām* is the cloud in which God comes in Paradise, so they claim." Al-Ḥasan said: "It is a veil between the sky and the earth, in which the angels ascend to copy out the deeds of the children of Adam so that they may be reckoned." It was said: it is a white, thin cloud like mist, which the Children of Israel did not have during their wandering in the wilderness.

Apparently *al-samāʾ* is the sky that shades us. It was said: "It will split, sky after sky," as Muqātil said. The *bāʾ* (in *bi-al-ghamām*) is the *bāʾ* of circumstance (*ḥāl*), meaning "clouded over." Or it is the *bāʾ* of cause, meaning "because of the rising of the cloud from it," as if the cloud is that by which the sky is split, just as one says: "the hump was split with the knife, and it split by it." A parallel to this is His words: ﴿the sky will be split by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18]. Or it has the sense of *ʿan* (from) according to three opinions.

The difference between the causal *bāʾ* and *ʿan* is that *inshaqqa ʿan kadhā* means "it opened from that," while *inshaqqa bi-kadhā* means that thing is the one that splits it.

(p-495) *Wa-nuzzila al-malāʾikatu* means: down to the earth, because the reward and reckoning are taking place. *Al-ḥaqq* is an attribute of *al-mulk*, meaning "the established," because all sovereignty will be annulled on that day, and nothing will remain except His sovereignty, may He be exalted. The predicate of *al-mulk* is *yawmaʾidhin*. *Al-Raḥmān* is connected to *al-ḥaqq*, or it is explanatory, that is *li-al-Raḥmān*. It was said: the predicate is *li-al-Raḥmān*, and *yawmaʾidhin* is governed by *al-mulk*. It was said: the predicate is *al-ḥaqq*, and *li-al-Raḥmān* is connected to it, or it is explanatory. That day was hard for the disbelievers because of their entering the Fire and the terrors that come with it. His words *ʿalā al-kāfirīna* ("for the disbelievers") indicate that it is made easy for the believers. There is a hadith that it will be eased until it is lighter for the believer than an obligatory prayer he prayed in the world.

The general sense of *al-ẓālim* ("the wrongdoer") is apparent, since the *alif-lām* in it is generic (*li-al-jins*). This was said by Mujāhid and Abū Rajāʾ, and they said: "Fulān" is a euphemism (*kināya*) for Satan.

Ibn ʿAbbās and a group said: *al-ẓālim* here is ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, since he had inclined toward Islam, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf is the one referred to by *Fulān*. There had been a close friendship between them, and he (Ubayy) forbade him from Islam, and he (ʿUqba) obeyed him. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās the opposite of this view. It was said: the occasion of revelation was ʿUqba and Ubayy. It was said: ʿUqba was a close friend of Umayya, and ʿUqba embraced Islam. Umayya said: "My face is forbidden to your face if you pledge allegiance to Muḥammad." So he disbelieved and apostatized to please Umayya, and so it was revealed. This was said by al-Shaʿbī. He mentioned ʿUqba's offensive conduct toward the Messenger, which was the reason the Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "I will not meet you outside Mecca without striking your head with the sword." So ʿUqba was killed on the Day of Badr, in cold blood; he commanded ʿAlī, who struck his neck. Ubayy ibn Khalaf was killed on the Day of Uḥud in single combat.

The purpose is to mention the terror of the Day of Resurrection, through the regret of the wrongdoer and his wish that he had not obeyed his friend who used to command him to wrongdoing. There is no wrongdoer except that he generally has a special friend, referred to as "Fulān." The apparent meaning is that the wrongdoer (*yaʿaḍḍu ʿalā yadayhi*) does the act of one who is regretful and grieving. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "He eats his hands up to the elbows, then they grow back, and he continues like this, whenever he eats them they grow back." It was said: it is a metaphor (*majāz*) used to express bewilderment, grief, regret, and sorrow. The lexicographers reported that one who is sorrowful, grieving, and remorseful bites his thumb out of regret. The poet said:

> *She slapped her cheek with light red (wine) cups;*
> *they received from them the torment of white, torturing ones.*
>
> *The jujube complained of the daisy's blossom,*
> *and the rose complained of the jujube's freshness.*

And in the proverb: "He eats his hands in regret and sheds tears of blood." Al-Zamakhsharī said: biting the fingertips and the hands, falling into the hand, eating the fingers, grinding the teeth, and their variants, are all euphemisms (*kināyāt*) for rage and anguish, because they are among their accompaniments. So the accompaniment is mentioned and the thing accompanied is indicated by it, and the speech is elevated thereby to a level of eloquence, and the listener finds in himself an awe and admiration that he does not find in the plain statement of the thing referred to. End of quotation. The poet said about grinding the teeth:

> *He refused humiliation, while al-Nuʿmān was grinding his teeth*
> *against him, and the swords were his refuges.*

*Yaqūlu* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: saying "Oh, would that I..." If the *alif-lām* in *al-rasūl* is for a known referent (*ʿahd*), the meaning is that ʿUqba wished that he had accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ) and followed the path of truth. If the *alif-lām* is generic, the meaning is that he wished to follow the path of the Messenger, which is faith. Then *al-rasūl* is generic, because every wrongdoer has been obligated to follow what a messenger from God brought, until the Muḥammadan community came and abrogated all previous religions, so after its coming no religion is accepted other than what it brought.

Then he calls out with woe and regret, saying: *yā waylatā*, meaning "Oh, my destruction!" Like His words: ﴿Oh, my regret over what I neglected in the side of God﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Quṭayb read *yā waylatī* with a *kasra* on the *tāʾ*, and the *yāʾ* is the *yāʾ* of possession (*iḍāfa*), which is the original form, because a man calls out to his woe, which is his destruction, saying to it: "Come, this is your time." A group read it with *imāla* (inclination of the vowel). Abū ʿAlī said: leaving out the *imāla* is better, because this word originally had a *yāʾ*, and the *kasra* was changed to a *fatḥa* and the *yāʾ* to an *alif*, fleeing from the *yāʾ*. Whoever uses *imāla* returns to what he originally fled from.

*Fulān* is a euphemism for a proper name and is inflected. *Fulu* is a euphemism for an indefinite human, like "O man (*yā rajul*)," and it is restricted to vocative use. *Fulah* in the sense of "O woman" is similar. The final letter of *fulu* is a *yāʾ* or a *wāw*, and it is not a truncated form of *Fulān*, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. Ibn ʿUṣfūr, Ibn Mālik, and the author of *al-Basīṭ* erred in saying that *fulu* is a euphemism for a proper name, like *Fulān*. Sībawayh's book contains what we have said, by transmission from the Arabs.

*Al-dhikr* is the remembrance of God, or the Qur'an, or the admonition. The apparent meaning is to take Satan in his literal sense, because it is he who whispered to him in the friendship of the one who misled him, so He named him Satan, because he misleads just as Satan misleads. Then He abandoned him and did not benefit him in the end. This sentence may be part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and it may be a report from God's speech, indicating the manner of their misguidance and warning against Satan, who brought them to that point. In the authentic hadith, the good companion is likened to musk and the bad companion to the one who blows the bellows.

The apparent meaning is that the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to his Lord, and his report that his people, the Quraysh, abandoned the Qur'an, is something that happened to him in the world. This is evident from his turning to it, consoling and comforting himself with His words: ﴿Thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, and that He is sufficient as a guide and helper. So it is a promise from Him of victory. This statement by the Messenger, and his complaint in it, is a warning to his people. A group, including Abū Muslim, said that it is his (ﷺ) statement in the Hereafter, like His words: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you against these as a witness?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 41].

The apparent meaning of *mahjūran* is "abandoned," meaning abandoned from belief in it, rejected and cast away from being heard, with a *fatḥa* on the *hāʾ*. This was said by Mujāhid, al-Nakhaʿī, and their followers. It was also said: it is from *al-hujr* (abuse or incoherent speech), and the implication is that it is *mahjūran fīhi* ("abused in it"), meaning that it is false. The myths of the ancients are that when they heard it they would make senseless noise in it, like His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise over it﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 26].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also possible that *al-mahjūr* has the sense of *al-hajr* (abandonment), like *al-malḥūd* and *al-maʿqūl*, and the meaning is that they took it as abandonment. And *al-ʿadūw* may be singular or plural. End of quotation.

And [the verb] (hādiyan) and (naṣīran) are in the accusative, either as ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) or as tamyīz (accusative of specification). "They said," that is, the disbelievers, in the manner of a demand (iqtirāḥ) and an objection (i'tirāḍ) that indicates their aversion to the truth. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Here (nuzzila) means only (unzila), like (khubbira) meaning (ukhbira). Otherwise it would be self-contradictory." End quote.

He said that (nuzzila) means (unzila) because (nuzzila), in his view, originally implies distribution (tafrīq). So if he left it with its original sense of distribution, he would contradict himself. As for His saying (jumlatan wāḥidatan), we have established that (nuzzila) does not necessarily imply distribution, because the doubling (taḍ'īf) in it, in our view, is synonymous with the hamza (of causation). We have explained this at the beginning of Āl ʿImrān. The speakers of this were the Quraysh disbelievers, who said: "If this were from Allah, it would have been sent down all at once, as the Torah and the Gospel were." It was also said that those who said this were the Jews, but this view is of no use, because the matter of the argument from it and its miraculous nature does not differ whether it is revealed all at once or in parts. Rather, its miraculous nature is more evident in its being revealed in parts, since they were challenged to produce a surah like it. Had it been revealed all at once and they were challenged to produce something like what was revealed, they would have been more incapable than when they were challenged to produce a surah of it and they failed.

The referent of "this" (al-mushār ilayhi) is not mentioned. It was said: it is from the words of the disbelievers, and they pointed to the Torah and the Gospel, meaning: a revelation like the revelation of those divine books, all at once. Then (linuthabbita bihi fu'adaka), "that We may strengthen your heart thereby," is a causal clause for an omitted element, meaning: We divided it over times, "that We may strengthen your heart thereby." It was also said: it is a new sentence from the speech of Allah, not from their speech. Since their statement implied the meaning "why was it revealed in parts?", the words "thus" (kadhālika) refer to the distribution, meaning: "thus" it was revealed in parts.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The wisdom in it is that by distributing it We strengthen your heart so that you understand it and memorise it, because the one who receives knowledge can only strengthen his heart to retain knowledge bit by bit, part after part. Had it been cast upon him all at once, he would have been unable to retain it. The Messenger (peace be upon him) differed in his condition from the condition of Dawūd, Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them), since he was unlettered and could not write, whereas they could read and write. So he had no choice but to receive and memorise, and it was revealed to him in portions over twenty years. It was also said: over twenty-three years. Also, it would descend according to events and in response to questioners, and because some of it was abrogated (mansūkh) and some of it abrogating (nāsikh), and this could only be done with what was revealed in parts. End quote.

The lām in (linuthabbita bihi) is the lām of purpose. Abū Ḥātim said: it is the lām of oath, and the implied meaning is "by Allah, He will surely strengthen," so the nūn was dropped and the lām was given a kasra. End quote. This is a view that is extremely weak. He (Abū Ḥātim) inclined toward the opinion of al-Akhfash that the answer of an oath may be introduced by the lām of kay (purpose), and he took as an example: "and that the hearts of [those who disbelieve in the Hereafter] may incline toward it" (al-Anʿām 6:113). But this is a weaker opinion. ʿAbdullah read (liyuthabbita) with the yā', meaning: that Allah may strengthen. (Wa-rattalnāhu), meaning: We made it distinct (faṣṣalnāhu). It was said: We made it clear (bayyannāhu). It was said: We explained it (fassarnāhu).

﴿And they will not bring you any example﴾ which they set forth by way of objection, as their comparison in this case with the Torah and the Gospel, except that We bring you the truth concerning it, and it is clearer in exposition and detail. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿And they will not bring you any example﴾, with a strange question among their false questions, as if it were an example of falsehood, except that We bring you the true answer, which cannot be evaded, and which is better in meaning and in what it conveys than their question. Since tafsīr (exegesis) is the disclosure of what the speech indicates, it is placed in the position of its meaning, so they say: the tafsīr of this speech is such-and-such, just as it is said: its meaning is such-and-such. Or (wa-lā yaʾtūnaka) means with a strange condition and attribute, as they say: why was not this your attribute and condition? For example, that an angel be sent with you to warn with you, or a treasure be cast to you, or that you have a garden, or that the Qur'an be sent down to you all at once. Except that We give you what befits you in Our wisdom and will to be given, and what is better in disclosing what you were sent with and in proving its soundness. End quote. It was also said: (wa-lā yaʾtūnaka) with a doubt aimed at nullifying your matter, except that We bring you the truth that refutes the doubt of the people of ignorance and nullifies the speech of the people of deviation. The comparative (muḍaḍal ʿalayhi) is omitted, meaning: ﴿and better in exposition﴾ than their example, and their example is their saying: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"

﴿Those who are gathered﴾ (alladhīna yuḥsharūn). Al-Kirmānī said: it is connected to His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day﴾ (al-Furqān 25:24), etc. It was said: it may also be connected to His saying: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy among the criminals﴾ (al-Furqān 25:31). End quote. For this reason they objected, so Allah, exalted is He, informed about their state and what their affair would lead to in the Hereafter, by describing them as ﴿worse in place and further astray from the way﴾. The *bāʾ* (in *bi-al-ghamām*) is the *bāʾ* of circumstance (*ḥāl*), meaning "clouded over." Or it is the *bāʾ* of cause, meaning "because of the rising of the cloud from it," as if the cloud is that by which the sky is split, just as one says: "the hump was split with the knife, and it split by it." A parallel to this is His words: ﴿the sky will be split by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18]. Or it has the sense of *ʿan* (from) according to three opinions.

The difference between the causal *bāʾ* and *ʿan* is that *inshaqqa ʿan kadhā* means "it opened from that," while *inshaqqa bi-kadhā* means that thing is the one that splits it.

(p-495) *Wa-nuzzila al-malāʾikatu* means: down to the earth, because the reward and reckoning are taking place. *Al-ḥaqq* is an attribute of *al-mulk*, meaning "the established," because all sovereignty will be annulled on that day, and nothing will remain except His sovereignty, may He be exalted. The predicate of *al-mulk* is *yawmaʾidhin*. *Al-Raḥmān* is connected to *al-ḥaqq*, or it is explanatory, that is *li-al-Raḥmān*. It was said: the predicate is *li-al-Raḥmān*, and *yawmaʾidhin* is governed by *al-mulk*. It was said: the predicate is *al-ḥaqq*, and *li-al-Raḥmān* is connected to it, or it is explanatory. That day was hard for the disbelievers because of their entering the Fire and the terrors that come with it. His words *ʿalā al-kāfirīna* ("for the disbelievers") indicate that it is made easy for the believers. There is a hadith that it will be eased until it is lighter for the believer than an obligatory prayer he prayed in the world.

The general sense of *al-ẓālim* ("the wrongdoer") is apparent, since the *alif-lām* in it is generic (*li-al-jins*). This was said by Mujāhid and Abū Rajāʾ, and they said: "Fulān" is a euphemism (*kināya*) for Satan.

Ibn ʿAbbās and a group said: *al-ẓālim* here is ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, since he had inclined toward Islam, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf is the one referred to by *Fulān*. There had been a close friendship between them, and he (Ubayy) forbade him from Islam, and he (ʿUqba) obeyed him. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās the opposite of this view. It was said: the occasion of revelation was ʿUqba and Ubayy. It was said: ʿUqba was a close friend of Umayya, and ʿUqba embraced Islam. Umayya said: "My face is forbidden to your face if you pledge allegiance to Muḥammad." So he disbelieved and apostatized to please Umayya, and so it was revealed. This was said by al-Shaʿbī. He mentioned ʿUqba's offensive conduct toward the Messenger, which was the reason the Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "I will not meet you outside Mecca without striking your head with the sword." So ʿUqba was killed on the Day of Badr, in cold blood; he commanded ʿAlī, who struck his neck. Ubayy ibn Khalaf was killed on the Day of Uḥud in single combat.

The purpose is to mention the terror of the Day of Resurrection, through the regret of the wrongdoer and his wish that he had not obeyed his friend who used to command him to wrongdoing. There is no wrongdoer except that he generally has a special friend, referred to as "Fulān." The apparent meaning is that the wrongdoer (*yaʿaḍḍu ʿalā yadayhi*) does the act of one who is regretful and grieving. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "He eats his hands up to the elbows, then they grow back, and he continues like this, whenever he eats them they grow back." It was said: it is a metaphor (*majāz*) used to express bewilderment, grief, regret, and sorrow. The lexicographers reported that one who is sorrowful, grieving, and remorseful bites his thumb out of regret. The poet said:

> *She slapped her cheek with light red (wine) cups;*
> *they received from them the torment of white, torturing ones.*
>
> *The jujube complained of the daisy's blossom,*
> *and the rose complained of the jujube's freshness.*

And in the proverb: "He eats his hands in regret and sheds tears of blood." Al-Zamakhsharī said: biting the fingertips and the hands, falling into the hand, eating the fingers, grinding the teeth, and their variants, are all euphemisms (*kināyāt*) for rage and anguish, because they are among their accompaniments. So the accompaniment is mentioned and the thing accompanied is indicated by it, and the speech is elevated thereby to a level of eloquence, and the listener finds in himself an awe and admiration that he does not find in the plain statement of the thing referred to. End of quotation. The poet said about grinding the teeth:

> *He refused humiliation, while al-Nuʿmān was grinding his teeth*
> *against him, and the swords were his refuges.*

*Yaqūlu* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: saying "Oh, would that I..." If the *alif-lām* in *al-rasūl* is for a known referent (*ʿahd*), the meaning is that ʿUqba wished that he had accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ) and followed the path of truth. If the *alif-lām* is generic, the meaning is that he wished to follow the path of the Messenger, which is faith. Then *al-rasūl* is generic, because every wrongdoer has been obligated to follow what a messenger from God brought, until the Muḥammadan community came and abrogated all previous religions, so after its coming no religion is accepted other than what it brought.

Then he calls out with woe and regret, saying: *yā waylatā*, meaning "Oh, my destruction!" Like His words: ﴿Oh, my regret over what I neglected in the side of God﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Quṭayb read *yā waylatī* with a *kasra* on the *tāʾ*, and the *yāʾ* is the *yāʾ* of possession (*iḍāfa*), which is the original form, because a man calls out to his woe, which is his destruction, saying to it: "Come, this is your time." A group read it with *imāla* (inclination of the vowel). Abū ʿAlī said: leaving out the *imāla* is better, because this word originally had a *yāʾ*, and the *kasra* was changed to a *fatḥa* and the *yāʾ* to an *alif*, fleeing from the *yāʾ*. Whoever uses *imāla* returns to what he originally fled from.

*Fulān* is a euphemism for a proper name and is inflected. *Fulu* is a euphemism for an indefinite human, like "O man (*yā rajul*)," and it is restricted to vocative use. *Fulah* in the sense of "O woman" is similar. The final letter of *fulu* is a *yāʾ* or a *wāw*, and it is not a truncated form of *Fulān*, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. Ibn ʿUṣfūr, Ibn Mālik, and the author of *al-Basīṭ* erred in saying that *fulu* is a euphemism for a proper name, like *Fulān*. Sībawayh's book contains what we have said, by transmission from the Arabs.

*Al-dhikr* is the remembrance of God, or the Qur'an, or the admonition. The apparent meaning is to take Satan in his literal sense, because it is he who whispered to him in the friendship of the one who misled him, so He named him Satan, because he misleads just as Satan misleads. Then He abandoned him and did not benefit him in the end. This sentence may be part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and it may be a report from God's speech, indicating the manner of their misguidance and warning against Satan, who brought them to that point. In the authentic hadith, the good companion is likened to musk and the bad companion to the one who blows the bellows.

The apparent meaning is that the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to his Lord, and his report that his people, the Quraysh, abandoned the Qur'an, is something that happened to him in the world. This is evident from his turning to it, consoling and comforting himself with His words: ﴿Thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾, and that He is sufficient as a guide and helper. So it is a promise from Him of victory. This statement by the Messenger, and his complaint in it, is a warning to his people. A group, including Abū Muslim, said that it is his (ﷺ) statement in the Hereafter, like His words: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you against these as a witness?﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 41].

The apparent meaning of *mahjūran* is "abandoned," meaning abandoned from belief in it, rejected and cast away from being heard, with a *fatḥa* on the *hāʾ*. This was said by Mujāhid, al-Nakhaʿī, and their followers. It was also said: it is from *al-hujr* (abuse or incoherent speech), and the implication is that it is *mahjūran fīhi* ("abused in it"), meaning that it is false. The myths of the ancients are that when they heard it they would make senseless noise in it, like His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise over it﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 26].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is also possible that *al-mahjūr* has the sense of *al-hajr* (abandonment), like *al-malḥūd* and *al-maʿqūl*, and the meaning is that they took it as abandonment. And *al-ʿadūw* may be singular or plural. End of quotation.

And [the verb] (hādiyan) and (naṣīran) are in the accusative, either as ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) or as tamyīz (accusative of specification). "They said," that is, the disbelievers, in the manner of a demand (iqtirāḥ) and an objection (i'tirāḍ) that indicates their aversion to the truth. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Here (nuzzila) means only (unzila), like (khubbira) meaning (ukhbira). Otherwise it would be self-contradictory." End quote.

He said that (nuzzila) means (unzila) because (nuzzila), in his view, originally implies distribution (tafrīq). So if he left it with its original sense of distribution, he would contradict himself. As for His saying (jumlatan wāḥidatan), we have established that (nuzzila) does not necessarily imply distribution, because the doubling (taḍ'īf) in it, in our view, is synonymous with the hamza (of causation). We have explained this at the beginning of Āl ʿImrān. The speakers of this were the Quraysh disbelievers, who said: "If this were from Allah, it would have been sent down all at once, as the Torah and the Gospel were." It was also said that those who said this were the Jews, but this view is of no use, because the matter of the argument from it and its miraculous nature does not differ whether it is revealed all at once or in parts. Rather, its miraculous nature is more evident in its being revealed in parts, since they were challenged to produce a surah like it. Had it been revealed all at once and they were challenged to produce something like what was revealed, they would have been more incapable than when they were challenged to produce a surah of it and they failed.

The referent of "this" (al-mushār ilayhi) is not mentioned. It was said: it is from the words of the disbelievers, and they pointed to the Torah and the Gospel, meaning: a revelation like the revelation of those divine books, all at once. Then (linuthabbita bihi fu'adaka), "that We may strengthen your heart thereby," is a causal clause for an omitted element, meaning: We divided it over times, "that We may strengthen your heart thereby." It was also said: it is a new sentence from the speech of Allah, not from their speech. Since their statement implied the meaning "why was it revealed in parts?", the words "thus" (kadhālika) refer to the distribution, meaning: "thus" it was revealed in parts.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The wisdom in it is that by distributing it We strengthen your heart so that you understand it and memorise it, because the one who receives knowledge can only strengthen his heart to retain knowledge bit by bit, part after part. Had it been cast upon him all at once, he would have been unable to retain it. The Messenger (peace be upon him) differed in his condition from the condition of Dawūd, Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them), since he was unlettered and could not write, whereas they could read and write. So he had no choice but to receive and memorise, and it was revealed to him in portions over twenty years. It was also said: over twenty-three years. Also, it would descend according to events and in response to questioners, and because some of it was abrogated (mansūkh) and some of it abrogating (nāsikh), and this could only be done with what was revealed in parts. End quote.

The lām in (linuthabbita bihi) is the lām of purpose. Abū Ḥātim said: it is the lām of oath, and the implied meaning is "by Allah, He will surely strengthen," so the nūn was dropped and the lām was given a kasra. End quote. This is a view that is extremely weak. He (Abū Ḥātim) inclined toward the opinion of al-Akhfash that the answer of an oath may be introduced by the lām of kay (purpose), and he took as an example: "and that the hearts of [those who disbelieve in the Hereafter] may incline toward it" (al-Anʿām 6:113). But this is a weaker opinion. ʿAbdullah read (liyuthabbita) with the yā', meaning: that Allah may strengthen. (Wa-rattalnāhu), meaning: We made it distinct (faṣṣalnāhu). It was said: We made it clear (bayyannāhu). It was said: We explained it (fassarnāhu).

﴿And they will not bring you any example﴾ which they set forth by way of objection, as their comparison in this case with the Torah and the Gospel, except that We bring you the truth concerning it, and it is clearer in exposition and detail. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿And they will not bring you any example﴾, with a strange question among their false questions, as if it were an example of falsehood, except that We bring you the true answer, which cannot be evaded, and which is better in meaning and in what it conveys than their question. Since tafsīr (exegesis) is the disclosure of what the speech indicates, it is placed in the position of its meaning, so they say: the tafsīr of this speech is such-and-such, just as it is said: its meaning is such-and-such. Or (wa-lā yaʾtūnaka) means with a strange condition and attribute, as they say: why was not this your attribute and condition? For example, that an angel be sent with you to warn with you, or a treasure be cast to you, or that you have a garden, or that the Qur'an be sent down to you all at once. Except that We give you what befits you in Our wisdom and will to be given, and what is better in disclosing what you were sent with and in proving its soundness. End quote. It was also said: (wa-lā yaʾtūnaka) with a doubt aimed at nullifying your matter, except that We bring you the truth that refutes the doubt of the people of ignorance and nullifies the speech of the people of deviation. The comparative (muḍaḍal ʿalayhi) is omitted, meaning: ﴿and better in exposition﴾ than their example, and their example is their saying: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"

﴿Those who are gathered﴾ (alladhīna yuḥsharūn). Al-Kirmānī said: it is connected to His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day﴾ (al-Furqān 25:24), etc. It was said: it may also be connected to His saying: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy among the criminals﴾ (al-Furqān 25:31). End quote. What appears evident is that when they objected concerning the discourse of the Qur'an and its being revealed in parts, their speech implied that they were people of guidance and goodness, and that they were on the straight path. For this reason they objected, so Allah, exalted is He, informed about their state and what their affair would lead to in the Hereafter, by describing them as ﴿worse in place and further astray from the way﴾. Apparently, the disbelievers will be gathered on their faces, by being dragged upon their faces. In a ḥadīth: "He who made them walk on their feet is able to make them walk on their faces." This is the view of the majority. It was also said that it is a metaphor for extreme humiliation, disgrace and shame. It was also said that it is from the Arab saying: "So-and-so passed on his face" when he did not know where he went. It is said: "He went on his face" when he hastened, heading for his destination. And (sharr) and (aḍall) are not in their usual sense of comparison. The words (sharrun makānan), meaning "worse in station," correspond to His saying (khayrun mustaqarran), "better in abode," and it is possible that by place (makān) is meant rank and nobility, not a dwelling. They parsed (alladhīna) as the subject, and the clause (ulāʾika) as the predicate. In my view it is also permissible that (alladhīna) be the predicate of an omitted subject, since the disbelievers and what they said were previously mentioned, so He said, to humiliate them and to make them hear of what their state will lead to: "They are those who will be gathered," then He resumed with informative speech about them, saying: ﴿Those are worse in place﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verse 35–44 (part 1 of 2):

(p-498) ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and appointed with him his brother Aaron as a minister.﴾ ﴿Then We said: "Go to the people who denied Our signs." So We destroyed them with complete destruction.﴾ ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind. And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them.﴾ ﴿And to each We presented examples, and to each We applied total destruction.﴾ ﴿And they have certainly passed by the town that was rained upon with a rain of evil. Did they not see it? Rather, they did not expect resurrection.﴾ ﴿And when they see you, they take you only in ridicule: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿He had almost led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in adhering to them. But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god? Would you be responsible for him?﴾ ﴿Or do you suppose that most of them hear or understand? They are not but like cattle; rather, they are further astray in the way.﴾

When the denial of the Quraysh and the disbelievers of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought had preceded, Allah, the Exalted, mentioned what contains consolation for the Messenger and intimidation for the deniers, and a reminder to them that there would befall them what befell the earlier nations of total annihilation when they denied their messengers. Therefore it was fitting that He first mentioned the one to whom His Book was sent all at once, and despite that they disbelieved and denied it; likewise, these people, if the Qur'an were sent down to him in one go, they would deny and disbelieve just as the people of Moses denied.

"Al-Kitab" here is the Torah, and "Harun" is a substitute (badal) or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan). It is possible that "ma'ahu" is the second object of "ja'alna," and that "wazIran" is a second object too. Ministry does not contradict prophethood, for at one time there were prophets who supported one another. Those sent to were the Copts and Pharaoh. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: they went and conveyed the message, but they denied them. "Fa-dammarnahum": destruction (tadmir) is the most severe annihilation, and its origin is breaking a thing in a way that it cannot be repaired. The story of Moses and those sent to him is mentioned in various places fully; here it is abridged, with a concise mention of its beginning and end, because by this it establishes the proof through the sending of the messengers and the deserving of destruction through their denial.

Ali, al-Hasan and Maslamah ibn Muharib read "fa-dammira-hum" as an imperative addressed to Moses and Aaron. Also from Ali, the same, except that it is emphasized with the heavy nun. Also from him "fa-dammira" as a command to both of them, with "bihim" with the preposition ba, and the meaning of the command is: be the cause of their destruction.

"Wa-qawma Nuh" is in the accusative by the rule of ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun), and the accusative is preferred because the verbal clauses preceded it. In this case "lamma" is an adverb according to the view of al-Farisi. But if it is a particle of obligation for obligation, then the apparent reading is that "aghraqnahum" is the answer of "lamma," so it does not explain a governing verb for "qawma," and it is then coordinated with the object in "fa-dammarnahum," or it is accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is "udhkur" (remember). Al-Hawfi permitted all three possibilities.

"Lamma kadhdhabu al-rusul": they denied Noah and those before him, or his denial is made a denial of all; or they did not see the sending of messengers, like the Brahmins. The apparent reading is that "wa-'Adan" is coordinated with "wa-qawma." Abu Ishaq said: it may be coordinated with the hā' and mīm in "wa-ja'alnahum li-l-nasi ayah." He said: it is also permissible that it is coordinated with "al-zalimin," since the interpretation is "We promised the wrongdoers punishment and promised 'Ad and Thamud." Abdullah, Amr ibn Maymun, al-Hasan and Isa read "wa-Thamud" as non-diptote (ghayr munsarif).

"Wa-ashab al-Rass." Ibn Abbas said: they are the people of Thamud. This is far-fetched because it is coordinated with Thamud, since coordination requires difference. Qatadah said: the people of a town in Yamamah called "al-Rass" and "al-Falaj." It is said: they killed their prophet and so were destroyed, and they were the remnant of Thamud and the people of Salih. Ka'b, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: a well in Antioch of Syria in which the companion of Ya-Sin was killed, who was Habib al-Najjar. It is said: they killed their prophet and threw him into a well, that is, they pushed him into it.

Wahb and al-Kalbi said: the companions of the Rass and the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah) are two peoples to whom a messenger was sent: Shu'ayb was sent to the companions of the Rass, and they were a people of idol-worshippers and owners of wells and livestock. He invited them to Islam, and they persisted in their rebellion and in harming him. Then while they were around the Rass, which is an unlined well, [the ground] collapsed beneath them. From Abu Ubaydah: it caved in on them, and they were swallowed up with their dwellings. Ali said, as related by al-Tha'labi: a people who worshipped a pine tree called Shah Darakht; they threw their prophet into a well they had dug for him, in a long narration. It is said: they were the companions of the Prophet Handhalah ibn Safwan (ﷺ). They were afflicted by the 'anqa', which is the largest of birds, named so for the length of its neck, and it used to dwell on their mountain called Fajj; it would swoop down on their children and snatch them when hunting was scarce for it. So Handhalah invoked against it and lightning struck it. Then they killed Handhalah and were destroyed. It is said: they are the people of the Trench (al-Ukhdud), and the Rass is the Trench. Ibn Abbas said: the Rass is the well of Adharbayjan. It is said: the Rass is the area between Najran, Yemen and Hadramawt. It is said: a people to whom Allah sent prophets, whom they killed, and they burned their bones in a well. It is said: a people to whom a prophet was sent, whom they ate. It is said: a people whose women were lesbians. It is said: the Rass is water and palm trees belonging to Banu Asad. It is said: the Rass is a river in the lands of the East, to which Allah sent a prophet from the offspring of Judah, son of Jacob, and they denied him. He remained among them for a time, then complained to Allah about them. They dug a well for him and lowered him into it, saying: "We hope that our God will be pleased with us." So for most of their day they would hear the groaning of their prophet. He prayed for his soul to be taken quickly, and he died, and a black cloud overshadowed them and melted them as lead melts.

Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The people of the Rass seized their prophet, threw him into a well, and sealed a rock over him. There was a black slave who had believed in him who used to bring food to that well, and Allah would help him lift that rock, and he would take out what would nourish him, then return the rock. Until Allah one day cast sleep upon the ears of that black man for fourteen years, and the people of the town brought out their prophet, and they believed in him." In a long narration. Al-Tabari said: it is possible that they disbelieved after that, so Allah mentioned them in this verse. The disagreement about the companions of the Rass is great; if what Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b related were sound, it would be the saying that cannot be disputed. (Summary of these sayings:) they are a people whom Allah destroyed for denying the one sent to them.

"Wa-qurunan bayna dhalika": this is a vagueness whose reality none knows except Allah. "Dhalika" refers to those previously mentioned; therefore "bayn" is fittingly applied to it without anything being coordinated to it, as if it were said: "between those mentioned." The speaker may mention various things and then point to them. The first "kullan" is in the accusative by ishtighal, meaning: "and We warned each" or "We admonished each"; the second is an object of "tabbarna," because it took no object; this is clear grammar. The meaning of "daraba al-amthal": He explained to them the wondrous stories of the ancients and described to them what their denial of their prophets led to, of Allah's punishment and His destruction of them, so that they might be guided by the striking of examples, but they were not guided. He who made the pronoun in "lahu" refer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is far off; he said: the meaning is "We struck for the Messenger every example," and on this "kullan" is accusative by "daraba-na," and "al-amthal" is a substitute for "kullan." The pronoun in "wa-laqad ataw" refers to the Quraysh, who used to pass by Sodom, one of the towns of the people of Lot, on their trade journeys to Syria. There were five towns; Allah destroyed four of them and one remained, which is Zughar, whose people did not do that deed; so said Ibn Abbas. "Matar al-su'" is the stones that were rained down on them from the sky, and they perished. Abraham (peace be upon him) used to call out advice to them: "O Sodom, a day from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is for you; I forbid you from exposing yourselves to punishment from Allah." The meaning of "ataw" is "passed by," therefore it is followed by "ʿala." He used the singular "al-qaryah" though they were towns, because Sodom was the mother of those (p-500) towns and the greatest of them. Makki said: the pronoun in "ataw" refers to those who took the Qur'an as abandoned. End of quote; they are the Quraysh. "Matar" is in the accusative as a second object of "ummirat," in the sense of "were given," or as a verbal noun with its extra letters omitted, meaning: the raining of evil.

"Afalam yakunu yarawnaha": that is, they look at what is in it of lessons and traces indicating what vengeance befell it, as He said: "And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night" [al-Saffat: 137], and He said: "And indeed they were on a clear highway" [al-Hijr: 79]. It is a question whose meaning is amazement. Despite that, they did not take warning by seeing it, that there would befall them in this world what befell those; rather they were disbelievers who did not believe in resurrection, so they did not anticipate the punishment of the Hereafter. He placed "hope" in the position of "expectation," because only one who believes expects the outcome; therefore they did not reflect or ponder, and passed by it as their caravans passed. Or: they do not hope for "nushur" (resurrection) as believers hope for it, out of their longing for the reward of their deeds. Or: they do not fear it, according to the Tihami dialect. Zayd ibn Ali read "muttirat" as triliteral in the passive voice, with "matara" being transitive. The poet said:

"Like one whose wadi after drought is rained upon."

Abu al-Simak read "matar al-su'" with a dammah on the sin.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-Furqan, verses 35–44 (part 2 of 2):

﴿When they see you, they take you only in mockery﴾. The polytheists did not confine themselves to denying the prophethood of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) and refusing to believe in him. They went further, adding ridicule and contempt, to the point that some of them would say to others: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The word ﴿in﴾ is a negating particle (in) and it is the response clause (jawab, the main clause that completes a conditional) of ﴿idha﴾ (when). ﴿Idha﴾ is distinctive in that when its response clause is negated by ﴿ma﴾ or ﴿la﴾, the particle ﴿fa'﴾ (then) does not enter it, unlike other conditional particles, which must take ﴿fa'﴾ with ﴿ma﴾ and ﴿la﴾. With ﴿idha﴾, the present-tense verb is in the indicative. So if the negating ﴿in﴾ occurs in the response to a conditional other than ﴿idha﴾, ﴿fa'﴾ is necessary, as with the negating ﴿ma﴾.

The meaning of ﴿huzuwan﴾ (in mockery) is "in the place of mockery," or "one who is mocked." Before ﴿a-hadha﴾ (Is this...?) there is an implied verb of saying, meaning "they say." Some hold that the response to ﴿idha﴾ is the implied speech: ﴿When they see you﴾ they say, ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The clause ﴿in yattakhidhunaka﴾ (they take you) is a parenthetical clause between ﴿idha﴾ and its response.

It is said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. Whenever he saw the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), he would say: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The verb is in the plural to magnify the ugliness of his act, or because a group was with him who said the same. The apparent meaning is that the sayers were a large group. This interrogative expresses belittlement and contempt on their part. They expressed it in the form of acknowledgment and affirmation, ﴿God has sent as a messenger﴾, while they were in utter denial and rejection, in mockery and ridicule. Had they not been mocking, they would have said: "This one claims or asserts that he has been sent as a messenger from God."

Their statement ﴿He almost led us astray﴾ is evidence of the great effort the Messenger of God (ﷺ) exerted in calling them, and of his expending the utmost of his strength and capacity in seeking their goodwill, along with presenting signs and miracles. To their own claim, they almost abandoned their religion for the religion of Islam, were it not for their excessive obstinacy and their clinging to worship of their gods. The particle ﴿law-la﴾ (were it not) in such speech functions, in meaning though not in form, as a restriction of an absolute ruling. This is stated by al-Zamakhshari.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Mockery is either of appearance, in which case he was better than them in physical form, or of attribute, which is impossible, because the attribute by which he was distinguished from them is the manifestation of the miracle upon him and not upon them. Since they could not discredit his argument, in reality they are the ones who deserve to be mocked. Then, out of their shamelessness, they reversed the matter and mocked the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). End of quotation.

It is said: The verse also indicates that, with the manifestation of his argument (peace and blessings be upon him), they became like madmen against whom he had prevailed. They first mocked him, then they described him as one who ﴿almost led us astray﴾ from our doctrine, were it not that we confronted him with stubbornness and persistence. This indicates that they conceded to him the strength of his argument and the perfection of his intellect. Their combining mockery with this perplexed claim shows that they were bewildered about his affair: at times they mocked him, and at other times they described him with what befits only a complete scholar.

﴿But they will soon know﴾ is a threat and an indication that they cannot escape Him, however long the respite lasts. The threat must befall them, so the delay should not deceive them. When they said ﴿He almost led us astray﴾, the statement ﴿Who is further astray in the way?﴾ came. That is: it will become clear to them who is the misleader and who is the one who goes astray, by witnessing the punishment from which there is no escape. The apparent reading is that ﴿man﴾ (who) is interrogative, and ﴿adall﴾ (more astray) is its predicate. The clause is in the position of the object of ﴿ya'lamun﴾ (they know), whether that verb takes one object or two. It is also possible that ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, the object of ﴿ya'lamun﴾, and ﴿adall﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "he is more astray." The omission of this pronoun results from the lengthening found in the Arab saying: "I am not the one who is saying to you, 'equal'."

﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ This is a statement of despair regarding their faith, and an indication to him (peace be upon him) that he should not grieve over them. It also informs that they, in their ignorance of benefits and their scant consideration of consequences, are like cattle. Then He mentions that they are ﴿further astray in the way﴾ than the livestock, in that they have understanding but abandon its use in what would save them from God's punishment. The livestock have no way to understand benefits. The word ﴿arayta﴾ (have you seen) is an interrogative of wonder at the ignorance of one in such a state. ﴿Ilahahu﴾ (his god) is the first object of ﴿ittakhadha﴾ (took), and ﴿hawahu﴾ (his desire) is the second, meaning he has placed his desire in the position of the god he worships, so it follows what is in his desire. The meaning is that he took as a god nothing but his desire. Reversing the construction (by making the desire the agent) is not good, since it would require that the one who took his desire as his god... and the verse is a case of poetic necessity and rare speech, so the speech of God is to be exonerated from it. A man used to worship an idol, and whenever he saw a better one, he threw it away and took the better one. It is said: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, who, whenever he desired something, worshipped it. Desire is the inclination of the heart toward something. ﴿Will you then be a guardian over him?﴾ means: will you compel him to abandon his desire, or will you protect him from his great ignorance?

Some people of Medina read ﴿man ittakhadha alihatan﴾ (whoever has taken gods), with tanwin (nunation) and in the plural. In it there is a shift in which ﴿hawahu﴾ becomes kinds, names of different genera, so that each genus of his desire is another god. Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿ilahatan﴾ (a deity) on the pattern fi'alah, and in it too there is a shift: his desire is a deity, in the sense of an object of worship, because it means "one who is worshipped." The ta' in it is for emphasis, which is why it takes tanwin. It is also said: Rather, ﴿ilahah﴾ is the sun, and it is called ﴿ulahah﴾ with a dammah on the hamza. It is not diptote, due to being a proper noun and feminine. But since it is among the words that take the definite article in some dialects, it came to be like what contains the article, and then it was removed. Therefore it takes tanwin and becomes like adjectives, so it is indefinite. This is stated by the author of al-Lawami'.

The first object of ﴿ara'ayta﴾ is ﴿man﴾, and the interrogative clause is in the position of the second object. The discussion of ﴿ara'ayta﴾ was presented at the beginning of al-An'am. The meaning of ﴿wakilan﴾ (a guardian) is: can you call them to guidance, so that you rely upon Him and compel them to Islam?

﴿Am﴾ (or) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and according to the correct view it is to be parsed as ﴿bal﴾ (rather) plus the interrogative hamza. As if He said: "Rather, do you suppose that..." This blame is so severe that it was introduced by turning away from the previous blame to it, namely that they are deprived of hearing and reason, since they do not lend an ear to hearing the truth, nor do they reflect with their intellect. They are likened to the livestock, which are a proverb for heedlessness and error. This is denied of most of them, because among them are those for whom happiness had preceded, so they became Muslims. They are described as further astray than the livestock, because the livestock submit to their owners, recognize who treats them well from who mistreats them, seek their benefit and avoid their harm, and find their way to their pastures and watering places. But they do not submit to their Lord, do not recognize His kindness to them, do not desire the reward which is the greatest benefit, do not guard against the punishment which is the greatest harm, and are not guided to the truth.
