Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The people of the Rass seized their prophet, threw him into a well, and sealed a rock over him. There was a black slave who had believed in him who used to bring food to that well, and Allah would help him lift that rock, and he would take out what would nourish him, then return the rock. Until Allah one day cast sleep upon the ears of that black man for fourteen years, and the people of the town brought out their prophet, and they believed in him." In a long narration. Al-Tabari said: it is possible that they disbelieved after that, so Allah mentioned them in this verse. The disagreement about the companions of the Rass is great; if what Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b related were sound, it would be the saying that cannot be disputed. (Summary of these sayings:) they are a people whom Allah destroyed for denying the one sent to them.

"Wa-qurunan bayna dhalika": this is a vagueness whose reality none knows except Allah. "Dhalika" refers to those previously mentioned; therefore "bayn" is fittingly applied to it without anything being coordinated to it, as if it were said: "between those mentioned." The speaker may mention various things and then point to them. The first "kullan" is in the accusative by ishtighal, meaning: "and We warned each" or "We admonished each"; the second is an object of "tabbarna," because it took no object; this is clear grammar. The meaning of "daraba al-amthal": He explained to them the wondrous stories of the ancients and described to them what their denial of their prophets led to, of Allah's punishment and His destruction of them, so that they might be guided by the striking of examples, but they were not guided. He who made the pronoun in "lahu" refer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is far off; he said: the meaning is "We struck for the Messenger every example," and on this "kullan" is accusative by "daraba-na," and "al-amthal" is a substitute for "kullan." The pronoun in "wa-laqad ataw" refers to the Quraysh, who used to pass by Sodom, one of the towns of the people of Lot, on their trade journeys to Syria. There were five towns; Allah destroyed four of them and one remained, which is Zughar, whose people did not do that deed; so said Ibn Abbas. "Matar al-su'" is the stones that were rained down on them from the sky, and they perished. Abraham (peace be upon him) used to call out advice to them: "O Sodom, a day from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is for you; I forbid you from exposing yourselves to punishment from Allah." The meaning of "ataw" is "passed by," therefore it is followed by "ʿala." He used the singular "al-qaryah" though they were towns, because Sodom was the mother of those (p-500) towns and the greatest of them. Makki said: the pronoun in "ataw" refers to those who took the Qur'an as abandoned. End of quote; they are the Quraysh. "Matar" is in the accusative as a second object of "ummirat," in the sense of "were given," or as a verbal noun with its extra letters omitted, meaning: the raining of evil.

"Afalam yakunu yarawnaha": that is, they look at what is in it of lessons and traces indicating what vengeance befell it, as He said: "And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night" [al-Saffat: 137], and He said: "And indeed they were on a clear highway" [al-Hijr: 79]. It is a question whose meaning is amazement. Despite that, they did not take warning by seeing it, that there would befall them in this world what befell those; rather they were disbelievers who did not believe in resurrection, so they did not anticipate the punishment of the Hereafter. He placed "hope" in the position of "expectation," because only one who believes expects the outcome; therefore they did not reflect or ponder, and passed by it as their caravans passed. Or: they do not hope for "nushur" (resurrection) as believers hope for it, out of their longing for the reward of their deeds. Or: they do not fear it, according to the Tihami dialect. Zayd ibn Ali read "muttirat" as triliteral in the passive voice, with "matara" being transitive. The poet said:

"Like one whose wadi after drought is rained upon."

Abu al-Simak read "matar al-su'" with a dammah on the sin.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-Furqan, verses 35–44 (part 2 of 2):

﴿When they see you, they take you only in mockery﴾. The polytheists did not confine themselves to denying the prophethood of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) and refusing to believe in him. They went further, adding ridicule and contempt, to the point that some of them would say to others: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The word ﴿in﴾ is a negating particle (in) and it is the response clause (jawab, the main clause that completes a conditional) of ﴿idha﴾ (when). ﴿Idha﴾ is distinctive in that when its response clause is negated by ﴿ma﴾ or ﴿la﴾, the particle ﴿fa'﴾ (then) does not enter it, unlike other conditional particles, which must take ﴿fa'﴾ with ﴿ma﴾ and ﴿la﴾. With ﴿idha﴾, the present-tense verb is in the indicative. So if the negating ﴿in﴾ occurs in the response to a conditional other than ﴿idha﴾, ﴿fa'﴾ is necessary, as with the negating ﴿ma﴾.

The meaning of ﴿huzuwan﴾ (in mockery) is "in the place of mockery," or "one who is mocked." Before ﴿a-hadha﴾ (Is this...?) there is an implied verb of saying, meaning "they say." Some hold that the response to ﴿idha﴾ is the implied speech: ﴿When they see you﴾ they say, ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The clause ﴿in yattakhidhunaka﴾ (they take you) is a parenthetical clause between ﴿idha﴾ and its response.

It is said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. Whenever he saw the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), he would say: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The verb is in the plural to magnify the ugliness of his act, or because a group was with him who said the same. The apparent meaning is that the sayers were a large group. This interrogative expresses belittlement and contempt on their part. They expressed it in the form of acknowledgment and affirmation, ﴿God has sent as a messenger﴾, while they were in utter denial and rejection, in mockery and ridicule. Had they not been mocking, they would have said: "This one claims or asserts that he has been sent as a messenger from God."

Their statement ﴿He almost led us astray﴾ is evidence of the great effort the Messenger of God (ﷺ) exerted in calling them, and of his expending the utmost of his strength and capacity in seeking their goodwill, along with presenting signs and miracles. To their own claim, they almost abandoned their religion for the religion of Islam, were it not for their excessive obstinacy and their clinging to worship of their gods. The particle ﴿law-la﴾ (were it not) in such speech functions, in meaning though not in form, as a restriction of an absolute ruling. This is stated by al-Zamakhshari.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Mockery is either of appearance, in which case he was better than them in physical form, or of attribute, which is impossible, because the attribute by which he was distinguished from them is the manifestation of the miracle upon him and not upon them. Since they could not discredit his argument, in reality they are the ones who deserve to be mocked. Then, out of their shamelessness, they reversed the matter and mocked the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). End of quotation.

It is said: The verse also indicates that, with the manifestation of his argument (peace and blessings be upon him), they became like madmen against whom he had prevailed. They first mocked him, then they described him as one who ﴿almost led us astray﴾ from our doctrine, were it not that we confronted him with stubbornness and persistence. This indicates that they conceded to him the strength of his argument and the perfection of his intellect. Their combining mockery with this perplexed claim shows that they were bewildered about his affair: at times they mocked him, and at other times they described him with what befits only a complete scholar.

﴿But they will soon know﴾ is a threat and an indication that they cannot escape Him, however long the respite lasts. The threat must befall them, so the delay should not deceive them. When they said ﴿He almost led us astray﴾, the statement ﴿Who is further astray in the way?﴾ came. That is: it will become clear to them who is the misleader and who is the one who goes astray, by witnessing the punishment from which there is no escape. The apparent reading is that ﴿man﴾ (who) is interrogative, and ﴿adall﴾ (more astray) is its predicate. The clause is in the position of the object of ﴿ya'lamun﴾ (they know), whether that verb takes one object or two. It is also possible that ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, the object of ﴿ya'lamun﴾, and ﴿adall﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "he is more astray." The omission of this pronoun results from the lengthening found in the Arab saying: "I am not the one who is saying to you, 'equal'."

﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ This is a statement of despair regarding their faith, and an indication to him (peace be upon him) that he should not grieve over them. It also informs that they, in their ignorance of benefits and their scant consideration of consequences, are like cattle. Then He mentions that they are ﴿further astray in the way﴾ than the livestock, in that they have understanding but abandon its use in what would save them from God's punishment. The livestock have no way to understand benefits. The word ﴿arayta﴾ (have you seen) is an interrogative of wonder at the ignorance of one in such a state. ﴿Ilahahu﴾ (his god) is the first object of ﴿ittakhadha﴾ (took), and ﴿hawahu﴾ (his desire) is the second, meaning he has placed his desire in the position of the god he worships, so it follows what is in his desire. The meaning is that he took as a god nothing but his desire. Reversing the construction (by making the desire the agent) is not good, since it would require that the one who took his desire as his god... and the verse is a case of poetic necessity and rare speech, so the speech of God is to be exonerated from it. A man used to worship an idol, and whenever he saw a better one, he threw it away and took the better one. It is said: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, who, whenever he desired something, worshipped it. Desire is the inclination of the heart toward something. ﴿Will you then be a guardian over him?﴾ means: will you compel him to abandon his desire, or will you protect him from his great ignorance?

Some people of Medina read ﴿man ittakhadha alihatan﴾ (whoever has taken gods), with tanwin (nunation) and in the plural. In it there is a shift in which ﴿hawahu﴾ becomes kinds, names of different genera, so that each genus of his desire is another god. Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿ilahatan﴾ (a deity) on the pattern fi'alah, and in it too there is a shift: his desire is a deity, in the sense of an object of worship, because it means "one who is worshipped." The ta' in it is for emphasis, which is why it takes tanwin. It is also said: Rather, ﴿ilahah﴾ is the sun, and it is called ﴿ulahah﴾ with a dammah on the hamza. It is not diptote, due to being a proper noun and feminine. But since it is among the words that take the definite article in some dialects, it came to be like what contains the article, and then it was removed. Therefore it takes tanwin and becomes like adjectives, so it is indefinite. This is stated by the author of al-Lawami'.

The first object of ﴿ara'ayta﴾ is ﴿man﴾, and the interrogative clause is in the position of the second object. The discussion of ﴿ara'ayta﴾ was presented at the beginning of al-An'am. The meaning of ﴿wakilan﴾ (a guardian) is: can you call them to guidance, so that you rely upon Him and compel them to Islam?

﴿Am﴾ (or) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and according to the correct view it is to be parsed as ﴿bal﴾ (rather) plus the interrogative hamza. As if He said: "Rather, do you suppose that..." This blame is so severe that it was introduced by turning away from the previous blame to it, namely that they are deprived of hearing and reason, since they do not lend an ear to hearing the truth, nor do they reflect with their intellect. They are likened to the livestock, which are a proverb for heedlessness and error. This is denied of most of them, because among them are those for whom happiness had preceded, so they became Muslims. They are described as further astray than the livestock, because the livestock submit to their owners, recognize who treats them well from who mistreats them, seek their benefit and avoid their harm, and find their way to their pastures and watering places. But they do not submit to their Lord, do not recognize His kindness to them, do not desire the reward which is the greatest benefit, do not guard against the punishment which is the greatest harm, and are not guided to the truth.

(p-501)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verse 35–44 (part 1 of 2):

(p-498) ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and appointed with him his brother Aaron as a minister.﴾ ﴿Then We said: "Go to the people who denied Our signs." So We destroyed them with complete destruction.﴾ ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind. And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them.﴾ ﴿And to each We presented examples, and to each We applied total destruction.﴾ ﴿And they have certainly passed by the town that was rained upon with a rain of evil. Did they not see it? Rather, they did not expect resurrection.﴾ ﴿And when they see you, they take you only in ridicule: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿He had almost led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in adhering to them. But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god? Would you be responsible for him?﴾ ﴿Or do you suppose that most of them hear or understand? They are not but like cattle; rather, they are further astray in the way.﴾

When the denial of the Quraysh and the disbelievers of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought had preceded, Allah, the Exalted, mentioned what contains consolation for the Messenger and intimidation for the deniers, and a reminder to them that there would befall them what befell the earlier nations of total annihilation when they denied their messengers. Therefore it was fitting that He first mentioned the one to whom His Book was sent all at once, and despite that they disbelieved and denied it; likewise, these people, if the Qur'an were sent down to him in one go, they would deny and disbelieve just as the people of Moses denied.

"Al-Kitab" here is the Torah, and "Harun" is a substitute (badal) or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan). It is possible that "ma'ahu" is the second object of "ja'alna," and that "wazIran" is a second object too. Ministry does not contradict prophethood, for at one time there were prophets who supported one another. Those sent to were the Copts and Pharaoh. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: they went and conveyed the message, but they denied them. "Fa-dammarnahum": destruction (tadmir) is the most severe annihilation, and its origin is breaking a thing in a way that it cannot be repaired. The story of Moses and those sent to him is mentioned in various places fully; here it is abridged, with a concise mention of its beginning and end, because by this it establishes the proof through the sending of the messengers and the deserving of destruction through their denial.

Ali, al-Hasan and Maslamah ibn Muharib read "fa-dammira-hum" as an imperative addressed to Moses and Aaron. Also from Ali, the same, except that it is emphasized with the heavy nun. Also from him "fa-dammira" as a command to both of them, with "bihim" with the preposition ba, and the meaning of the command is: be the cause of their destruction.

"Wa-qawma Nuh" is in the accusative by the rule of ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun), and the accusative is preferred because the verbal clauses preceded it. In this case "lamma" is an adverb according to the view of al-Farisi. But if it is a particle of obligation for obligation, then the apparent reading is that "aghraqnahum" is the answer of "lamma," so it does not explain a governing verb for "qawma," and it is then coordinated with the object in "fa-dammarnahum," or it is accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is "udhkur" (remember). Al-Hawfi permitted all three possibilities.

"Lamma kadhdhabu al-rusul": they denied Noah and those before him, or his denial is made a denial of all; or they did not see the sending of messengers, like the Brahmins. The apparent reading is that "wa-'Adan" is coordinated with "wa-qawma." Abu Ishaq said: it may be coordinated with the hā' and mīm in "wa-ja'alnahum li-l-nasi ayah." He said: it is also permissible that it is coordinated with "al-zalimin," since the interpretation is "We promised the wrongdoers punishment and promised 'Ad and Thamud." Abdullah, Amr ibn Maymun, al-Hasan and Isa read "wa-Thamud" as non-diptote (ghayr munsarif).

"Wa-ashab al-Rass." Ibn Abbas said: they are the people of Thamud. This is far-fetched because it is coordinated with Thamud, since coordination requires difference. Qatadah said: the people of a town in Yamamah called "al-Rass" and "al-Falaj." It is said: they killed their prophet and so were destroyed, and they were the remnant of Thamud and the people of Salih. Ka'b, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: a well in Antioch of Syria in which the companion of Ya-Sin was killed, who was Habib al-Najjar. It is said: they killed their prophet and threw him into a well, that is, they pushed him into it.

Wahb and al-Kalbi said: the companions of the Rass and the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah) are two peoples to whom a messenger was sent: Shu'ayb was sent to the companions of the Rass, and they were a people of idol-worshippers and owners of wells and livestock. He invited them to Islam, and they persisted in their rebellion and in harming him. Then while they were around the Rass, which is an unlined well, [the ground] collapsed beneath them. From Abu Ubaydah: it caved in on them, and they were swallowed up with their dwellings. Ali said, as related by al-Tha'labi: a people who worshipped a pine tree called Shah Darakht; they threw their prophet into a well they had dug for him, in a long narration. It is said: they were the companions of the Prophet Handhalah ibn Safwan (ﷺ). They were afflicted by the 'anqa', which is the largest of birds, named so for the length of its neck, and it used to dwell on their mountain called Fajj; it would swoop down on their children and snatch them when hunting was scarce for it. So Handhalah invoked against it and lightning struck it. Then they killed Handhalah and were destroyed. It is said: they are the people of the Trench (al-Ukhdud), and the Rass is the Trench. Ibn Abbas said: the Rass is the well of Adharbayjan. It is said: the Rass is the area between Najran, Yemen and Hadramawt. It is said: a people to whom Allah sent prophets, whom they killed, and they burned their bones in a well. It is said: a people to whom a prophet was sent, whom they ate. It is said: a people whose women were lesbians. It is said: the Rass is water and palm trees belonging to Banu Asad. It is said: the Rass is a river in the lands of the East, to which Allah sent a prophet from the offspring of Judah, son of Jacob, and they denied him. He remained among them for a time, then complained to Allah about them. They dug a well for him and lowered him into it, saying: "We hope that our God will be pleased with us." So for most of their day they would hear the groaning of their prophet. He prayed for his soul to be taken quickly, and he died, and a black cloud overshadowed them and melted them as lead melts.

The omission of this pronoun results from the lengthening found in the Arab saying: "I am not the one who is saying to you, 'equal'."

﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ This is a statement of despair regarding their faith, and an indication to him (peace be upon him) that he should not grieve over them. It also informs that they, in their ignorance of benefits and their scant consideration of consequences, are like cattle. Then He mentions that they are ﴿further astray in the way﴾ than the livestock, in that they have understanding but abandon its use in what would save them from God's punishment. The livestock have no way to understand benefits. The word ﴿arayta﴾ (have you seen) is an interrogative of wonder at the ignorance of one in such a state. ﴿Ilahahu﴾ (his god) is the first object of ﴿ittakhadha﴾ (took), and ﴿hawahu﴾ (his desire) is the second, meaning he has placed his desire in the position of the god he worships, so it follows what is in his desire. The meaning is that he took as a god nothing but his desire. Reversing the construction (by making the desire the agent) is not good, since it would require that the one who took his desire as his god... and the verse is a case of poetic necessity and rare speech, so the speech of God is to be exonerated from it. A man used to worship an idol, and whenever he saw a better one, he threw it away and took the better one. It is said: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, who, whenever he desired something, worshipped it. Desire is the inclination of the heart toward something. ﴿Will you then be a guardian over him?﴾ means: will you compel him to abandon his desire, or will you protect him from his great ignorance?

Some people of Medina read ﴿man ittakhadha alihatan﴾ (whoever has taken gods), with tanwin (nunation) and in the plural. In it there is a shift in which ﴿hawahu﴾ becomes kinds, names of different genera, so that each genus of his desire is another god. Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿ilahatan﴾ (a deity) on the pattern fi'alah, and in it too there is a shift: his desire is a deity, in the sense of an object of worship, because it means "one who is worshipped." The ta' in it is for emphasis, which is why it takes tanwin. It is also said: Rather, ﴿ilahah﴾ is the sun, and it is called ﴿ulahah﴾ with a dammah on the hamza. It is not diptote, due to being a proper noun and feminine. But since it is among the words that take the definite article in some dialects, it came to be like what contains the article, and then it was removed. Therefore it takes tanwin and becomes like adjectives, so it is indefinite. This is stated by the author of al-Lawami'.

The first object of ﴿ara'ayta﴾ is ﴿man﴾, and the interrogative clause is in the position of the second object. The discussion of ﴿ara'ayta﴾ was presented at the beginning of al-An'am. The meaning of ﴿wakilan﴾ (a guardian) is: can you call them to guidance, so that you rely upon Him and compel them to Islam?

﴿Am﴾ (or) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and according to the correct view it is to be parsed as ﴿bal﴾ (rather) plus the interrogative hamza. As if He said: "Rather, do you suppose that..." This blame is so severe that it was introduced by turning away from the previous blame to it, namely that they are deprived of hearing and reason, since they do not lend an ear to hearing the truth, nor do they reflect with their intellect. They are likened to the livestock, which are a proverb for heedlessness and error. This is denied of most of them, because among them are those for whom happiness had preceded, so they became Muslims. They are described as further astray than the livestock, because the livestock submit to their owners, recognize who treats them well from who mistreats them, seek their benefit and avoid their harm, and find their way to their pastures and watering places. But they do not submit to their Lord, do not recognize His kindness to them, do not desire the reward which is the greatest benefit, do not guard against the punishment which is the greatest harm, and are not guided to the truth.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verse 35–44 (part 1 of 2):

(p-498) ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and appointed with him his brother Aaron as a minister.﴾ ﴿Then We said: "Go to the people who denied Our signs." So We destroyed them with complete destruction.﴾ ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind. And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them.﴾ ﴿And to each We presented examples, and to each We applied total destruction.﴾ ﴿And they have certainly passed by the town that was rained upon with a rain of evil. Did they not see it? Rather, they did not expect resurrection.﴾ ﴿And when they see you, they take you only in ridicule: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿He had almost led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in adhering to them. But they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in the way.﴾ ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god? Would you be responsible for him?﴾ ﴿Or do you suppose that most of them hear or understand? They are not but like cattle; rather, they are further astray in the way.﴾

When the denial of the Quraysh and the disbelievers of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought had preceded, Allah, the Exalted, mentioned what contains consolation for the Messenger and intimidation for the deniers, and a reminder to them that there would befall them what befell the earlier nations of total annihilation when they denied their messengers. Therefore it was fitting that He first mentioned the one to whom His Book was sent all at once, and despite that they disbelieved and denied it; likewise, these people, if the Qur'an were sent down to him in one go, they would deny and disbelieve just as the people of Moses denied.

"Al-Kitab" here is the Torah, and "Harun" is a substitute (badal) or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan). It is possible that "ma'ahu" is the second object of "ja'alna," and that "wazIran" is a second object too. Ministry does not contradict prophethood, for at one time there were prophets who supported one another. Those sent to were the Copts and Pharaoh. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: they went and conveyed the message, but they denied them. "Fa-dammarnahum": destruction (tadmir) is the most severe annihilation, and its origin is breaking a thing in a way that it cannot be repaired. The story of Moses and those sent to him is mentioned in various places fully; here it is abridged, with a concise mention of its beginning and end, because by this it establishes the proof through the sending of the messengers and the deserving of destruction through their denial.

Ali, al-Hasan and Maslamah ibn Muharib read "fa-dammira-hum" as an imperative addressed to Moses and Aaron. Also from Ali, the same, except that it is emphasized with the heavy nun. Also from him "fa-dammira" as a command to both of them, with "bihim" with the preposition ba, and the meaning of the command is: be the cause of their destruction.

"Wa-qawma Nuh" is in the accusative by the rule of ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun), and the accusative is preferred because the verbal clauses preceded it. In this case "lamma" is an adverb according to the view of al-Farisi. But if it is a particle of obligation for obligation, then the apparent reading is that "aghraqnahum" is the answer of "lamma," so it does not explain a governing verb for "qawma," and it is then coordinated with the object in "fa-dammarnahum," or it is accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is "udhkur" (remember). Al-Hawfi permitted all three possibilities.

"Lamma kadhdhabu al-rusul": they denied Noah and those before him, or his denial is made a denial of all; or they did not see the sending of messengers, like the Brahmins. The apparent reading is that "wa-'Adan" is coordinated with "wa-qawma." Abu Ishaq said: it may be coordinated with the hā' and mīm in "wa-ja'alnahum li-l-nasi ayah." He said: it is also permissible that it is coordinated with "al-zalimin," since the interpretation is "We promised the wrongdoers punishment and promised 'Ad and Thamud." Abdullah, Amr ibn Maymun, al-Hasan and Isa read "wa-Thamud" as non-diptote (ghayr munsarif).

"Wa-ashab al-Rass." Ibn Abbas said: they are the people of Thamud. This is far-fetched because it is coordinated with Thamud, since coordination requires difference. Qatadah said: the people of a town in Yamamah called "al-Rass" and "al-Falaj." It is said: they killed their prophet and so were destroyed, and they were the remnant of Thamud and the people of Salih. Ka'b, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: a well in Antioch of Syria in which the companion of Ya-Sin was killed, who was Habib al-Najjar. It is said: they killed their prophet and threw him into a well, that is, they pushed him into it.

Wahb and al-Kalbi said: the companions of the Rass and the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah) are two peoples to whom a messenger was sent: Shu'ayb was sent to the companions of the Rass, and they were a people of idol-worshippers and owners of wells and livestock. He invited them to Islam, and they persisted in their rebellion and in harming him. Then while they were around the Rass, which is an unlined well, [the ground] collapsed beneath them. From Abu Ubaydah: it caved in on them, and they were swallowed up with their dwellings. Ali said, as related by al-Tha'labi: a people who worshipped a pine tree called Shah Darakht; they threw their prophet into a well they had dug for him, in a long narration. It is said: they were the companions of the Prophet Handhalah ibn Safwan (ﷺ). They were afflicted by the 'anqa', which is the largest of birds, named so for the length of its neck, and it used to dwell on their mountain called Fajj; it would swoop down on their children and snatch them when hunting was scarce for it. So Handhalah invoked against it and lightning struck it. Then they killed Handhalah and were destroyed. It is said: they are the people of the Trench (al-Ukhdud), and the Rass is the Trench. Ibn Abbas said: the Rass is the well of Adharbayjan. It is said: the Rass is the area between Najran, Yemen and Hadramawt. It is said: a people to whom Allah sent prophets, whom they killed, and they burned their bones in a well. It is said: a people to whom a prophet was sent, whom they ate. It is said: a people whose women were lesbians. It is said: the Rass is water and palm trees belonging to Banu Asad. It is said: the Rass is a river in the lands of the East, to which Allah sent a prophet from the offspring of Judah, son of Jacob, and they denied him. He remained among them for a time, then complained to Allah about them. They dug a well for him and lowered him into it, saying: "We hope that our God will be pleased with us." So for most of their day they would hear the groaning of their prophet. He prayed for his soul to be taken quickly, and he died, and a black cloud overshadowed them and melted them as lead melts.

Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The people of the Rass seized their prophet, threw him into a well, and sealed a rock over him. There was a black slave who had believed in him who used to bring food to that well, and Allah would help him lift that rock, and he would take out what would nourish him, then return the rock. Until Allah one day cast sleep upon the ears of that black man for fourteen years, and the people of the town brought out their prophet, and they believed in him." In a long narration. Al-Tabari said: it is possible that they disbelieved after that, so Allah mentioned them in this verse. The disagreement about the companions of the Rass is great; if what Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b related were sound, it would be the saying that cannot be disputed. (Summary of these sayings:) they are a people whom Allah destroyed for denying the one sent to them.

"Wa-qurunan bayna dhalika": this is a vagueness whose reality none knows except Allah. "Dhalika" refers to those previously mentioned; therefore "bayn" is fittingly applied to it without anything being coordinated to it, as if it were said: "between those mentioned." The speaker may mention various things and then point to them. The first "kullan" is in the accusative by ishtighal, meaning: "and We warned each" or "We admonished each"; the second is an object of "tabbarna," because it took no object; this is clear grammar. The meaning of "daraba al-amthal": He explained to them the wondrous stories of the ancients and described to them what their denial of their prophets led to, of Allah's punishment and His destruction of them, so that they might be guided by the striking of examples, but they were not guided. He who made the pronoun in "lahu" refer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is far off; he said: the meaning is "We struck for the Messenger every example," and on this "kullan" is accusative by "daraba-na," and "al-amthal" is a substitute for "kullan." The pronoun in "wa-laqad ataw" refers to the Quraysh, who used to pass by Sodom, one of the towns of the people of Lot, on their trade journeys to Syria. There were five towns; Allah destroyed four of them and one remained, which is Zughar, whose people did not do that deed; so said Ibn Abbas. "Matar al-su'" is the stones that were rained down on them from the sky, and they perished. Abraham (peace be upon him) used to call out advice to them: "O Sodom, a day from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is for you; I forbid you from exposing yourselves to punishment from Allah." The meaning of "ataw" is "passed by," therefore it is followed by "ʿala." He used the singular "al-qaryah" though they were towns, because Sodom was the mother of those (p-500) towns and the greatest of them. Makki said: the pronoun in "ataw" refers to those who took the Qur'an as abandoned. End of quote; they are the Quraysh. "Matar" is in the accusative as a second object of "ummirat," in the sense of "were given," or as a verbal noun with its extra letters omitted, meaning: the raining of evil.

"Afalam yakunu yarawnaha": that is, they look at what is in it of lessons and traces indicating what vengeance befell it, as He said: "And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night" [al-Saffat: 137], and He said: "And indeed they were on a clear highway" [al-Hijr: 79]. It is a question whose meaning is amazement. Despite that, they did not take warning by seeing it, that there would befall them in this world what befell those; rather they were disbelievers who did not believe in resurrection, so they did not anticipate the punishment of the Hereafter. He placed "hope" in the position of "expectation," because only one who believes expects the outcome; therefore they did not reflect or ponder, and passed by it as their caravans passed. Or: they do not hope for "nushur" (resurrection) as believers hope for it, out of their longing for the reward of their deeds. Or: they do not fear it, according to the Tihami dialect. Zayd ibn Ali read "muttirat" as triliteral in the passive voice, with "matara" being transitive. The poet said:

"Like one whose wadi after drought is rained upon."

Abu al-Simak read "matar al-su'" with a dammah on the sin.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-Furqan, verses 35–44 (part 2 of 2):

﴿When they see you, they take you only in mockery﴾. The polytheists did not confine themselves to denying the prophethood of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) and refusing to believe in him. They went further, adding ridicule and contempt, to the point that some of them would say to others: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The word ﴿in﴾ is a negating particle (in) and it is the response clause (jawab, the main clause that completes a conditional) of ﴿idha﴾ (when). ﴿Idha﴾ is distinctive in that when its response clause is negated by ﴿ma﴾ or ﴿la﴾, the particle ﴿fa'﴾ (then) does not enter it, unlike other conditional particles, which must take ﴿fa'﴾ with ﴿ma﴾ and ﴿la﴾. With ﴿idha﴾, the present-tense verb is in the indicative. So if the negating ﴿in﴾ occurs in the response to a conditional other than ﴿idha﴾, ﴿fa'﴾ is necessary, as with the negating ﴿ma﴾.

The meaning of ﴿huzuwan﴾ (in mockery) is "in the place of mockery," or "one who is mocked." Before ﴿a-hadha﴾ (Is this...?) there is an implied verb of saying, meaning "they say." Some hold that the response to ﴿idha﴾ is the implied speech: ﴿When they see you﴾ they say, ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The clause ﴿in yattakhidhunaka﴾ (they take you) is a parenthetical clause between ﴿idha﴾ and its response.

It is said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. Whenever he saw the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), he would say: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The verb is in the plural to magnify the ugliness of his act, or because a group was with him who said the same. The apparent meaning is that the sayers were a large group. This interrogative expresses belittlement and contempt on their part. They expressed it in the form of acknowledgment and affirmation, ﴿God has sent as a messenger﴾, while they were in utter denial and rejection, in mockery and ridicule. Had they not been mocking, they would have said: "This one claims or asserts that he has been sent as a messenger from God."

Their statement ﴿He almost led us astray﴾ is evidence of the great effort the Messenger of God (ﷺ) exerted in calling them, and of his expending the utmost of his strength and capacity in seeking their goodwill, along with presenting signs and miracles. To their own claim, they almost abandoned their religion for the religion of Islam, were it not for their excessive obstinacy and their clinging to worship of their gods. The particle ﴿law-la﴾ (were it not) in such speech functions, in meaning though not in form, as a restriction of an absolute ruling. This is stated by al-Zamakhshari.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Mockery is either of appearance, in which case he was better than them in physical form, or of attribute, which is impossible, because the attribute by which he was distinguished from them is the manifestation of the miracle upon him and not upon them. Since they could not discredit his argument, in reality they are the ones who deserve to be mocked. Then, out of their shamelessness, they reversed the matter and mocked the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). End of quotation.

It is said: The verse also indicates that, with the manifestation of his argument (peace and blessings be upon him), they became like madmen against whom he had prevailed. They first mocked him, then they described him as one who ﴿almost led us astray﴾ from our doctrine, were it not that we confronted him with stubbornness and persistence. This indicates that they conceded to him the strength of his argument and the perfection of his intellect. Their combining mockery with this perplexed claim shows that they were bewildered about his affair: at times they mocked him, and at other times they described him with what befits only a complete scholar.

﴿But they will soon know﴾ is a threat and an indication that they cannot escape Him, however long the respite lasts. The threat must befall them, so the delay should not deceive them. When they said ﴿He almost led us astray﴾, the statement ﴿Who is further astray in the way?﴾ came. That is: it will become clear to them who is the misleader and who is the one who goes astray, by witnessing the punishment from which there is no escape. The apparent reading is that ﴿man﴾ (who) is interrogative, and ﴿adall﴾ (more astray) is its predicate. The clause is in the position of the object of ﴿ya'lamun﴾ (they know), whether that verb takes one object or two. It is also possible that ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, the object of ﴿ya'lamun﴾, and ﴿adall﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "he is more astray." The omission of this pronoun results from the lengthening found in the Arab saying: "I am not the one who is saying to you, 'equal'."

﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ This is a statement of despair regarding their faith, and an indication to him (peace be upon him) that he should not grieve over them. It also informs that they, in their ignorance of benefits and their scant consideration of consequences, are like cattle. Then He mentions that they are ﴿further astray in the way﴾ than the livestock, in that they have understanding but abandon its use in what would save them from God's punishment. The livestock have no way to understand benefits. The word ﴿arayta﴾ (have you seen) is an interrogative of wonder at the ignorance of one in such a state. ﴿Ilahahu﴾ (his god) is the first object of ﴿ittakhadha﴾ (took), and ﴿hawahu﴾ (his desire) is the second, meaning he has placed his desire in the position of the god he worships, so it follows what is in his desire. The meaning is that he took as a god nothing but his desire. Reversing the construction (by making the desire the agent) is not good, since it would require that the one who took his desire as his god... and the verse is a case of poetic necessity and rare speech, so the speech of God is to be exonerated from it. A man used to worship an idol, and whenever he saw a better one, he threw it away and took the better one. It is said: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, who, whenever he desired something, worshipped it. Desire is the inclination of the heart toward something. ﴿Will you then be a guardian over him?﴾ means: will you compel him to abandon his desire, or will you protect him from his great ignorance?

In it there is a shift in which ﴿hawahu﴾ becomes kinds, names of different genera, so that each genus of his desire is another god. The ta' in it is for emphasis, which is why it takes tanwin. It is also said: Rather, ﴿ilahah﴾ is the sun, and it is called ﴿ulahah﴾ with a dammah on the hamza. It is said: they killed their prophet and so were destroyed, and they were the remnant of Thamud and the people of Salih. Ka'b, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: a well in Antioch of Syria in which the companion of Ya-Sin was killed, who was Habib al-Najjar. It is said: they killed their prophet and threw him into a well, that is, they pushed him into it.

Wahb and al-Kalbi said: the companions of the Rass and the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah) are two peoples to whom a messenger was sent: Shu'ayb was sent to the companions of the Rass, and they were a people of idol-worshippers and owners of wells and livestock. He invited them to Islam, and they persisted in their rebellion and in harming him. Then while they were around the Rass, which is an unlined well, [the ground] collapsed beneath them. From Abu Ubaydah: it caved in on them, and they were swallowed up with their dwellings. Ali said, as related by al-Tha'labi: a people who worshipped a pine tree called Shah Darakht; they threw their prophet into a well they had dug for him, in a long narration. It is said: they were the companions of the Prophet Handhalah ibn Safwan (ﷺ). They were afflicted by the 'anqa', which is the largest of birds, named so for the length of its neck, and it used to dwell on their mountain called Fajj; it would swoop down on their children and snatch them when hunting was scarce for it. So Handhalah invoked against it and lightning struck it. Then they killed Handhalah and were destroyed. It is said: they are the people of the Trench (al-Ukhdud), and the Rass is the Trench. Ibn Abbas said: the Rass is the well of Adharbayjan. It is said: the Rass is the area between Najran, Yemen and Hadramawt. It is said: a people to whom Allah sent prophets, whom they killed, and they burned their bones in a well. It is said: a people to whom a prophet was sent, whom they ate. It is said: a people whose women were lesbians. It is said: the Rass is water and palm trees belonging to Banu Asad. It is said: the Rass is a river in the lands of the East, to which Allah sent a prophet from the offspring of Judah, son of Jacob, and they denied him. He remained among them for a time, then complained to Allah about them. They dug a well for him and lowered him into it, saying: "We hope that our God will be pleased with us." So for most of their day they would hear the groaning of their prophet. He prayed for his soul to be taken quickly, and he died, and a black cloud overshadowed them and melted them as lead melts.

Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The people of the Rass seized their prophet, threw him into a well, and sealed a rock over him. There was a black slave who had believed in him who used to bring food to that well, and Allah would help him lift that rock, and he would take out what would nourish him, then return the rock. Until Allah one day cast sleep upon the ears of that black man for fourteen years, and the people of the town brought out their prophet, and they believed in him." In a long narration. Al-Tabari said: it is possible that they disbelieved after that, so Allah mentioned them in this verse. The disagreement about the companions of the Rass is great; if what Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b related were sound, it would be the saying that cannot be disputed. (Summary of these sayings:) they are a people whom Allah destroyed for denying the one sent to them.

"Wa-qurunan bayna dhalika": this is a vagueness whose reality none knows except Allah. "Dhalika" refers to those previously mentioned; therefore "bayn" is fittingly applied to it without anything being coordinated to it, as if it were said: "between those mentioned." The speaker may mention various things and then point to them. The first "kullan" is in the accusative by ishtighal, meaning: "and We warned each" or "We admonished each"; the second is an object of "tabbarna," because it took no object; this is clear grammar. The meaning of "daraba al-amthal": He explained to them the wondrous stories of the ancients and described to them what their denial of their prophets led to, of Allah's punishment and His destruction of them, so that they might be guided by the striking of examples, but they were not guided. He who made the pronoun in "lahu" refer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is far off; he said: the meaning is "We struck for the Messenger every example," and on this "kullan" is accusative by "daraba-na," and "al-amthal" is a substitute for "kullan." The pronoun in "wa-laqad ataw" refers to the Quraysh, who used to pass by Sodom, one of the towns of the people of Lot, on their trade journeys to Syria. There were five towns; Allah destroyed four of them and one remained, which is Zughar, whose people did not do that deed; so said Ibn Abbas. "Matar al-su'" is the stones that were rained down on them from the sky, and they perished. Abraham (peace be upon him) used to call out advice to them: "O Sodom, a day from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is for you; I forbid you from exposing yourselves to punishment from Allah." The meaning of "ataw" is "passed by," therefore it is followed by "ʿala." He used the singular "al-qaryah" though they were towns, because Sodom was the mother of those (p-500) towns and the greatest of them. Makki said: the pronoun in "ataw" refers to those who took the Qur'an as abandoned. End of quote; they are the Quraysh. "Matar" is in the accusative as a second object of "ummirat," in the sense of "were given," or as a verbal noun with its extra letters omitted, meaning: the raining of evil.

"Afalam yakunu yarawnaha": that is, they look at what is in it of lessons and traces indicating what vengeance befell it, as He said: "And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night" [al-Saffat: 137], and He said: "And indeed they were on a clear highway" [al-Hijr: 79]. It is a question whose meaning is amazement. Despite that, they did not take warning by seeing it, that there would befall them in this world what befell those; rather they were disbelievers who did not believe in resurrection, so they did not anticipate the punishment of the Hereafter. He placed "hope" in the position of "expectation," because only one who believes expects the outcome; therefore they did not reflect or ponder, and passed by it as their caravans passed. Or: they do not hope for "nushur" (resurrection) as believers hope for it, out of their longing for the reward of their deeds. Or: they do not fear it, according to the Tihami dialect. Zayd ibn Ali read "muttirat" as triliteral in the passive voice, with "matara" being transitive. The poet said:

"Like one whose wadi after drought is rained upon."

Abu al-Simak read "matar al-su'" with a dammah on the sin.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-Furqan, verses 35–44 (part 2 of 2):

﴿When they see you, they take you only in mockery﴾. The polytheists did not confine themselves to denying the prophethood of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) and refusing to believe in him. They went further, adding ridicule and contempt, to the point that some of them would say to others: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The word ﴿in﴾ is a negating particle (in) and it is the response clause (jawab, the main clause that completes a conditional) of ﴿idha﴾ (when). ﴿Idha﴾ is distinctive in that when its response clause is negated by ﴿ma﴾ or ﴿la﴾, the particle ﴿fa'﴾ (then) does not enter it, unlike other conditional particles, which must take ﴿fa'﴾ with ﴿ma﴾ and ﴿la﴾. With ﴿idha﴾, the present-tense verb is in the indicative. So if the negating ﴿in﴾ occurs in the response to a conditional other than ﴿idha﴾, ﴿fa'﴾ is necessary, as with the negating ﴿ma﴾.

The meaning of ﴿huzuwan﴾ (in mockery) is "in the place of mockery," or "one who is mocked." Before ﴿a-hadha﴾ (Is this...?) there is an implied verb of saying, meaning "they say." Some hold that the response to ﴿idha﴾ is the implied speech: ﴿When they see you﴾ they say, ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The clause ﴿in yattakhidhunaka﴾ (they take you) is a parenthetical clause between ﴿idha﴾ and its response.

It is said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. Whenever he saw the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), he would say: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ The verb is in the plural to magnify the ugliness of his act, or because a group was with him who said the same. The apparent meaning is that the sayers were a large group. This interrogative expresses belittlement and contempt on their part. They expressed it in the form of acknowledgment and affirmation, ﴿God has sent as a messenger﴾, while they were in utter denial and rejection, in mockery and ridicule. Had they not been mocking, they would have said: "This one claims or asserts that he has been sent as a messenger from God."

Their statement ﴿He almost led us astray﴾ is evidence of the great effort the Messenger of God (ﷺ) exerted in calling them, and of his expending the utmost of his strength and capacity in seeking their goodwill, along with presenting signs and miracles. To their own claim, they almost abandoned their religion for the religion of Islam, were it not for their excessive obstinacy and their clinging to worship of their gods. The particle ﴿law-la﴾ (were it not) in such speech functions, in meaning though not in form, as a restriction of an absolute ruling. This is stated by al-Zamakhshari.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Mockery is either of appearance, in which case he was better than them in physical form, or of attribute, which is impossible, because the attribute by which he was distinguished from them is the manifestation of the miracle upon him and not upon them. Since they could not discredit his argument, in reality they are the ones who deserve to be mocked. Then, out of their shamelessness, they reversed the matter and mocked the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). End of quotation.

It is said: The verse also indicates that, with the manifestation of his argument (peace and blessings be upon him), they became like madmen against whom he had prevailed. They first mocked him, then they described him as one who ﴿almost led us astray﴾ from our doctrine, were it not that we confronted him with stubbornness and persistence. This indicates that they conceded to him the strength of his argument and the perfection of his intellect. Their combining mockery with this perplexed claim shows that they were bewildered about his affair: at times they mocked him, and at other times they described him with what befits only a complete scholar.

﴿But they will soon know﴾ is a threat and an indication that they cannot escape Him, however long the respite lasts. The threat must befall them, so the delay should not deceive them. When they said ﴿He almost led us astray﴾, the statement ﴿Who is further astray in the way?﴾ came. That is: it will become clear to them who is the misleader and who is the one who goes astray, by witnessing the punishment from which there is no escape. The apparent reading is that ﴿man﴾ (who) is interrogative, and ﴿adall﴾ (more astray) is its predicate. The clause is in the position of the object of ﴿ya'lamun﴾ (they know), whether that verb takes one object or two. It is also possible that ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun, the object of ﴿ya'lamun﴾, and ﴿adall﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "he is more astray." The omission of this pronoun results from the lengthening found in the Arab saying: "I am not the one who is saying to you, 'equal'."

﴿Have you seen him who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ This is a statement of despair regarding their faith, and an indication to him (peace be upon him) that he should not grieve over them. It also informs that they, in their ignorance of benefits and their scant consideration of consequences, are like cattle. Then He mentions that they are ﴿further astray in the way﴾ than the livestock, in that they have understanding but abandon its use in what would save them from God's punishment. The livestock have no way to understand benefits. The word ﴿arayta﴾ (have you seen) is an interrogative of wonder at the ignorance of one in such a state. ﴿Ilahahu﴾ (his god) is the first object of ﴿ittakhadha﴾ (took), and ﴿hawahu﴾ (his desire) is the second, meaning he has placed his desire in the position of the god he worships, so it follows what is in his desire. The meaning is that he took as a god nothing but his desire. Reversing the construction (by making the desire the agent) is not good, since it would require that the one who took his desire as his god... and the verse is a case of poetic necessity and rare speech, so the speech of God is to be exonerated from it. A man used to worship an idol, and whenever he saw a better one, he threw it away and took the better one. It is said: It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, who, whenever he desired something, worshipped it. Desire is the inclination of the heart toward something. ﴿Will you then be a guardian over him?﴾ means: will you compel him to abandon his desire, or will you protect him from his great ignorance?

Some people of Medina read ﴿man ittakhadha alihatan﴾ (whoever has taken gods), with tanwin (nunation) and in the plural. In it there is a shift in which ﴿hawahu﴾ becomes kinds, names of different genera, so that each genus of his desire is another god. Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿ilahatan﴾ (a deity) on the pattern fi'alah, and in it too there is a shift: his desire is a deity, in the sense of an object of worship, because it means "one who is worshipped." The ta' in it is for emphasis, which is why it takes tanwin. It is also said: Rather, ﴿ilahah﴾ is the sun, and it is called ﴿ulahah﴾ with a dammah on the hamza. It is not diptote, due to being a proper noun and feminine. But since it is among the words that take the definite article in some dialects, it came to be like what contains the article, and then it was removed. Therefore it takes tanwin and becomes like adjectives, so it is indefinite. This is stated by the author of al-Lawami'.

The first object of ﴿ara'ayta﴾ is ﴿man﴾, and the interrogative clause is in the position of the second object. The discussion of ﴿ara'ayta﴾ was presented at the beginning of al-An'am. The meaning of ﴿wakilan﴾ (a guardian) is: can you call them to guidance, so that you rely upon Him and compel them to Islam?

﴿Am﴾ (or) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and according to the correct view it is to be parsed as ﴿bal﴾ (rather) plus the interrogative hamza. As if He said: "Rather, do you suppose that..." This blame is so severe that it was introduced by turning away from the previous blame to it, namely that they are deprived of hearing and reason, since they do not lend an ear to hearing the truth, nor do they reflect with their intellect. They are likened to the livestock, which are a proverb for heedlessness and error. This is denied of most of them, because among them are those for whom happiness had preceded, so they became Muslims. They are described as further astray than the livestock, because the livestock submit to their owners, recognize who treats them well from who mistreats them, seek their benefit and avoid their harm, and find their way to their pastures and watering places. But they do not submit to their Lord, do not recognize His kindness to them, do not desire the reward which is the greatest benefit, do not guard against the punishment which is the greatest harm, and are not guided to the truth.

(p-501)

[p. 502]

ألم تر إلى ربك كيف مد الظل ولو شاء لجعله ساكنا ثم جعلنا الشمس عليه دليلا

*"Have you not considered your Lord, how He extended the shade? Had He willed, He would have made it still. Then We made the sun its indicator."*

ثم قبضناه إلينا قبضا يسيرا

*"Then We withdrew it to Us, a gradual withdrawal."*

وهو الذي جعل لكم الليل لباسا والنوم سباتا وجعل النهار نشورا

*"It is He who made the night a garment for you, and sleep a rest, and made the day a resurrection."*

وهو الذي أرسل الرياح بشرا بين يدي رحمته وأنزلنا من السماء ماء طهورا

*"It is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, and We send down from the sky pure water."*

لنحيي به بلدة ميتا ونسقيه مما خلقنا أنعاما وأناسي كثيرا

*"That We may give life thereby to a dead land and give it to drink, of what We have created, cattle and many people."*

ولقد صرفناه بينهم ليذكروا فأبى أكثر الناس إلا كفورا

*"We have indeed diversified it among them that they may remember, but most people refused except disbelief."*

ولو شئنا لبعثنا في كل قرية نذيرا

*"Had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town."* [al-Furqan: 51]

فلا تطع الكافرين وجاهدهم به جهادا كبيرا

*"So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it, a great striving."* [al-Furqan: 52]

وهو الذي مرج البحرين هذا عذب فرات وهذا ملح أجاج وجعل بينهما برزخا وحجرا محجورا

*"It is He who released the two seas, this one sweet and palatable, and this one salty and bitter; and He placed between them a barrier and a forbidding partition."* [al-Furqan: 53]

وهو الذي خلق من الماء بشرا فجعله نسبا وصهرا وكان ربك قديرا

*"It is He who created a human from water and made him kin by blood and by marriage; and your Lord is ever Powerful."* [al-Furqan: 54]

ويعبدون من دون الله ما لا ينفعهم ولا يضرهم وكان الكافر على ربه ظهيرا

*"They worship besides God what neither benefits them nor harms them; and the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord."* [al-Furqan: 55]

وما أرسلناك إلا مبشرا ونذيرا

*"We have not sent you except as a bearer of good tidings and a warner."* [al-Furqan: 56]

قل ما أسألكم عليه من أجر إلا من شاء أن يتخذ إلى ربه سبيلا

*"Say: I ask of you no wage for it, except that whoever wills may take a path to his Lord."* [al-Furqan: 57]

وتوكل على الحي الذي لا يموت وسبح بحمده وكفى به بذنوب عباده خبيرا

*"Put your trust in the Living who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise; and sufficient is He as Knower of the sins of His servants."* [al-Furqan: 58]

الذي خلق السماوات والأرض وما بينهما في ستة أيام ثم استوى على العرش الرحمن فاسأل به خبيرا

*"He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself on the Throne, the Most Merciful; so ask about Him one who is informed."* [al-Furqan: 59]

وإذا قيل لهم اسجدوا للرحمن قالوا وما الرحمن أنسجد لما تأمرنا وزادهم نفورا

*"And when it is said to them, 'Prostrate to the Most Merciful,' they say, 'What is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?' And it increases them in aversion."* [al-Furqan: 60]

لَمّا بيَّن تعالى جهل المعترضين على دلائل الصانع وفساد طريقتهم، ذكر أنواعا من الدلائل الواضحة التي تدل على قدرته التامة، لعلهم يتدبرونها ويؤمنون بمن هذه قدرته وتصرفه في عالمه، فبدأ بحال الظل في زيادته ونقصانه وتغيره من حال إلى حال، وأن ذلك جار على مشيئته. وتقدم الكلام على (ألم تر) في البقرة في قصة الذي حاج إبراهيم. والمعنى: ألم تر إلى صنع ربك وقدرته. و(كيف): سؤال عن حال في موضع نصب (p-٥٠٣) بـ(مد). والجملة في موضع متعلق (ألم تر)؛ لأن (تر) معلقة [mu'allaqah: the verb of perception is suspended, meaning it governs no direct object here]، والجملة الاستفهامية التي هي معلَّق عنها فعل القلب ليس باقيا على حقيقة الاستفهام. فالمعنى: ألم تر إلى مد ربك الظل.

وقال الجمهور: الظل هنا من طلوع الفجر إلى طلوع الشمس، مثل ظل الجنة: ظل ممدود لا شمس فيه ولا ظلمة. واعترض بأنه في غير النهار بل في بقايا الليل، ولا يسمى ظلا. وقيل: الظل الليل لا ظل الأرض، وهو يغمر الدنيا كلها. وقيل: من غيبوبة الشمس إلى طلوعها، وهذا هو القول الذي قبله ولكن أورده كذا. وقيل: ظلال الأشياء كلها، كقوله: ﴿أولم يروا إلى ما خلق الله من شيء يتفيأ ظلاله﴾ [al-Nahl: 48] [*"Have they not considered what things God has created, whose shadows turn from the right and the left?"*]. وقال أبو عبيدة: الظل بالغداة والفيء بالعشي. وقال ابن السكيت: الظل ما نسخته الشمس، والفيء ما نسخ الشمس. وقيل: ما لم تكن عليه الشمس ظل، وما كانت عليه فزالت فيء.

﴿ولو شاء لجعله ساكنا﴾: قال ابن عباس وقتادة وابن زيد: كظل الجنة الذي لا شمس تذهبه. وقال مجاهد: لا تصيبه الشمس ولا تزول. وقال الحسن: لو شاء لتركه ظلا كما هو. وقيل: لأدامه أبدا بمنع طلوع الشمس بعد غيبوبتها، فلما طلعت الشمس دلت على زوال الظل وبدا فيه النقصان، فبطلوع الشمس يبدو النقصان في الظل، وبغروبها تبدو الزيادة في الظل، فبالشمس استدل أهل الأرض على الظل وزيادته ونقصه، وكلما علت الشمس نقص الظل، وكلما دنت للغروب زاد، وهو قوله: ﴿ثم قبضناه إلينا قبضا يسيرا﴾، يعني في وقت علو الشمس بالنهار ينقص الظل نقصانا يسيرا بعد يسير، وكذلك زيادته بعد نصف النهار يزيد يسيرا بعد يسير حتى يعم الأرض كلها، فأما زوال الظل كله فإنما يكون في البلدان المتوسطة في وقت.

وقال الزمخشري: ومعنى (مد الظل) أن جعله يمتد وينبسط فينتفع به الناس.

﴿ولو شاء لجعله ساكنا﴾، أي: لاصقا بأصل كل مظل من جبل وبناء وشجر وغير منبسط، فلم ينتفع به أحد. سمي انبساط الظل وامتداده تحركا منه، وعدم ذلك سكونا. ومعنى كون الشمس دليلا أن الناس يستدلون بالشمس وبأحوالها في مسيرها على أحوال الظل، من كونه ثابتا في مكان وزائلا ومتسعا ومتقلصا، فيبنون حاجتهم إلى الظل واستغناءهم عنه على حسب ذلك. وقبضه إليه أن ينسخه بظل الشمس (يسيرا)، أي: على مهل، وفي هذا القبض اليسير شيئا بعد شيء من المنافع ما لا يعد ولا يحصى، ولو قبض دفعة لتعطلت أكثر مرافق الناس بالظل والشمس جميعا. (فإن قلت): ثم في هذين الموضعين كيف موقعها؟ (قلت): موقعها لبيان تفاضل الأمور الثلاثة، كأن الثاني أعظم من الأول، والثالث أعظم من الثاني؛ تشبيها لتباعد ما بينهما في الفضل بتباعد ما بين الحوادث في الوقت. ووجه آخر وهو أنه بنى الظل حين بنى السماء، كالقبة المضروبة، ودحا الأرض تحتها، فألقت القبة ظلها على الأرض لعدم النير.

﴿ولو شاء لجعله ساكنا﴾ مستقرا على تلك الحالة، ثم خلق الشمس وجعله على ذلك الظل سلطها عليه وجعلها دليلا متبوعا لهم كما يتبع الدليل في الطريق، فهو يزيد بها وينقص ويمتد ويقلص، ثم نسخه بها قبضه قبضا سهلا يسيرا غير عسير. ويحتمل أن يريد قبضه عند قيام الساعة بقبض أسبابه، وهي الأجرام التي تلقي الظل، فيكون قد ذكر إعدامه بإعدام أسبابه، كما ذكر إنشاءه بإنشاء أسبابه، وقوله: (قبضناه إلينا) يدل عليه، وكذلك قوله: (يسيرا)، كما قال: ﴿ذلك حشر علينا يسير﴾ [Qaf: 44] [*"That is a gathering easy for Us."*]، انتهى. وقوله: سمى انبساط الظل وامتداده تحركا منه، لم يسم الله ذلك، إنما قال: (كيف مد الظل). وقوله: ويحتمل أن يريد قبضه عند قيام الساعة، فهذا يبعد احتماله؛ لأنه إنما ذكر آثار صنعته وقدرته لتشاهد، ثم قال: (مد الظل) وعطف عليه ماضيا مثله، فيبعد أن يكون التقدير: ثم قبضه عند قيام الساعة، مع ظهور كونه ماضيا مستدامًا أمثاله.

وقال ابن عطية: ﴿ولو شاء لجعله ساكنا﴾، أي: ثابتا غير متحرك ولا منسوخ، لكنه جعل الشمس ونسخها إياه (p-٥٠٤) بطردها له من موضع إلى موضع دليلا عليه، مبينا لوجوده ولوجه العبرة فيه. وحكى الطبري: أنه لولا الشمس لم يعلم أن الظل شيء، إذ الأشياء إنما تعرف بأضدادها. وقال ابن عباس: (يسيرا) معجلا. وقال مجاهد: لطيفا، أي: شيئا بعد شيء، ويحتمل أن يريد سهلا قريب التناول. وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: أكثر الناس في تأويل هذه الآية، ويُرفع الكلام فيها إلى وجهين.

الأول: أن الظل لا ضوء خالص ولا ظلمة خالصة، وهو ما بين طلوع الفجر وطلوع الشمس، وكذلك الكيفيات الحاصلة داخل السقف وأبنية الجدارات، وهي أطيب الأحوال؛ لأن الظلمة الخالصة يكرهها الطبع وينفر عنها الحس، والضوء الخالص يحير الحس البصري ويحدث السخونة القوية، وهي مؤذية، ولهذا قيل في الجنة: ﴿وظل ممدود﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30] [*"and extended shade"*]، والناظر إلى الجسم الملون كأنه يشاهد بالظل شيئا سوى الجسم وسوى اللون، والظل ليس أمرا ثالثا ولا معرفة به إلا أنه إذا طلعت الشمس ووقع ضوؤها على الجسم ثم مال، عرف للظل وجود وماهية، ولولاها ما عرف؛ لأن الأشياء تدرك بأضدادها، فظهر للعقل أن الظل كيفية زائدة على الجسم واللون؛ ولذلك قال: ﴿ثم جعلنا الشمس عليه دليلا﴾، أي: جعلنا الظل أولا بما فيه من المنافع واللذات، ثم هدينا العقول إلى معرفة وجوده بأن أطلعنا الشمس فكانت دليلا على وجود الظل. (ثم قبضناه) أي: أزلناه لا دفعة بل (يسيرا) يسيرا، كلما ازداد ارتفاع الشمس ازداد نقصان الظل من جانب المغرب، ولما كانت الحركات المكانية لا توجد دفعة بل يسيرا يسيرا كان زوال الأظلال كذلك.

والثاني: أنه لما خلق السماء والأرض وقع ظل السماء على الأرض، فجعل الشمس دليلا؛ لأنه بحسب حركات الأضواء تتحرك الأظلال، فهما متعاقبان متلازمان لا واسطة بينهما، فبمقدار ما يزداد أحدهما ينقص الآخر، فكما أن المهتدي يقتدي بالهادي والدليل ويلازمه فكذلك الأظلال ملازمة للأضواء، ولذلك جعل الشمس دليلا عليه، انتهى ملخصا. وهو مأخوذ من كلام الزمخشري، ومحسن بعض تحسين. والآية في غاية الظهور ولا تحتاج إلى هذا التكثير.

وقال أيضا: الظل ليس عدما محضا، بل هو أضواء مخلوطة بظلام، فهو أمر وجودي، وفي تحقيقه دقيق يرجع فيه إلى الكتب العقلية، انتهى. والآية في غاية الوضوح ولا تحتاج إلى هذا التكثير، وقد تركت أشياء من كلام المفسرين مما لا تمس إليه الحاجة. (جعل الليل لباسا) تشبيها بالثوب الذي يغطي البدن ويستره؛ من حيث الليل يستر الأشياء. والسبات: ضرب من الإغماء يعتري اليقظان مرضا، فشبه النوم به، والسبت الإقامة في المكان، فكان السبات سكونا تاما، والنشور هنا الإحياء، شبه اليقظة به ليتطابق الإحياء مع الإماتة، اللذين يتضمنهما النوم والسبات، انتهى من كلام ابن عطية. وقال غيره: السبات الراحة، جعل النوم سباتا أي: سبب راحة.

وقال الزمخشري: السبات الموت، وهو كقوله: ﴿وهو الذي يتوفاكم بالليل﴾ [al-An'am: 60] [*"It is He who takes you in death by night."*]. (فإن قلت): هلا فسرته بالراحة؟ (قلت): النشور في مقابلته يأباه، انتهى. ولا يأباه إلا لو تعين تفسير النشور بالحياة. وقال أبو مسلم: (نشورا) هو بمعنى الانتشار والحركة. وقال ابن عطية: ويحتمل أن يريد بالنشور وقت انتشار وتفرق لطلب المعاش وابتغاء فضل الله. و(النهار نشورا) وما قبله من باب: ليل نائم ونهار صائم، وهذه الآية مع دلالتها على قدرة الخالق، فيها إظهار لنعمته على خلقه؛ لأن الاحتجاب بستر الليل كم فيه لكثير من الناس فوائد دينية ودنيوية. وقال الشاعر:

*وكم لظلام الليل عندي من يد* 
*تخبر أن المانوية تكذب*

[*"How many a favour of the darkness of night is mine, which proves that the Manichaeans lie."*]

والنوم واليقظة وشبههما بالموت والحياة، أي: عبرة فيهما لمن اعتبر. وعن لقمان أنه قال لابنه: يا بني كما (p-٥٠٥) تنام فتوقظ فكذلك تموت فتنشر.

The disagreement over the recitation of **al-rīḥ** (the wind) as singular or plural was discussed earlier, in al-Baqarah. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The plural recitation is more apt, because the usage of *al-rīḥ* in the Qur'an, whenever it appears in the singular, refers to punishment, while whenever it refers to rain and mercy it appears as *riyāḥ* (winds). This is because the wind of rain spreads out, shifts, scatters, and comes gently, from here and there and one thing after another, whereas the wind of punishment comes out without shifting, arriving as one solid body. Do you not see that it smashes and demolishes whatever it finds? Al-Rummānī said: The winds of mercy are plural because there are three fertilizing (*lawāqiḥ*) winds: the south wind, the east wind, and the north wind. The wind of punishment is singular because it is one wind that does not fertilize, namely the west wind (*al-dabūr*). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ refutes this, when a wind blew: "O Allah, make it winds (*riyāḥan*) and do not make it a single wind (*rīḥan*)." End of quote. It is not appropriate to say that this recitation is more apt, because each of the two recitations is *mutawātir* (transmitted by a large number of narrators through every stage, so that its authenticity is certain), and the *alif* and *lām* in *al-rīḥ* are for the category, so they are generalizing. As for what was mentioned, that al-Rummānī's statement is refuted by the hadith, this is not evident, because it is possible that by his words ﷺ "*riyāḥan*" he meant the three fertilizing winds, and by "do not make it a single wind" he meant the west wind. Thus what al-Rummānī said agrees with the hadith on this understanding.

The disagreement over the recitation of **nushran** (spreading out) and its meaning was discussed in al-Aʿrāf. The phrase ﴿before His mercy﴾ is a fine metaphor, meaning in front of the rain, because it comes heralded by it. *Ṭahūr* is on the pattern *faʿūl*, either for emphasis, like *naʾūm* (very sleepy), in which case it is derived from *ṭāhir* (pure); or it is a noun for what is used for purification, like *saḥūr* (pre-dawn meal) and *faṭūr* (breakfast); or it is a verbal noun of *tatahhara* (to purify oneself), coming in a form other than the regular verbal noun, as transmitted by Sībawayh. The apparent sense of His words ﴿pure water﴾ is that it is for emphasis on its purity. The basis of the emphasis is that nothing has mixed with it, unlike water that springs from the earth and the like, which is mixed with earthy particles from its place of rest, its course, or what is thrown into it. It may be described as a noun or as a verbal noun. Thaʿlab said: It is what is pure in itself and purifies others. If what he said is an explanation of its intensified purity, it is sound, and it is supported by His words ﴿and He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you by it﴾ [al-Anfāl: 11]. Otherwise, *faʿūl* does not mean *mufaʿʿil* (causative form). An example of the use of *ṭahūr* for emphasis is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And their Lord will give them a pure drink﴾ [al-Insān: 21]. The poet said:

*To smooth-hipped gazelles of the deer, with sweet teeth, whose saliva is pure*

The recitation of ʿĪsā and Abū Jaʿfar was "*mayyitan*" (with a shadda), and they described *baldatan* (town) with a masculine adjective, because *al-baldah* has the meaning of *al-balad* in His words ﴿so We drove it to a dead land﴾ [Fāṭir: 9]. The majority preferred the lightened form, because it resembles a verbal noun of the form *faʿl*; just as the masculine and feminine are described by a verbal noun, so too by what resembles it, unlike the doubled form, which resembles the active participle *fāʿil* in accepting the feminine *tāʾ*, except in what is specific to the feminine, such as *ṭāmith* (menstruating).

ʿAbd Allāh, Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Abī ʿAbla, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Abū ʿAmr, in one narration from them, recited "*wa-nasqiyahu*" (and We give it to drink) with a fatḥa on the nūn. It is also narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith al-Dhimārī recited "*wa-anāsiya*" with the yāʾ lightened. It is narrated from al-Kisāʾī: "*wa-anāsiyya*," the plural of *insān* in the view of Sībawayh, and the plural of *insī* in the view of al-Farrāʾ, al-Mubarrad, and al-Zajjāj. The regular plural would be *anāsiyya*, as they said for *muhallabī* the plural *mahālibah*. It is also reported that the plural of *insān* is *anāsīn*, like *sirḥān* and *sarāḥīn*.

He described the water as pure and gave as the reason for sending it down the giving of life and drink, because since the humans are among those for whom the water was sent down, it was described as pure, both as an honor to them and as completing the blessing upon them. The causal clause implies that purity is a condition for the validity of this, just as you would say: "The prince mounted me on a swift horse so that I might hunt wild game on it."

He placed the reviving of the land and the watering of livestock before the watering of humans, because their life depends on the life of their land and the life of their livestock. So He mentioned first what is the cause of that. Also, when they find what waters their land and their livestock, they find their own drink.

*Al-anʿām* (livestock) and *al-anāsī* were made indefinite and described as numerous, because many of them are sustained only by the rain that Allah sends down. Likewise, ﴿that We may revive by it a dead town﴾ refers to some of the lands of these people who are far from the places where water is found, unlike the inhabitants of cities, who are near to valleys, rivers, and springs, and so are generally independent of rainwater for irrigation. He singled out livestock from among the drinking animals He created, because birds and wild beasts go far in search of water, so drinking does not fail them, unlike livestock, which are the property of humans, and their benefits depend on them. So bestowing favor upon them by watering their livestock is like bestowing favor upon them by watering them.

The pronoun in "*ṣarrafnāhu*" (We have diversified it) refers to the water sent down from the sky. That is, We made the sending down of water a reminder, by turning it from some places to others. It occurs each year in the same amount; this was said by the majority, including Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Mujāhid. According to this interpretation, "*illā kufūran*" (except disbelief) is their saying that rain comes by the stars and constellations (*anwāʾ*); this was said by ʿIkrima. It was also said that "*kufūran*" is unrestricted disbelief, since they abandoned reflection.

Ibn ʿAbbās also said: It refers to the Qur'an, even though it has not been mentioned before, because the matter is clear. This is supported by His words "*wa-jāhidhum bihi*" (and strive against them with it), for the pronouns are consistent. And if it refers to the rain, then "*bihi*" refers to the Qur'an.

Abū Muslim said: It refers to the rain, the winds, the clouds, and all the other signs mentioned in it.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: We have diversified this statement among people in the Qur'an and in all the other books and scriptures sent down to the messengers, namely the mention of the creation of clouds and the sending down of rain, so that they might reflect, take heed, recognize the right of the blessing in it, and give thanks. But most of them refused except to deny the blessing, reject it, and care little for it.

It was also said: We diversified the rain among them in different lands and different times, and in varying forms: heavy downpour, drizzle, light rain, mist, steady rain, and fine rain. But they refused except disbelief, and that they should say, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star," and not mention His mercy and His craftsmanship.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: No year has less rain than another, but Allah distributes it among His servants as He wills, and he recited this verse.

It is narrated that the angels know the number and quantity of the rain each year, because it does not vary, but it varies among the lands.

From this a response can be drawn regarding the indefiniteness of *al-baldah*, *al-anʿām*, and *al-anāsī*, as if He said: "That He may revive by it some dead lands, and that We may give to drink some of the livestock and humans, and that portion is many." End of quote.

ʿIkrima recited "*ṣarafnāhu*" with the rāʾ lightened.
