وهُوَ قَوْلُ الأخْفَشِ والزَّجّاجِ. ويَكُونَ (خَبِيرًا) لَيْسَ مِن صِفاتِ اللَّهِ هُنا، كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: اسْألْ عَنِ الرَّحْمَنِ الخُبَراءَ جِبْرِيلَ والعُلَماءَ وأهْلَ الكُتُبِ المُنَزَّلَةِ، وإنْ جَعَلْتَ (بِهِ) مُتَعَلِّقًا بِخَبِيرًا كانَ المَعْنى (فاسْألْ) عَنِ اللَّهِ الخُبَراءَ بِهِ. وقالَ الكَلْبِيُّ: مَعْناهُ (فاسْألْ) خَبِيرًا بِهِ، و(بِهِ) يَعُودُ إلى ما ذُكِرَ مِن خَلْقِ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ [p-٥٠٩] والِاسْتِواءِ عَلى العَرْشِ، وذَلِكَ الخَبِيرُ هو اللَّهُ تَعالى؛ لِأنَّهُ لا دَلِيلَ في العَقْلِ عَلى كَيْفِيَّةِ خَلْقِ ذَلِكَ، فَلا يَعْلَمُها إلّا اللَّهُ. وعَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ: الخَبِيرُ جِبْرِيلُ وقُدِّمَ لِرُءُوسِ الآيِ. وقالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: الباءُ في (بِهِ) صِلَةُ سَلْ، كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿سَألَ سائِلٌ بِعَذابٍ﴾ [المعارج: ١] (أي: "سأل سائل عن عذاب واقع")، كَما يَكُونُ (عَنْ) صِلَتَهُ في نَحْوِ ﴿ثُمَّ لَتُسْألُنَّ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَنِ النَّعِيمِ﴾ [التكاثر: ٨] ("ثم لتُسألُنّ يومئذٍ عن النعيم")، أوْ صِلَةُ (خَبِيرًا) بِهِ، فَتَجْعَلُ (خَبِيرًا) مَفْعُولًا، أيْ: فَسَلْ عَنْهُ رَجُلًا عارِفًا يُخْبِرْكَ بِرَحْمَتِهِ، أوْ فَسَلْ رَجُلًا خَبِيرًا بِهِ وبِرَحْمَتِهِ، أوْ فَسَلْ بِسُؤالِهِ خَبِيرًا. كَقَوْلِكَ: رَأيْتُ بِهِ أسَدًا، أيْ: رَأيْتُ بِرُؤْيَتِهِ، والمَعْنى إنْ سَألْتَهُ وجَدْتَهُ خَبِيرًا بِجَعْلِهِ حالًا عَنْ بِهِ تُرِيدُ فَسَلْ عَنْهُ عالِمًا بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ. وقِيلَ: (الرَّحْمَنُ) اسْمٌ مِن أسْماءِ اللَّهِ مَذْكُورٌ في الكُتُبِ المُتَقَدِّمَةِ ولَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَهُ. فَقِيلَ: فَسَلْ بِهَذا الِاسْمِ مَن يُخْبِرُكَ مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ حَتّى يُعْرَفَ مَن يُنْكِرُهُ، ومِن ثَمَّ كانُوا يَقُولُونَ: ما نَعْرِفُ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا الَّذِي في اليَمامَةِ يَعْنُونَ مُسَيْلِمَةَ، وكانَ يُقالُ لَهُ رَحْمَنُ اليَمامَةِ، انْتَهى.

﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ اسْجُدُوا لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾ وكانَتْ قُرَيْشٌ لا تَعْرِفُ هَذا في أسْماءِ اللَّهِ غالَطَتْ قُرَيْشٌ بِذَلِكَ فَقالَتْ: إنَّ مُحَمَّدًا يَأْمُرُنا بِعِبادَةِ رَحْمَنِ اليَمامَةِ، نَزَلَتْ ﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ﴾، و(ما) سُؤالٌ عَنِ المَجْهُولِ، فَيَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ سُؤالًا عَنِ المُسَمّى بِهِ؛ لِأنَّهم ما كانُوا يَعْرِفُونَهُ بِهَذا الِاسْمِ، ويَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ سُؤالًا عَنْ مَعْناهُ؛ لِأنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُسْتَعْمَلًا في كَلامِهِمْ كَما يُسْتَعْمَلُ الرَّحِيمُ والرَّحُومُ والرّاحِمُ، أوْ لِأنَّهم أنْكَرُوا إطْلاقَهُ عَلى اللَّهِ؛ قالَهُ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ. والَّذِي يَظْهَرُ أنَّهم لَمّا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ﴿اسْجُدُوا لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾ فَذُكِرَتِ الصِّفَةُ المُقْتَضِيَةُ لِلْمُبالَغَةِ في الرَّحْمَةِ، والكَلِمَةُ عَرَبِيَّةٌ لا يُنْكَرُ وضْعُها، أظْهَرُوا التَّجاهُلَ بِهَذِهِ الصِّفَةِ الَّتِي لِلَّهِ مُغالَطَةً مِنهم ووَقاحَةً فَقالُوا: ﴿وما الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ ("And what is the Most Merciful?")، وهم عارِفُونَ بِهِ وبِصِفَتِهِ الرَّحْمانِيَّةِ، وهَذا كَما قالَ فِرْعَوْنُ: ﴿وما رَبُّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ("And what is the Lord of the worlds?") [الشعراء: ٢٣] حِينَ قالَ لَهُ مُوسى: ﴿إنّى رَسُولٌ مِن رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ("I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds") [الأعراف: ١٠٤]، عَلى سَبِيلِ المُناكَرَةِ، وهو عالِمٌ بِرَبِّ العالَمِينَ. كَما قالَ مُوسى: ﴿لَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ ما أنْزَلَ هَؤُلاءِ إلّا رَبُّ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ بَصائِرَ﴾ ("You certainly know that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence") [الإسراء: ١٠٢] فَكَذَلِكَ كُفّارُ قُرَيْشٍ اسْتَفْهَمُوا عَنِ الرَّحْمَنِ اسْتِفْهامَ مَن يَجْهَلُهُ، وهم عالِمُونَ بِهِ، فَعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا مُسَيْلِمَةَ، وعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: مَن لا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا مُسَيْلِمَةَ. فالمَعْنى أنَسْجَدُ لِمُسَيْلِمَةَ، وعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: لا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ بِالكُلِّيَّةِ فالمَعْنى ﴿أنَسْجُدُ لِما تَأْمُرُنا﴾ ("Shall we prostrate to what you command us?") مِن غَيْرِ عِلْمٍ بِبَيانِهِ. والقائِلُ (اسْجُدُوا) الرَّسُولُ أوِ اللَّهُ عَلى لِسانِ رَسُولِهِ. وقَرَأ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ والأسْوَدُ بْنُ يَزِيدَ وحَمْزَةُ والكِسائِيُّ ”يَأْمُرُ“ بِالياءِ مِن تَحْتُ، أيْ: يَأْمُرُنا مُحَمَّدٌ، والكِنايَةُ عَنْهُ أوِ المُسَمّى الرَّحْمَنَ ولا نَعْرِفُهُ. وقَرَأ باقِي السَّبْعَةِ بِالتّاءِ خِطابًا لِلرَّسُولِ. ومَفْعُولُ (تَأْمُرُنا) الثّانِي مَحْذُوفٌ لِدَلالَةِ الكَلامِ عَلَيْهِ، تَقْدِيرُهُ يَأْمُرُنا سُجُودَهُ نَحْوَ قَوْلِهِمْ: أمَرْتُكَ الخَيْرَ. (وزادَهم) أيْ: هَذا القَوْلُ، وهو الأمْرُ بِالسُّجُودِ لِلرَّحْمَنِ، (زادَهم) ضَلالًا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ مَعَ ضَلالِهِمُ السّابِقِ، وكانَ حَقُّهُ أنْ يَكُونَ باعِثًا عَلى فِعْلِ السُّجُودِ والقَبُولِ. وقالَ الضَّحّاكُ: سَجَدَ أبُو بَكْرٍ وعُمَرُ وعُثْمانُ وعَلِيٌّ وعُثْمانُ بْنُ مَظْعُونٍ وعَمْرُو ابْنُ غَلَسَةَ، فَرَآهُمُ المُشْرِكُونَ فَأخَذُوا في ناحِيَةِ المَسْجِدِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ، فَهَذا المُرادُ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وزادَهم نُفُورًا﴾ ("and it increased them in aversion")، ومَعْنى (نُفُورًا): فِرارًا.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verses 51–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town.﴾ When the Exalted knew what the Messenger endured of harm from his people, He informed him that, had He willed, He would have sent a warner to every town, so that the matter would be lighter for you. But He magnified your reward and your rank, since He made your warning general to all of mankind, and singled you out with it so that your reward would increase, for reward comes in proportion to the abundance of striving, and so that He would gather for you the good deeds of those who believe in you, since you are their founder.

﴿So do not obey the disbelievers.﴾ This means the disbelievers of Quraysh. They had listened to him and desired that he return to the religion of their forefathers, and they would make him king over them and gather great wealth for him. So the Exalted forbade him to obey them, until he would show them that he had no desire for any of that, for his desire was only in calling to God and believing in Him.

﴿And strive against them with it.﴾ That is, with the Qur'an, or with Islam, or with the sword, or by abandoning their obedience. The word *jihadan* (struggle) is a verbal noun described by *kabiran* (great), because it is incumbent upon him, peace be upon him, to strive against the entire world, so it is a great struggle.

*Maraja* (he mixed them) means: he mixed the two together, or he poured one of them into the other, or he let them flow; these are opinions. The apparent meaning is that by "the two seas" is meant abundant sweet water and abundant salt water. It has also been said that they are two specific seas: the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome. It has been said that they are the sea of the heavens and the sea of the earth, which meet every year; this was reported from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: the waters of the rivers that fall into the salt sea, and this is close to the first opinion. Ibn Atiyyah said: the purpose of the verse is to draw attention to the power of God and the perfection of His creation of things, in that He spread in the earth abundant sweet waters from rivers, springs and wells, and placed them amid the bitter water, and placed the bitter water amid them; so you see the sea surrounded on its two banks by sweet waters, and the sea's water reaching the islands and the like, surrounded by bitter water. *Al-barzakh* and *al-hijr* are that which separates the two of them, of earth and barrier; this was said by al-Hasan. This accords with the view of those who say that *maraja* means *ajra* (he let flow). It has also been said that *al-barzakh* refers to the lands and deserts, so the two do not differ except through the removal of the barrier on the Day of Resurrection. Most of the scholars said: the barrier is a prevention from the power of God. Al-Zajjaj said: they are mixed in the sight of the eye, yet separated by the power of God. In Basra, the sweet water flows down from it into the Tigris toward the sea, and the tide comes from the sea, [p. 507] and the two meet without mixing: the sea's water is intensely green, and the Tigris's water is reddish. The water-drawer draws from the Tigris water here with us, and nothing mixes with it. The Nile of Egypt, in its flood, cuts through the salt sea, cutting it in such a way that it remains a flowing reddish river in the middle of the salt water, so that people may draw water from it. The waters appear as pieces in the middle of the salt sea, and people say: this is ice-water, and they give drink from it from the middle of the sea.

Talha and Qutayba, from al-Kisa'i, read *malih* with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *lam*, and likewise in Fatir. Abu Hatim said: this is an objectionable reading. Abu al-Fath said: he meant *malih* and deleted the alif, as it was deleted from *barad* (cold), meaning *barid*. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in the book *al-Lawami*: it is an anomalous and rare dialect. It has been said: he meant *malih* and shortened it by deleting the alif. *Al-malih* is permissible as a description of water, because water is found in the flowing channels being salted by something else, and salty by its own nature. But it is more proper to say *ma'un milh*, described by a verbal noun, meaning: water possessing saltness; and description by this is like *hilf* and *nidw* among attributes.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): what is the meaning of ﴿a forbidding ban﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:22)? (I answer): it is the phrase that one who seeks refuge says, and we have explained it. Here it is used figuratively, as if each of the two seas seeks refuge from its companion and says to it: ﴿a forbidding ban﴾, just as He said: ﴿they do not transgress﴾ (Ar-Rahman 55:20), meaning: neither of them transgresses upon its companion by mingling. So the negation of transgression there is like seeking refuge here; He made each of them in the form of one transgressing against its companion, so it seeks refuge from it. This is among the finest metaphors and the clearest evidence of eloquence. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that ﴿a forbidding ban﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:22) is conjoined to *barzakh* (a barrier), as an object conjoined to an object; al-Hawfi also parsed it this way. According to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, it would be by implying an allegorical speech, meaning: and they say—each of the two to its companion—﴿a forbidding ban﴾.

The apparent meaning is the generality of humankind, who are the children of Adam, and *bashar* (human) applies to the singular and the plural. It has been said: by *nasab* (lineage) is meant Adam, and by *sihr* (marriage kinship) is meant Eve. It has been said: *nasab* is the sons and *sihr* the daughters. As for *min al-ma'* (from water), it is either the drop of semen, or that it is the origin of the creation of every living thing. Lineage and marriage kinship cover every relationship between two human beings: lineage is that one shares with another a father and mother, whether near or distant; and marriage kinship is the bonds of marriage. Ali ibn Abi Talib said: lineage is what marriage with it is not permitted, and marriage kinship is the kinship of nursing. From Tawus: nursing is of marriage kinship. From Ali: marriage kinship is what marriage with it is permitted, and lineage is what marriage with it is not permitted. Al-Dahhak said: marriage kinship is the kinship of nursing. Ibn Sirin said: it was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and Ali, because lineage and marriage kinship were combined in him. Ibn Atiyyah said: their combining is a sanctity of prohibition until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful.﴾ In that He created from one drop of semen a human being of two kinds: male and female.

When He mentioned the signs of His power, and what He bestowed upon His servants of wondrous creations, it was thereby established that He is the one deserving of worship, for He benefits and harms, and this refutes the corrupt intellects of the polytheists who worship idols. The apparent meaning is that *al-kafir* (the disbeliever) is a generic noun, and thus it is general. It has been said: it is Abu Jahl, and the verse was revealed concerning him. Ikrimah said: *al-kafir* here is Iblis. *Al-zahir* and *al-mudahir* are like *al-mu'in* and *al-mu'awin* (helper and assistant); this was said by Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. The form *fa'il* in the sense of *mufa'il* is common. The meaning is that the disbeliever aids Satan against his Lord through enmity and associating partners with Him. It has been said: the meaning is that the one who does this act, namely worshipping what neither benefits nor harms, is against his Lord, insignificant and despised, from their saying: "I put him behind me (*zahartu bihi*)" when you leave him behind your back and do not turn to him. This is like His saying: ﴿those have no portion﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:77), and the verse continues; this was said by al-Tabari. It has also been said: "against his Lord" means: a helper against the friends of God. It has been said: a helper for the polytheists in preventing God from being declared One.

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bearer of good news and a warner.﴾ He consoled His Prophet with this, meaning: do not be concerned about them, and do not let your soul go to waste over them in sorrows. You are only a Messenger who gives good news to the believers of Paradise and warns the disbelievers of the Fire, and you are not held responsible for their faith, all of them. Then the Exalted commanded him to argue against them, removing the aspects of accusation, with His saying: ﴿Say: I do not ask of you any wage for it﴾, meaning: I do not seek wealth or any benefit that is specifically for me. The pronoun in *'alayhi* (for it) refers to the good news and warning, or to the Qur'an, or to the conveying of the message; there are opinions. The apparent meaning of *illa man sha'a* (except whoever wills) is that it is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception not of the same kind), and this is what the majority said. Accordingly, it has been said: "But whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, let him do so." It has been said: "But whoever spends in the way of God and in striving against His enemies, he is my reward." It has been said that it is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*) with an elided noun, its estimate being: except the wage of one who takes a way to his Lord, meaning: except the wage of one who believes, that is, the wage accruing to me for calling him to faith and his acceptance of it, since the Exalted rewards me for that. It has been said: except the wage of one who believes, meaning by the wage the spending in the way of God; that is, I do not ask you for any wage except spending in the way of God, so He made spending the wage.

When He informed that he had weaned himself from asking them for anything, the Exalted commanded him to entrust his affair to Him, to trust Him, and to rely upon Him; He is the one who undertakes His support and the manifestation of His religion. The Exalted described Himself with the attribute which entails trust, in His saying: ﴿the Living who does not die﴾, because this meaning belongs specifically to the Exalted and to no other living being, as He said: ﴿everything perishes except His Face﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:88). One of the early scholars recited this verse and said: it is not valid for a person of intellect to trust, after it, in any created being. Then He commanded him to glorify Him and to praise Him, combined with extolling Him; because glorification has its place in the belief of the heart, and praise has its place in the tongue agreeing with belief. In a hadith: "Whoever says: Glory be to God and praise be to Him, one hundred times, his sins are forgiven even if they were like the foam of the sea." These are the two words that are light upon the tongue and heavy in the scale. ﴿And sufficient is He as one who is aware of the sins of His servants.﴾ He meant that nothing of the affairs of His servants is entrusted to him, whether they believe or disbelieve, and that He is aware of their conditions, sufficient for the recompense of their deeds. In this sentence is consolation for the Messenger and a warning for the disbeliever. In some reports: "Sufficient for you as victory is that your enemy is disobedient." It is an expression intended for emphasis; you say: "Knowledge is sufficient as beauty," and "Good manners are sufficient as wealth," meaning: it is enough for you, you need nothing beyond it, because He is aware of their conditions and able to requite them.

When He commanded him with trust and glorification, and mentioned the attribute of everlasting life, He mentioned what indicates complete power, which is the bringing into being of this world. The discussion of a similar statement has preceded. *Alladhi* (the one who) may be an attribute of *al-Hayy alladhi la yamutu* (the Living who does not die). It becomes definite with the reading of Zayd ibn Ali, *al-Rahmani* in the genitive. As for the reading of the majority, *al-Rahmanu* in the nominative, then *alladhi* may be an attribute of *al-Hayy*, and *al-Rahmanu* the predicate of an elided subject. It may also be that *alladhi* is the subject and *al-Rahmanu* its predicate; or that *alladhi* is the predicate of an elided subject, and *al-Rahmanu* an attribute of it; or that *alladhi* is in the accusative by an implied "I mean." According to the view of al-Akhfash, *al-Rahmanu* may be the subject, and *fas'al* (then ask) its predicate, and it is parsed according to the principle of the poet's saying:

*And a sayer said: "Khawlan, marry their young woman."*

They also permitted that *al-Rahmanu* be a substitute for the concealed pronoun in *istawa* (He established Himself). The apparent meaning is that *bihi* (about Him) is attached to *fas'al* (then ask), and the *ba'* remains un-transposed in the sense of *'an* (about). *Khabiran* (aware) is one of the attributes of God, as you say: "I met Zayd, a lion," and "I met Zayd, the sea," meaning that he is the lion in courage and the sea in generosity. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, is the Subtle, the Knowing, the Aware, and the meaning is: "then ask" God, the Aware of things, the Knower of their realities. Ibn Atiyyah said: *khabiran* on this reading is in the accusative either by the occurrence of the asking, or as a emphasizing circumstantial accusative (*hal mu'akkida*), as He said: ﴿and it is the truth confirming﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:91). This circumstance is not a changing one, since the lofty attribute does not change. End of quotation. This parsing is built on the premise that it is as you say: "If you met so-and-so, you would meet the sea through him in generosity," meaning: you would meet from him. The meaning is: "then ask God about every matter," and its being accusative as an emphasizing circumstantial accusative on this estimate is not valid; it is only valid that it be a direct object. It is permitted that the *ba'* be in the sense of *'an*, meaning: "then ask" about Him, "aware," as the poet said:

*If you ask me about women, then I am knowing of the ailments of women, a physician.*

وهُوَ قَوْلُ الأخْفَشِ والزَّجّاجِ. ويَكُونَ (خَبِيرًا) لَيْسَ مِن صِفاتِ اللَّهِ هُنا، كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: اسْألْ عَنِ الرَّحْمَنِ الخُبَراءَ جِبْرِيلَ والعُلَماءَ وأهْلَ الكُتُبِ المُنَزَّلَةِ، وإنْ جَعَلْتَ (بِهِ) مُتَعَلِّقًا بِخَبِيرًا كانَ المَعْنى (فاسْألْ) عَنِ اللَّهِ الخُبَراءَ بِهِ. وقالَ الكَلْبِيُّ: مَعْناهُ (فاسْألْ) خَبِيرًا بِهِ، و(بِهِ) يَعُودُ إلى ما ذُكِرَ مِن خَلْقِ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ [p-٥٠٩] والِاسْتِواءِ عَلى العَرْشِ، وذَلِكَ الخَبِيرُ هو اللَّهُ تَعالى؛ لِأنَّهُ لا دَلِيلَ في العَقْلِ عَلى كَيْفِيَّةِ خَلْقِ ذَلِكَ، فَلا يَعْلَمُها إلّا اللَّهُ. وعَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ: الخَبِيرُ جِبْرِيلُ وقُدِّمَ لِرُءُوسِ الآيِ. وقالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: الباءُ في (بِهِ) صِلَةُ سَلْ، كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿سَألَ سائِلٌ بِعَذابٍ﴾ [المعارج: ١] (أي: "سأل سائل عن عذاب واقع")، كَما يَكُونُ (عَنْ) صِلَتَهُ في نَحْوِ ﴿ثُمَّ لَتُسْألُنَّ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَنِ النَّعِيمِ﴾ [التكاثر: ٨] ("ثم لتُسألُنّ يومئذٍ عن النعيم")، أوْ صِلَةُ (خَبِيرًا) بِهِ، فَتَجْعَلُ (خَبِيرًا) مَفْعُولًا، أيْ: فَسَلْ عَنْهُ رَجُلًا عارِفًا يُخْبِرْكَ بِرَحْمَتِهِ، أوْ فَسَلْ رَجُلًا خَبِيرًا بِهِ وبِرَحْمَتِهِ، أوْ فَسَلْ بِسُؤالِهِ خَبِيرًا. كَقَوْلِكَ: رَأيْتُ بِهِ أسَدًا، أيْ: رَأيْتُ بِرُؤْيَتِهِ، والمَعْنى إنْ سَألْتَهُ وجَدْتَهُ خَبِيرًا بِجَعْلِهِ حالًا عَنْ بِهِ تُرِيدُ فَسَلْ عَنْهُ عالِمًا بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ. وقِيلَ: (الرَّحْمَنُ) اسْمٌ مِن أسْماءِ اللَّهِ مَذْكُورٌ في الكُتُبِ المُتَقَدِّمَةِ ولَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَهُ. فَقِيلَ: فَسَلْ بِهَذا الِاسْمِ مَن يُخْبِرُكَ مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ حَتّى يُعْرَفَ مَن يُنْكِرُهُ، ومِن ثَمَّ كانُوا يَقُولُونَ: ما نَعْرِفُ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا الَّذِي في اليَمامَةِ يَعْنُونَ مُسَيْلِمَةَ، وكانَ يُقالُ لَهُ رَحْمَنُ اليَمامَةِ، انْتَهى.

﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ اسْجُدُوا لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾ وكانَتْ قُرَيْشٌ لا تَعْرِفُ هَذا في أسْماءِ اللَّهِ غالَطَتْ قُرَيْشٌ بِذَلِكَ فَقالَتْ: إنَّ مُحَمَّدًا يَأْمُرُنا بِعِبادَةِ رَحْمَنِ اليَمامَةِ، نَزَلَتْ ﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ﴾، و(ما) سُؤالٌ عَنِ المَجْهُولِ، فَيَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ سُؤالًا عَنِ المُسَمّى بِهِ؛ لِأنَّهم ما كانُوا يَعْرِفُونَهُ بِهَذا الِاسْمِ، ويَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ سُؤالًا عَنْ مَعْناهُ؛ لِأنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُسْتَعْمَلًا في كَلامِهِمْ كَما يُسْتَعْمَلُ الرَّحِيمُ والرَّحُومُ والرّاحِمُ، أوْ لِأنَّهم أنْكَرُوا إطْلاقَهُ عَلى اللَّهِ؛ قالَهُ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ. والَّذِي يَظْهَرُ أنَّهم لَمّا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ﴿اسْجُدُوا لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾ فَذُكِرَتِ الصِّفَةُ المُقْتَضِيَةُ لِلْمُبالَغَةِ في الرَّحْمَةِ، والكَلِمَةُ عَرَبِيَّةٌ لا يُنْكَرُ وضْعُها، أظْهَرُوا التَّجاهُلَ بِهَذِهِ الصِّفَةِ الَّتِي لِلَّهِ مُغالَطَةً مِنهم ووَقاحَةً فَقالُوا: ﴿وما الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ ("And what is the Most Merciful?")، وهم عارِفُونَ بِهِ وبِصِفَتِهِ الرَّحْمانِيَّةِ، وهَذا كَما قالَ فِرْعَوْنُ: ﴿وما رَبُّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ("And what is the Lord of the worlds?") [الشعراء: ٢٣] حِينَ قالَ لَهُ مُوسى: ﴿إنّى رَسُولٌ مِن رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ("I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds") [الأعراف: ١٠٤]، عَلى سَبِيلِ المُناكَرَةِ، وهو عالِمٌ بِرَبِّ العالَمِينَ. كَما قالَ مُوسى: ﴿لَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ ما أنْزَلَ هَؤُلاءِ إلّا رَبُّ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ بَصائِرَ﴾ ("You certainly know that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence") [الإسراء: ١٠٢] فَكَذَلِكَ كُفّارُ قُرَيْشٍ اسْتَفْهَمُوا عَنِ الرَّحْمَنِ اسْتِفْهامَ مَن يَجْهَلُهُ، وهم عالِمُونَ بِهِ، فَعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا مُسَيْلِمَةَ، وعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: مَن لا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا مُسَيْلِمَةَ. فالمَعْنى أنَسْجَدُ لِمُسَيْلِمَةَ، وعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: لا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ بِالكُلِّيَّةِ فالمَعْنى ﴿أنَسْجُدُ لِما تَأْمُرُنا﴾ ("Shall we prostrate to what you command us?") مِن غَيْرِ عِلْمٍ بِبَيانِهِ. والقائِلُ (اسْجُدُوا) الرَّسُولُ أوِ اللَّهُ عَلى لِسانِ رَسُولِهِ. وقَرَأ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ والأسْوَدُ بْنُ يَزِيدَ وحَمْزَةُ والكِسائِيُّ ”يَأْمُرُ“ بِالياءِ مِن تَحْتُ، أيْ: يَأْمُرُنا مُحَمَّدٌ، والكِنايَةُ عَنْهُ أوِ المُسَمّى الرَّحْمَنَ ولا نَعْرِفُهُ. وقَرَأ باقِي السَّبْعَةِ بِالتّاءِ خِطابًا لِلرَّسُولِ. ومَفْعُولُ (تَأْمُرُنا) الثّانِي مَحْذُوفٌ لِدَلالَةِ الكَلامِ عَلَيْهِ، تَقْدِيرُهُ يَأْمُرُنا سُجُودَهُ نَحْوَ قَوْلِهِمْ: أمَرْتُكَ الخَيْرَ. (وزادَهم) أيْ: هَذا القَوْلُ، وهو الأمْرُ بِالسُّجُودِ لِلرَّحْمَنِ، (زادَهم) ضَلالًا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ مَعَ ضَلالِهِمُ السّابِقِ، وكانَ حَقُّهُ أنْ يَكُونَ باعِثًا عَلى فِعْلِ السُّجُودِ والقَبُولِ. وقالَ الضَّحّاكُ: سَجَدَ أبُو بَكْرٍ وعُمَرُ وعُثْمانُ وعَلِيٌّ وعُثْمانُ بْنُ مَظْعُونٍ وعَمْرُو ابْنُ غَلَسَةَ، فَرَآهُمُ المُشْرِكُونَ فَأخَذُوا في ناحِيَةِ المَسْجِدِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ، فَهَذا المُرادُ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وزادَهم نُفُورًا﴾ ("and it increased them in aversion")، ومَعْنى (نُفُورًا): فِرارًا.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verses 51–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town.﴾ When the Exalted knew what the Messenger endured of harm from his people, He informed him that, had He willed, He would have sent a warner to every town, so that the matter would be lighter for you. But He magnified your reward and your rank, since He made your warning general to all of mankind, and singled you out with it so that your reward would increase, for reward comes in proportion to the abundance of striving, and so that He would gather for you the good deeds of those who believe in you, since you are their founder.

﴿So do not obey the disbelievers.﴾ This means the disbelievers of Quraysh. They had listened to him and desired that he return to the religion of their forefathers, and they would make him king over them and gather great wealth for him. So the Exalted forbade him to obey them, until he would show them that he had no desire for any of that, for his desire was only in calling to God and believing in Him.

﴿And strive against them with it.﴾ That is, with the Qur'an, or with Islam, or with the sword, or by abandoning their obedience. The word *jihadan* (struggle) is a verbal noun described by *kabiran* (great), because it is incumbent upon him, peace be upon him, to strive against the entire world, so it is a great struggle.

*Maraja* (he mixed them) means: he mixed the two together, or he poured one of them into the other, or he let them flow; these are opinions. The apparent meaning is that by "the two seas" is meant abundant sweet water and abundant salt water. It has also been said that they are two specific seas: the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome. It has been said that they are the sea of the heavens and the sea of the earth, which meet every year; this was reported from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: the waters of the rivers that fall into the salt sea, and this is close to the first opinion. Ibn Atiyyah said: the purpose of the verse is to draw attention to the power of God and the perfection of His creation of things, in that He spread in the earth abundant sweet waters from rivers, springs and wells, and placed them amid the bitter water, and placed the bitter water amid them; so you see the sea surrounded on its two banks by sweet waters, and the sea's water reaching the islands and the like, surrounded by bitter water. *Al-barzakh* and *al-hijr* are that which separates the two of them, of earth and barrier; this was said by al-Hasan. This accords with the view of those who say that *maraja* means *ajra* (he let flow). It has also been said that *al-barzakh* refers to the lands and deserts, so the two do not differ except through the removal of the barrier on the Day of Resurrection. Most of the scholars said: the barrier is a prevention from the power of God. Al-Zajjaj said: they are mixed in the sight of the eye, yet separated by the power of God. In Basra, the sweet water flows down from it into the Tigris toward the sea, and the tide comes from the sea, [p. 507] and the two meet without mixing: the sea's water is intensely green, and the Tigris's water is reddish. The water-drawer draws from the Tigris water here with us, and nothing mixes with it. The Nile of Egypt, in its flood, cuts through the salt sea, cutting it in such a way that it remains a flowing reddish river in the middle of the salt water, so that people may draw water from it. The waters appear as pieces in the middle of the salt sea, and people say: this is ice-water, and they give drink from it from the middle of the sea.

Talha and Qutayba, from al-Kisa'i, read *malih* with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *lam*, and likewise in Fatir. Abu Hatim said: this is an objectionable reading. Abu al-Fath said: he meant *malih* and deleted the alif, as it was deleted from *barad* (cold), meaning *barid*. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in the book *al-Lawami*: it is an anomalous and rare dialect. It has been said: he meant *malih* and shortened it by deleting the alif. *Al-malih* is permissible as a description of water, because water is found in the flowing channels being salted by something else, and salty by its own nature. But it is more proper to say *ma'un milh*, described by a verbal noun, meaning: water possessing saltness; and description by this is like *hilf* and *nidw* among attributes.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): what is the meaning of ﴿a forbidding ban﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:22)? (I answer): it is the phrase that one who seeks refuge says, and we have explained it. Here it is used figuratively, as if each of the two seas seeks refuge from its companion and says to it: ﴿a forbidding ban﴾, just as He said: ﴿they do not transgress﴾ (Ar-Rahman 55:20), meaning: neither of them transgresses upon its companion by mingling. So the negation of transgression there is like seeking refuge here; He made each of them in the form of one transgressing against its companion, so it seeks refuge from it. This is among the finest metaphors and the clearest evidence of eloquence. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that ﴿a forbidding ban﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:22) is conjoined to *barzakh* (a barrier), as an object conjoined to an object; al-Hawfi also parsed it this way. According to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, it would be by implying an allegorical speech, meaning: and they say—each of the two to its companion—﴿a forbidding ban﴾.

The apparent meaning is the generality of humankind, who are the children of Adam, and *bashar* (human) applies to the singular and the plural. It has been said: by *nasab* (lineage) is meant Adam, and by *sihr* (marriage kinship) is meant Eve. It has been said: *nasab* is the sons and *sihr* the daughters. As for *min al-ma'* (from water), it is either the drop of semen, or that it is the origin of the creation of every living thing. Lineage and marriage kinship cover every relationship between two human beings: lineage is that one shares with another a father and mother, whether near or distant; and marriage kinship is the bonds of marriage. Ali ibn Abi Talib said: lineage is what marriage with it is not permitted, and marriage kinship is the kinship of nursing. From Tawus: nursing is of marriage kinship. From Ali: marriage kinship is what marriage with it is permitted, and lineage is what marriage with it is not permitted. Al-Dahhak said: marriage kinship is the kinship of nursing. Ibn Sirin said: it was revealed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and Ali, because lineage and marriage kinship were combined in him. Ibn Atiyyah said: their combining is a sanctity of prohibition until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful.﴾ In that He created from one drop of semen a human being of two kinds: male and female.

When He mentioned the signs of His power, and what He bestowed upon His servants of wondrous creations, it was thereby established that He is the one deserving of worship, for He benefits and harms, and this refutes the corrupt intellects of the polytheists who worship idols. The apparent meaning is that *al-kafir* (the disbeliever) is a generic noun, and thus it is general. It has been said: it is Abu Jahl, and the verse was revealed concerning him. Ikrimah said: *al-kafir* here is Iblis. *Al-zahir* and *al-mudahir* are like *al-mu'in* and *al-mu'awin* (helper and assistant); this was said by Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. The form *fa'il* in the sense of *mufa'il* is common. The meaning is that the disbeliever aids Satan against his Lord through enmity and associating partners with Him. It has been said: the meaning is that the one who does this act, namely worshipping what neither benefits nor harms, is against his Lord, insignificant and despised, from their saying: "I put him behind me (*zahartu bihi*)" when you leave him behind your back and do not turn to him. This is like His saying: ﴿those have no portion﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:77), and the verse continues; this was said by al-Tabari. It has also been said: "against his Lord" means: a helper against the friends of God. It has been said: a helper for the polytheists in preventing God from being declared One.

﴿And We have not sent you except as a bearer of good news and a warner.﴾ He consoled His Prophet with this, meaning: do not be concerned about them, and do not let your soul go to waste over them in sorrows. You are only a Messenger who gives good news to the believers of Paradise and warns the disbelievers of the Fire, and you are not held responsible for their faith, all of them. Then the Exalted commanded him to argue against them, removing the aspects of accusation, with His saying: ﴿Say: I do not ask of you any wage for it﴾, meaning: I do not seek wealth or any benefit that is specifically for me. The pronoun in *'alayhi* (for it) refers to the good news and warning, or to the Qur'an, or to the conveying of the message; there are opinions. The apparent meaning of *illa man sha'a* (except whoever wills) is that it is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception not of the same kind), and this is what the majority said. Accordingly, it has been said: "But whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, let him do so." It has been said: "But whoever spends in the way of God and in striving against His enemies, he is my reward." It has been said that it is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*) with an elided noun, its estimate being: except the wage of one who takes a way to his Lord, meaning: except the wage of one who believes, that is, the wage accruing to me for calling him to faith and his acceptance of it, since the Exalted rewards me for that. It has been said: except the wage of one who believes, meaning by the wage the spending in the way of God; that is, I do not ask you for any wage except spending in the way of God, so He made spending the wage.

When He informed that he had weaned himself from asking them for anything, the Exalted commanded him to entrust his affair to Him, to trust Him, and to rely upon Him; He is the one who undertakes His support and the manifestation of His religion. The Exalted described Himself with the attribute which entails trust, in His saying: ﴿the Living who does not die﴾, because this meaning belongs specifically to the Exalted and to no other living being, as He said: ﴿everything perishes except His Face﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:88). One of the early scholars recited this verse and said: it is not valid for a person of intellect to trust, after it, in any created being. Then He commanded him to glorify Him and to praise Him, combined with extolling Him; because glorification has its place in the belief of the heart, and praise has its place in the tongue agreeing with belief. In a hadith: "Whoever says: Glory be to God and praise be to Him, one hundred times, his sins are forgiven even if they were like the foam of the sea." These are the two words that are light upon the tongue and heavy in the scale. ﴿And sufficient is He as one who is aware of the sins of His servants.﴾ He meant that nothing of the affairs of His servants is entrusted to him, whether they believe or disbelieve, and that He is aware of their conditions, sufficient for the recompense of their deeds. In this sentence is consolation for the Messenger and a warning for the disbeliever. In some reports: "Sufficient for you as victory is that your enemy is disobedient." It is an expression intended for emphasis; you say: "Knowledge is sufficient as beauty," and "Good manners are sufficient as wealth," meaning: it is enough for you, you need nothing beyond it, because He is aware of their conditions and able to requite them.

When He commanded him with trust and glorification, and mentioned the attribute of everlasting life, He mentioned what indicates complete power, which is the bringing into being of this world. The discussion of a similar statement has preceded. *Alladhi* (the one who) may be an attribute of *al-Hayy alladhi la yamutu* (the Living who does not die). It becomes definite with the reading of Zayd ibn Ali, *al-Rahmani* in the genitive. As for the reading of the majority, *al-Rahmanu* in the nominative, then *alladhi* may be an attribute of *al-Hayy*, and *al-Rahmanu* the predicate of an elided subject. It may also be that *alladhi* is the subject and *al-Rahmanu* its predicate; or that *alladhi* is the predicate of an elided subject, and *al-Rahmanu* an attribute of it; or that *alladhi* is in the accusative by an implied "I mean." According to the view of al-Akhfash, *al-Rahmanu* may be the subject, and *fas'al* (then ask) its predicate, and it is parsed according to the principle of the poet's saying:

*And a sayer said: "Khawlan, marry their young woman."*

They also permitted that *al-Rahmanu* be a substitute for the concealed pronoun in *istawa* (He established Himself). The apparent meaning is that *bihi* (about Him) is attached to *fas'al* (then ask), and the *ba'* remains un-transposed in the sense of *'an* (about). *Khabiran* (aware) is one of the attributes of God, as you say: "I met Zayd, a lion," and "I met Zayd, the sea," meaning that he is the lion in courage and the sea in generosity. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, is the Subtle, the Knowing, the Aware, and the meaning is: "then ask" God, the Aware of things, the Knower of their realities. Ibn Atiyyah said: *khabiran* on this reading is in the accusative either by the occurrence of the asking, or as a emphasizing circumstantial accusative (*hal mu'akkida*), as He said: ﴿and it is the truth confirming﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:91). This circumstance is not a changing one, since the lofty attribute does not change. End of quotation. This parsing is built on the premise that it is as you say: "If you met so-and-so, you would meet the sea through him in generosity," meaning: you would meet from him. The meaning is: "then ask God about every matter," and its being accusative as an emphasizing circumstantial accusative on this estimate is not valid; it is only valid that it be a direct object. It is permitted that the *ba'* be in the sense of *'an*, meaning: "then ask" about Him, "aware," as the poet said:

*If you ask me about women, then I am knowing of the ailments of women, a physician.*

وهُوَ قَوْلُ الأخْفَشِ والزَّجّاجِ. ويَكُونَ (خَبِيرًا) لَيْسَ مِن صِفاتِ اللَّهِ هُنا، كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: اسْألْ عَنِ الرَّحْمَنِ الخُبَراءَ جِبْرِيلَ والعُلَماءَ وأهْلَ الكُتُبِ المُنَزَّلَةِ، وإنْ جَعَلْتَ (بِهِ) مُتَعَلِّقًا بِخَبِيرًا كانَ المَعْنى (فاسْألْ) عَنِ اللَّهِ الخُبَراءَ بِهِ. وقالَ الكَلْبِيُّ: مَعْناهُ (فاسْألْ) خَبِيرًا بِهِ، و(بِهِ) يَعُودُ إلى ما ذُكِرَ مِن خَلْقِ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ [p-٥٠٩] والِاسْتِواءِ عَلى العَرْشِ، وذَلِكَ الخَبِيرُ هو اللَّهُ تَعالى؛ لِأنَّهُ لا دَلِيلَ في العَقْلِ عَلى كَيْفِيَّةِ خَلْقِ ذَلِكَ، فَلا يَعْلَمُها إلّا اللَّهُ. وعَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ: الخَبِيرُ جِبْرِيلُ وقُدِّمَ لِرُءُوسِ الآيِ. وقالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: الباءُ في (بِهِ) صِلَةُ سَلْ، كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿سَألَ سائِلٌ بِعَذابٍ﴾ [المعارج: ١] (أي: "سأل سائل عن عذاب واقع")، كَما يَكُونُ (عَنْ) صِلَتَهُ في نَحْوِ ﴿ثُمَّ لَتُسْألُنَّ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَنِ النَّعِيمِ﴾ [التكاثر: ٨] ("ثم لتُسألُنّ يومئذٍ عن النعيم")، أوْ صِلَةُ (خَبِيرًا) بِهِ، فَتَجْعَلُ (خَبِيرًا) مَفْعُولًا، أيْ: فَسَلْ عَنْهُ رَجُلًا عارِفًا يُخْبِرْكَ بِرَحْمَتِهِ، أوْ فَسَلْ رَجُلًا خَبِيرًا بِهِ وبِرَحْمَتِهِ، أوْ فَسَلْ بِسُؤالِهِ خَبِيرًا. كَقَوْلِكَ: رَأيْتُ بِهِ أسَدًا، أيْ: رَأيْتُ بِرُؤْيَتِهِ، والمَعْنى إنْ سَألْتَهُ وجَدْتَهُ خَبِيرًا بِجَعْلِهِ حالًا عَنْ بِهِ تُرِيدُ فَسَلْ عَنْهُ عالِمًا بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ. وقِيلَ: (الرَّحْمَنُ) اسْمٌ مِن أسْماءِ اللَّهِ مَذْكُورٌ في الكُتُبِ المُتَقَدِّمَةِ ولَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَهُ. فَقِيلَ: فَسَلْ بِهَذا الِاسْمِ مَن يُخْبِرُكَ مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ حَتّى يُعْرَفَ مَن يُنْكِرُهُ، ومِن ثَمَّ كانُوا يَقُولُونَ: ما نَعْرِفُ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا الَّذِي في اليَمامَةِ يَعْنُونَ مُسَيْلِمَةَ، وكانَ يُقالُ لَهُ رَحْمَنُ اليَمامَةِ، انْتَهى.

﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ اسْجُدُوا لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾ وكانَتْ قُرَيْشٌ لا تَعْرِفُ هَذا في أسْماءِ اللَّهِ غالَطَتْ قُرَيْشٌ بِذَلِكَ فَقالَتْ: إنَّ مُحَمَّدًا يَأْمُرُنا بِعِبادَةِ رَحْمَنِ اليَمامَةِ، نَزَلَتْ ﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ﴾، و(ما) سُؤالٌ عَنِ المَجْهُولِ، فَيَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ سُؤالًا عَنِ المُسَمّى بِهِ؛ لِأنَّهم ما كانُوا يَعْرِفُونَهُ بِهَذا الِاسْمِ، ويَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ سُؤالًا عَنْ مَعْناهُ؛ لِأنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُسْتَعْمَلًا في كَلامِهِمْ كَما يُسْتَعْمَلُ الرَّحِيمُ والرَّحُومُ والرّاحِمُ، أوْ لِأنَّهم أنْكَرُوا إطْلاقَهُ عَلى اللَّهِ؛ قالَهُ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ. والَّذِي يَظْهَرُ أنَّهم لَمّا قِيلَ لَهُمُ ﴿اسْجُدُوا لِلرَّحْمَنِ﴾ فَذُكِرَتِ الصِّفَةُ المُقْتَضِيَةُ لِلْمُبالَغَةِ في الرَّحْمَةِ، والكَلِمَةُ عَرَبِيَّةٌ لا يُنْكَرُ وضْعُها، أظْهَرُوا التَّجاهُلَ بِهَذِهِ الصِّفَةِ الَّتِي لِلَّهِ مُغالَطَةً مِنهم ووَقاحَةً فَقالُوا: ﴿وما الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ ("And what is the Most Merciful?")، وهم عارِفُونَ بِهِ وبِصِفَتِهِ الرَّحْمانِيَّةِ، وهَذا كَما قالَ فِرْعَوْنُ: ﴿وما رَبُّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ("And what is the Lord of the worlds?") [الشعراء: ٢٣] حِينَ قالَ لَهُ مُوسى: ﴿إنّى رَسُولٌ مِن رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ("I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds") [الأعراف: ١٠٤]، عَلى سَبِيلِ المُناكَرَةِ، وهو عالِمٌ بِرَبِّ العالَمِينَ. كَما قالَ مُوسى: ﴿لَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ ما أنْزَلَ هَؤُلاءِ إلّا رَبُّ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ بَصائِرَ﴾ ("You certainly know that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence") [الإسراء: ١٠٢] فَكَذَلِكَ كُفّارُ قُرَيْشٍ اسْتَفْهَمُوا عَنِ الرَّحْمَنِ اسْتِفْهامَ مَن يَجْهَلُهُ، وهم عالِمُونَ بِهِ، فَعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا مُسَيْلِمَةَ، وعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: مَن لا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ إلّا مُسَيْلِمَةَ. فالمَعْنى أنَسْجَدُ لِمُسَيْلِمَةَ، وعَلى قَوْلِ مَن قالَ: لا يَعْرِفُونَ الرَّحْمَنَ بِالكُلِّيَّةِ فالمَعْنى ﴿أنَسْجُدُ لِما تَأْمُرُنا﴾ ("Shall we prostrate to what you command us?") مِن غَيْرِ عِلْمٍ بِبَيانِهِ. والقائِلُ (اسْجُدُوا) الرَّسُولُ أوِ اللَّهُ عَلى لِسانِ رَسُولِهِ. وقَرَأ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ والأسْوَدُ بْنُ يَزِيدَ وحَمْزَةُ والكِسائِيُّ ”يَأْمُرُ“ بِالياءِ مِن تَحْتُ، أيْ: يَأْمُرُنا مُحَمَّدٌ، والكِنايَةُ عَنْهُ أوِ المُسَمّى الرَّحْمَنَ ولا نَعْرِفُهُ. وقَرَأ باقِي السَّبْعَةِ بِالتّاءِ خِطابًا لِلرَّسُولِ. ومَفْعُولُ (تَأْمُرُنا) الثّانِي مَحْذُوفٌ لِدَلالَةِ الكَلامِ عَلَيْهِ، تَقْدِيرُهُ يَأْمُرُنا سُجُودَهُ نَحْوَ قَوْلِهِمْ: أمَرْتُكَ الخَيْرَ. (وزادَهم) أيْ: هَذا القَوْلُ، وهو الأمْرُ بِالسُّجُودِ لِلرَّحْمَنِ، (زادَهم) ضَلالًا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ مَعَ ضَلالِهِمُ السّابِقِ، وكانَ حَقُّهُ أنْ يَكُونَ باعِثًا عَلى فِعْلِ السُّجُودِ والقَبُولِ. وقالَ الضَّحّاكُ: سَجَدَ أبُو بَكْرٍ وعُمَرُ وعُثْمانُ وعَلِيٌّ وعُثْمانُ بْنُ مَظْعُونٍ وعَمْرُو ابْنُ غَلَسَةَ، فَرَآهُمُ المُشْرِكُونَ فَأخَذُوا في ناحِيَةِ المَسْجِدِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ، فَهَذا المُرادُ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وزادَهم نُفُورًا﴾ ("and it increased them in aversion")، ومَعْنى (نُفُورًا): فِرارًا.

(p-510) ﴿Blessed is He who placed constellations (buruj) in the sky, and placed within it a lamp and a luminous moon.﴾ ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeed each other, for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.﴾ ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing.﴾ [al-Furqan: 64] ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever a lasting torment.﴾ [al-Furqan: 65] ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and as a station.﴾ [al-Furqan: 66] ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but keep a balance between that.﴾ [al-Furqan: 67] ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit adultery; and whoever does that will meet a penalty.﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation.﴾ [al-Furqan: 69] ﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds, and Allah is ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ [al-Furqan: 70] ﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, indeed he turns back to Allah with a [sincere] return.﴾ [al-Furqan: 71] ﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity.﴾ [al-Furqan: 72] ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind.﴾ [al-Furqan: 73] ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous.﴾ [al-Furqan: 74] ﴿Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for what they endured, and they will be met therein with greeting and peace.﴾ [al-Furqan: 75] ﴿Abiding therein; excellent is it as a place of settlement and as a station.﴾ [al-Furqan: 76] ﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so the punishment will be inevitable."﴾ [al-Furqan: 77].

(p-511) When the Quraysh made their question about His name, which is "al-Rahman," a question about something unknown, this verse was revealed explicitly describing His attributes by which He is known and which necessitate acknowledging His divinity. Its connection to what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and described Himself as "al-Rahman," and they asked about what He placed in the sky of luminaries and what He arranged of the state of night and day, they would have hastened to prostrate and worship the Most Merciful. Then He alerted them to what they have a complete interest in: observing the stars, their conditions, and assigning names to them. The apparent meaning is that "al-buruj" refers to the well-known constellations among the Arabs, which are the stations of the wandering stars, and they are: Aries (al-Hamal), Taurus (al-Thawr), Gemini (al-Jawza'), Cancer (al-Saratan), Leo (al-Asad), Virgo (al-Sunbula), Libra (al-Mizan), Scorpio (al-'Aqrab), Sagittarius (al-Qaws), Capricorn (al-Jady), Aquarius (al-Dalw), and Pisces (al-Hut). They were called so because of their resemblance to what they were compared to. They were also called "buruj," which are high palaces, because for these stars they are like dwellings for their inhabitants. The derivation of "burj" is from "tabarruj" (display) because of its prominence.

It is also said: "al-buruj" here means palaces in Paradise. Al-A'mash said: The companions of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) used to recite it as ﴿fi al-sama'﴾ [in the sky] "qusuran" [palaces]. Abu Salih said: "al-buruj" here means the great stars. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The view that they are palaces in Paradise diminishes the purpose of the verse, which is to draw attention to perceptible things by which proof is established against every denier of Allah or ignorant person.

"Barada flows, clapping with the pure, flowing wine."

He means the water of Barada. It is also said: it is a noun of form, like "rikbah" (manner of riding), and the noun of form is used as a state in their saying: "I passed by water in the manner of a man's sitting (qi'dat rajul)." "Upon them the she-camels and the gazelles walk in succession."

And another says, describing a woman who moved from one dwelling in winter to another in summer habitually:

"And for her, at al-Matirun, when the ant has eaten what it gathered,
She has a succession, until when it rises high, she settles from Jilliq at Bay'a,
In houses in the midst of a village, around which olives have ripened."

It is also said: "khilfatan" refers to increase and decrease. Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Kisa'i said: this one is black and this one is white, this one is tall and this one is short.

﴿li-man arada an yadhdhakkara﴾ [for whoever wishes to remember]. 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan said: its meaning is: for whoever wishes to remember what he missed of good and of prayer and the like in one of them, so that he makes it up in the one following it. Mujahid and others said: that is, he would take lessons from the created things (p-512) and thank Allah, exalted is He, for His blessings upon him in intellect, thought, and understanding. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "yatadhakkaru" (he remembers). The meaning is that the observer looks into their alternation and knows that there must be a transition from state to state for them, and their change from a changer and an alterer, and he derives proof from that of the greatness of His power, and the grateful one gives thanks for the blessing of rest at night and activity by day, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you night and day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73], and so that they may be two times for the one who remembers and the one who is grateful, such that whoever missed his portion of worship in one of them can perform it in the other. Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wathhab, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Talha, and Hamza read "tadhkura," the imperfect of "dhakara" in its light form.

Since the mention of the disbelievers and their condemnation came first, "for whoever wishes to remember or wishes gratitude" came, and then He mentioned the states of the believers who remember and give thanks, saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 63]. This is an idafa (annexation) of honor and favor, and it is the plural of "'abd" (servant). Ibn Bahr said: it is the plural of "'abid" (worshipper), like "sahib" and "sihab," "tajir" and "tijar," "rajil" and "rijal," meaning: those who worship Him with the true worship due to Him. The apparent view is that "wa-'ibad" is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿alladhina yamshuna﴾ [those who walk] is the predicate (khabar). It is also said: "ula'ika" is the predicate and "alladhina" is an attribute. A group of 'Abd al-Qays called the 'Ibad because Khosrow (Kisra) ruled over them, not the Arabs. It is also said that they were called that because they became devoted with the Christians of al-Hira, so they became the servants of Allah. Al-Yamani read "wa-'ubbad," the plural of "'abid" like "darib" and "durrab." Al-Hasan read "wa-'ubud" with a damma on the 'ayn and the ba'. Al-Sulami and al-Yamani read "yumashshawna," in the passive form with shaddah.

"Hawnan" means gentleness and softness. "Hawnan" is in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "walking in gentleness," or as a state, meaning they walk gently, with deliberation, tranquility, and good bearing, not stamping their feet nor flapping their sandals out of insolence and arrogance. For this reason some scholars disliked riding in the markets. Mujahid said: with forbearance and dignity. Ibn 'Abbas said: with obedience, chastity, and humility. Al-Hasan said: they are forbearing; if they are treated with ignorance, they do not respond with ignorance. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "hawnan" is an expression about their life, the duration of their lives, and their conduct; He mentioned the most important part of that, especially since walking on the earth is the mingling and association with people. Then he said: "hawnan," meaning that their whole affair is gentle, i.e., not harsh. A group went to the view that "hawnan" is linked to His saying ﴿walk upon the earth﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], meaning that walking itself is gentleness. It may be interpreted in this way: that the character of that walker is gentle, suited to his walk, so the statement returns to what we have explained. But if the intended meaning is the description of walking alone, it is invalid, because many a walker is gentle and unhurried, and yet he is a fox with a flat tail. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to lean forward slightly in his walk, as if he were walking downhill. And he, peace be upon him, is the foremost in this verse. His saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever among you walks in greed, let him walk slowly." He intended in the state of the heart and did not mean walking alone. Do you not see that the frivolous, who are lax in religion, clung only to the appearance of walking, until the poet said about them:

"All of them walk slowly, all of them seek prey."

Al-Zuhri said: the speed of walking takes away the radiance of the face, meaning slight haste, because it undermines dignity, and the good lies in moderation. Zayd ibn Aslam said: He saw in a dream someone who explained to him ﴿those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] as meaning those who do not wish to cause corruption on the earth. 'Iyad ibn Musa said: He, peace be upon him, used to lift his feet quickly in his walk, and the stride of his step was unlike the gait of one who is proud, and his bearing was intended, and all of that was with gentleness and steadiness, without haste, as he said: "Indeed, one descends only from a slope." 'Umar used to walk quickly by nature, not by affectation.

(p-510) ﴿Blessed is He who placed constellations (buruj) in the sky, and placed within it a lamp and a luminous moon.﴾ ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeed each other, for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.﴾ ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing.﴾ [al-Furqan: 64] ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever a lasting torment.﴾ [al-Furqan: 65] ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and as a station.﴾ [al-Furqan: 66] ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but keep a balance between that.﴾ [al-Furqan: 67] ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit adultery; and whoever does that will meet a penalty.﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation.﴾ [al-Furqan: 69] ﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds, and Allah is ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ [al-Furqan: 70] ﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, indeed he turns back to Allah with a [sincere] return.﴾ [al-Furqan: 71] ﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity.﴾ [al-Furqan: 72] ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind.﴾ [al-Furqan: 73] ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous.﴾ [al-Furqan: 74] ﴿Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for what they endured, and they will be met therein with greeting and peace.﴾ [al-Furqan: 75] ﴿Abiding therein; excellent is it as a place of settlement and as a station.﴾ [al-Furqan: 76] ﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so the punishment will be inevitable."﴾ [al-Furqan: 77].

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 25, verses 63–66:**

﴿When the ignorant address them﴾, i.e., with what is not fitting to address them with, ﴿they say, "Peace"﴾, i.e., a farewell peace, not a greeting, like the saying of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to his father: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ (Maryam 19:47). This is related by al-Asamm. Mujahid said: "a sound word," so it is in the accusative as the object of "they say." It was also said: it is on the assumption of an implied verb, its estimated form being "we bid peace" (sallamna): (salaman), so it is a part of the complement of the quoted clause. Ibn Atiyya said: "What I say is that 'they say' is the governing verb of (salaman), because the meaning is 'they say this utterance.'" Al-Zamakhshari said: "a greeting of peace from you," so "peace" (al-salam) is put in the place of "greeting" (al-taslim). It was also said: "they say a correct word (sadaadan) from speech by which they are safe from harm and sin." By ignorance is meant foolishness, lack of courtesy, and bad conduct, from the saying of the poet:

*Surely let no one among us act ignorantly toward us, lest we act more ignorantly than the ignorant.*

End. Al-Kalbi and Abu al-Aliyah said that it was abrogated (naskh, i.e., replaced by a later ruling) by the verse of fighting. Ibn Atiyya said: "This verse was before the verse of the sword, and what concerned the disbelievers was abrogated from it, while its ruling remained for the Muslims until the Day of Resurrection." Sibawayh mentioned this verse in his book in this context, and he spoke of no other abrogation. He preferred from it that what is meant is safety (al-salamah), not greeting (al-taslim), because the believers were never ordered to offer peace to the disbelievers. The verse is Meccan, and the verse of the sword abrogated it. In history there is a report to the effect that Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi was inclined away from Ali ibn Abi Talib. He saw in a dream that (Ali) had gone ahead of him to cross a bridge, and said to him: "You only claim this matter through a woman, while we are more entitled to it than you." He had related this to al-Ma'mun. (Al-Ma'mun) said: "I did not see in his answer the eloquence that is attributed to him." Al-Ma'mun said to him: "What did he answer you with?" He said: "He would say to me, 'Peace, peace.'" Al-Ma'mun drew his attention to this verse and said: "O uncle, he answered you with the most eloquent answer." Ibrahim was humiliated and ashamed. It seems that Ibrahim had not memorized the verse, or it had escaped him at the time of relating the story.

**Al-baytutah** (spending the night) is that the night overtakes you, whether you sleep or do not sleep, and it is the opposite of the afternoon (al-zuluf). The tribes of Bajilah and Azd al-Sarat say *bayat*, while the rest of the Arabs say *yabit*. When (Allah) mentioned their conduct by day, that they conduct themselves in the best manner, He mentioned their conduct by night. The apparent meaning is that He means the enlivening of the night with prayer, or most of it. It was also said: whoever recites any part of the Qur'an at night in prayer has spent the night prostrating and standing. It was also said: they are the two rak'ahs after maghrib and the two rak'ahs after 'isha'. It was also said: whoever performs an even number of rak'ahs and then the witr after having prayed 'isha' has entered into this verse. In this verse there is encouragement to stand in prayer at night.

He placed prostration first, although it comes later in the action, for the sake of the rhyme (al-fawasil) and because of the excellence of prostration, for it is a state in which the servant is closest to Allah. Abu al-Barhasam recited (sujudan), on the pattern of (qu'udan). He praised them by their supplication that He turn away from them the punishment of Hell, and in this is affirmation of their faith in the Resurrection and recompense. Ibn Abbas said: (gharaman) means "grievous, painful." Al-Khudri said: "constant, insistent, lasting." Al-Hasan said: "Every creditor parts from his debtor except the creditor of Hell." Al-Suddi said: "severe." They cited, as evidence that (gharaman) means "lasting," the verse of the poet, who is Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

*The day of al-yasar and the day of al-jifar were a punishment, and they were a lasting one.*

And al-A'sha said:

*If He punishes, it will be a lasting one; and if He gives abundantly, He is not concerned.*

He described them as enlivening the night while prostrating, then followed it with the mention of this their supplication, as a notice that they, despite their diligence, are fearful and entreat Allah to turn away the punishment from them.

(**Saa'at**) may mean "evil is" (bi'sat). The object of blame is omitted, and in (sa'at) there is an unspecified pronoun, and it is necessary that ﴿a dwelling place and a station﴾ be a specification (tamyiz). The estimated form is "it is evil as a dwelling place and a station," and this object of blame is the link to the clause which is the predicate of *inna*. It is also permissible that (sa'at) means "grieved," in which case the object is omitted, i.e., "it grieved them," and the subject is the pronoun of Hell. It is permissible for ﴿a dwelling place and a station﴾ to be two specifications, or to be two circumstantial clauses, one of them coordinated with the other. The apparent meaning is that the two causes are not synonymous: first He mentioned the perpetuity of its punishment, and second the evil of its place, and these are different, even though the perpetuity of punishment in a place entails blame of that place. It was also said: they are synonymous, and the apparent meaning is that it is from the speech of the supplicants and a quotation of their words. It was also said: it is from the speech of Allah, and it appears that His saying "and a station" is conjoined by way of emphasis, since settling (al-istiqrar) and dwelling (al-iqamah) are as if they were synonymous. It was also said: the "dwelling place" (al-mustaqarr) is for the sinners among the people of faith, for they settle in it but do not remain, while "dwelling" (al-iqamah) is for the disbelievers. A group recited (wa-maqaman), with a fatha on the mim, meaning "a place of standing," while the majority recite it with a damma, meaning "a place of dwelling."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verse 67–77 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They are neither extravagant nor niggardly﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jili said: Spending in what is not obedience to God is extravagance (israf), and withholding from obedience is niggardliness (iqtar). The same meaning was given by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. A man heard another man say: "There is no good in extravagance," so he said: "There is no extravagance in good." 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba said: Extravagance is that you spend the property of another. Al-Nakha'i said: It is the one who does not let anyone go hungry or naked, and does not spend an outlay which people say is extravagant. Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: They are those who do not wear clothes for beauty and do not eat food for pleasure. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz when he married him to his daughter Fatima: "What is your expenditure?" 'Umar said to him: "The good deed between the two evil ones," and then he recited the verse. Extravagance (israf) is exceeding the limit in spending, and qatr (niggardliness) is constriction, which is the opposite of extravagance. It is reported from Anas in the Sunan of Ibn Majah that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, among extravagance is that you eat whatever you desire." A poet said:

"Do not go to excess in any matter, but moderate: both extremes of the affairs are blameworthy."

Another said:

"When a man gives his soul whatever it desires, and does not restrain it, it reaches out to every falsehood.
And it drives him toward sin and shame by means of the sweetness of the fleeting thing that calls him to it."

Hatim said:

"If you have given your belly its desire, and your private part too, then you have attained the furthest point of blame, all of it."

Al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read (yaqturu) with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ta'. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ta'. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ta' with shadda, and all of these are dialects meaning constriction. Abu Hatim denied the use of the quadriliteral aqtara here, and said aqtara means became poor. From it comes ﴿And upon the straitened man according to his means﴾ [al-Baqara: 236]. He overlooked what al-Asma'i and others reported: from aqtara meaning constricted. Qiwam (the balance) is moderation between the two states. Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read (qiwaman) with a kasra. It was said: both are dialects with one meaning. It was also said: with the kasra, qiwam is that by which a thing is sustained; one says: "You are our qiwam," meaning that by which need is met, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It was said: (qiwaman) with a kasra means a limit, sufficiency and the basis of a state. And ﴿between that﴾ and (qiwaman) may be two predicates according to those who permit multiple predicates for kana; or (bayna) may be the predicate and (qiwaman) a emphatic circumstantial phrase; or (qiwaman) may be the predicate and (bayna dhalika) either an object of kana according to the view of those who hold that the defective kana governs the adverbial phrase, or a circumstantial phrase of (qiwaman), since if it were postponed it would be an attribute. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿bayna dhalika﴾ be the subject of (kana) and built because it is added to a built word, like His saying: ﴿and from the disgrace of that day﴾ [Hud: 66] in the reading of one who pronounces the mim with a fatha, with (qiwaman) as the predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Grammatically there is no harm in it, but the meaning is not strong, because what lies between extravagance and niggardliness is necessarily a balance, so there is no benefit in the predicate, which is the basis of the benefit.

He, may He be exalted, described them with the moderation that lies between excess and deficiency, and the Messenger (ﷺ) was addressed with the like in His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾ [al-Isra': 29], etc.

﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. Ibn Mas'ud asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to God while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." So God revealed its confirmation: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. It was said: Polytheists came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who had killed much and committed much adultery, and they said: "What you say and call to is indeed good; would you tell us that there is an expiation for what we have done?" Then it was revealed up to ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. It was also said: the occasion of revelation was the story of Wahshi in his Islam, in a long hadith.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He negated these great abominations from those described with those great qualities in religion, as a contrast with what the enemies of the believers, from Quraysh and others, were upon, as if it were said: "And those whom God has cleared and purified from what you are upon."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a removal of His believing servants from the attributes of the disbelievers in their worship of idols, their killing of souls by burying daughters alive, and other injustice, assassination and raids, and fornication which was permitted among them.

The explanation of the like of ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except with right﴾ [al-An'am: 151] has preceded in Surat al-An'am.

It was read (yulaqqa) with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the lam and the qaf with shadda. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Raja' read (yalqa) with an alif, as if he intended to delete the presumed damma on the alif and kept the alif.

Al-Athām in the language means punishment, and it is the recompense of sin. The poet said:

"May God recompense Ibn 'Urwa, since he became disobedient, and disobedience for him is athām."

That is: a prescribed punishment and a penalty, and Qatada and Ibn Zayd explained it thus. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Ibn Jubayr said: Athām is a valley in Hell bearing this name, which God made a punishment for the disbelievers. Abu Muslim said: al-athām is sin, and its meaning is (yalqa) the recompense of athām, so the name of the thing is applied to its recompense. Al-Hasan said: athām is one of the names of Hell. It was said: a well in it. It was said: a mountain. Ibn Mas'ud read: (yalqa ayyaman), plural of yawm, meaning hardships. One says: "a day of days" for a grievous day.

As for His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾, it appears that it refers to the whole of calling upon another god, killing a soul without right, and adultery, so the doubling is ordered upon the totality of these sins, and that doubling does not necessarily apply to each one of them. There is no doubt that the punishment of the disbelievers varies according to their crimes.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ in the passive with an alif, and (wa yakhlud) in the active. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Ibn Kathir likewise, except that they doubled the 'ayn and dropped the alif. Abu Ja'far also, and Shayba and Talha ibn Sulayman, read (nudaʻʻif) with a nun, damma, and a doubled kasra on the 'ayn, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Musarrif read (yudaʻif) with a ya' in the active, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Sulayman read (wa takhludu) with a ta' of address by way of iltifat, in the nominative, meaning: "and you, O disbeliever, will abide." Abu Haywa read (wa yukhalladu) in the passive, with a doubled lam, jussive. It was also reported from Abu 'Amr and on his authority likewise, with a single lam. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (yudaʻafu) and (wa yakhludu) with the nominative for both; likewise Ibn 'Amir and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim (yudaʻafu) and (wa yakhludu) in the passive, nominative, with a single lam. Al-A'mash with a damma on the ya' in the passive, doubled, nominative: the nominative is on resumption or circumstance, and the jussive is on substitution for (yalqa), as the poet said:

"Whenever you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firm wood and a blazing fire."

The pronoun in (fihi) refers to the punishment. The apparent view is that the repentance of a believing man who kills a soul without right is accepted, contrary to Ibn 'Abbas, and this was discussed in al-Nisa'. As for the changing of their evil deeds into good deeds, it means making their deeds in place of their former sins into obedience, and that will be the cause of God's mercy toward them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, and they refuted those who said it refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: The evil deed itself does not become a good deed, but the evil deed is erased by repentance, and the good deed is recorded along with repentance, while the disbeliever's deed is nullified and his evil deeds are established against him. Ibn al-Musayyab and Makhul interpreted that it is on the Day of Resurrection, and it has the sense of the generosity of pardon. In Muslim's book: God will, on the Day of Resurrection, change for whomever among the monotheists He wishes to forgive, his evil deeds into good deeds. They said: the evil deed is erased and a good deed is established in its place. Al-Qaffal and al-Qadi said: the punishment is changed into reward, mentioning both, and meaning what is deserved by each.

﴿Except one who repents﴾ is a connected exception from the genus, and it does not appear, because the excepted-from is judged to be one for whom ﴿the punishment will be doubled﴾, so the sense becomes: ﴿except one who repents and believes and does righteous deeds﴾, so the punishment is not doubled for him. The absence of doubling does not entail the absence of punishment other than the doubled punishment, so in my view it is better that it be a disconnected exception, meaning: but whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, ﴿those, God will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾, and when it is so, he does not suffer punishment at all. (Their evil deeds) is the second object, which originally should be restricted by a preposition, i.e., (bi-sayyi'atihim). (Good deeds) is the first object, which is the stated one, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We replaced them with two gardens, two gardens﴾ [Saba': 16]. A poet said:

"The sister of the one with two jars laughs at me: 'May God replace you with two colours: the blackness of a face and the whiteness of two eyes.'"

It appears that (whoever repents), meaning initiates repentance, will repent to God, meaning returns to His reward and His kindness. Ibn 'Atiyya said: (whoever repents) has truly grasped a firm matter, just as you say to one whose speech about a matter is praised: "Indeed you have spoken a word, O so-and-so," so likewise the verse means the praise of repentance, as if He said: he will find relief and great forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: Whoever abandons sins, regrets them and enters into righteous deeds, is by that a repenter to God, who knows the right of the repenters and does with them what they deserve; and God loves the repenting and loves the purified. It was said: whoever resolves on repentance will repent to God, so let him hasten to it and turn to God with it. It was said: (whoever repents) from his sins, he repents to Him who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evil deeds. It was said: (whoever repents) continues steadfast in repentance, so he is the true penitent before God.

﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾ returns to the mention of the attributes of the servants of the Merciful. The apparent meaning is that they do not testify to falsehood, or the testimony of falsehood; so said 'Ali and al-Baqir, and it is from testimony. It was said: the meaning is that they do not attend a gathering, from presence. Falsehood (al-zur) is idolatry and an idol, or lying, or musical instruments, or the festivals of the Christians, or a game that was in the Jahiliyya, or wailing, or gatherings in which the righteous are disparaged: these are sayings. Idolatry was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, singing by Mujahid, lying by Ibn Jurayj. In al-Kashshaf, from Qatada: gatherings of falsehood. From Ibn al-Hanafiyya: play and singing. From Mujahid: the festivals of the polytheists; and "idle talk" (laghw) is everything that should be cast aside and discarded. The meaning is: (and when they pass) by people of idle talk, (they pass by) turning away from them, honouring themselves against stopping over them or engaging with them; by His saying: ﴿And when they hear idle talk they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. End.

﴿with the signs of their Lord﴾: these are the Qur'an.

﴿لَمْ يَخِرُّوا عَلَيْها صُمًّا وعُمْيانًا﴾ The negation applies to the qualifier that follows, which is "deaf and blind," and not to the falling down (khurur) that the negation particle precedes. In the usage of the Arabs, the most common view is that the negation applies to the qualifier. The meaning is that when they are reminded of these verses, they bend over them eagerly to listen, and they turn toward the one who reminds them with attentive ears and watchful eyes. This is unlike the hypocrites and others like them, who, when reminded, are bent over the verses and turned toward the one who reminds them only outwardly, and they are "deaf and blind" in that they do not grasp them and do not perceive what is in them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rather, their falling down is in prostration and weeping, just as you say: "Zayd did not go out to war in fear," meaning that he went out only boldly and resolutely. The listener who is reminded is one whose ear is upright and whose affair is sound, so when he turns away, that is a khurur, which is a falling without order or arrangement. Although it resembles one who falls down in prostration, its basic sense is falling without order. End of quote. al-Suddi said: "They do not fall down" and "deaf and blind" describe the disbelievers, and it is an expression of their turning away and their exertion in that. He paired this with your saying: "So-and-so sat wishing," and "So-and-so stood weeping," while you did not intend to report sitting or standing, but these are preparatory phrases in speech and expression.

﴿قُرَّةَ أعْيُنٍ﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for joy and happiness, and it is derived from qurr, which means coolness. It is said: "The tears of joy are cool, and the tears of sorrow are hot." It is also said: "God cool your eye," and "God heat the eye of the enemy." Abu Tammam said:
As for the eyes of lovers, they were heated (with tears),
and as for the eyes of the gloaters, they were cooled.
It was also said that it is derived from qarar, meaning that the gaze rests on it and does not look at anything else. Abu 'Amr said: "The comfort of the eye is sleep," meaning security, because security does not come with fear. This was related by al-Qaffal. The comfort of the eyes, regarding those whose righteousness they mention, is seeing them obedient to God (p-517). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Hadrami. In the early period of Islam, a father would be guided while his son was a disbeliever, or a husband while his wife was a disbeliever, and the comfort of their eyes was in the faith of their beloved ones. Ibn 'Abbas said: The comfort of a child's eye is that you see him writing jurisprudence (fiqh). The apparent meaning is that they prayed for this so that they would be obeyed in this world and they would be gladdened by them. It was also said: They asked that God join those people with them in Paradise so that their joy would be complete. End of quote. This second view includes the first, which concerns this world, because that is the result of their faith in this world. It is clear that min here is for the inception of the end point (ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning: ﴿هَبْ لَنا﴾ grant us, from their side, what cools our eyes of obedience and righteousness. It is also permitted that min be for specification (bayan), as al-Zamakhshari said. He said: It is as if it were said: "Grant us ﴿قُرَّةَ أعْيُنٍ﴾ (comfort of the eyes)," and then the comfort was specified and explained by His saying: ﴿مِن أزْواجِنا وذُرِّيّاتِنا﴾ (from our spouses and our offspring). Its meaning is that God makes them, for them, a comfort of the eyes, from your saying: "I saw from you a lion," meaning: you are a lion. End of quote. We have previously noted that min which is for specifying the genus (bayan al-jins) must come before what it specifies, and then it comes with min of specification. This is according to the view of those who affirmed that it can be for specifying the genus. The correct view is that this meaning is not established for min.

Ibn 'Amir, the two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), and Hafs read ﴿وذُرِّيّاتِنا﴾ in the plural. The rest of the seven read it in the singular, and Talhah also read it in the singular. 'Abdullah, Abu al-Darda', and Abu Hurayrah read (qurrat) in the plural, while the majority read it in the singular. The word qurrah is indefinite to match the indefiniteness of a'yun (eyes), as if he said: "Grant us from them joy and happiness." The word a'yun comes in the form of the paucity plural (jam' qillah) rather than 'uyun, which is the form of the plurality plural (jam' kathrah), because what is meant is the eyes of the righteous, and they are few in comparison to the eyes of others. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, but it is not sound, because a'yun applies to ten and less of plurals, while the righteous do not have ten eyes; rather, their eyes are very many. Even if their eyes are few in comparison to the eyes of others, they are so many as to be uncountable. The word imaman is in the singular, either because the singular is sufficient in place of the plural, and it is made good by its being a rhyme-final (fasilah), and it indicates the genus without ambiguity; or because the meaning is "make each one of them an imam"; or it may be the plural of amm, like hall and hilal; or because they were united and their word was agreed upon. They said: "Make us one imam," they asked God that they would be exemplars in religion, and they did not seek leadership. This was said by al-Nakha'i. It was also said: the verse contains what indicates that leadership in religion must be sought. It was revealed concerning the ten who were given glad tidings of Paradise.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ (those) is a reference to those described with these ten qualities. ﴿الغُرْفَةَ﴾ (the chamber) is a definite noun with the article al, so it is general, meaning the chambers, as in His saying: ﴿وهم في الغُرُفاتِ آمِنُونَ﴾ (and they will be secure in the upper chambers) [Saba' 34:37], and they are the lofty places.
