It is reported from Anas in the Sunan of Ibn Majah that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, among extravagance is that you eat whatever you desire." A poet said:

"Do not go to excess in any matter, but moderate: both extremes of the affairs are blameworthy."

Another said:

"When a man gives his soul whatever it desires, and does not restrain it, it reaches out to every falsehood.
And it drives him toward sin and shame by means of the sweetness of the fleeting thing that calls him to it."

Hatim said:

"If you have given your belly its desire, and your private part too, then you have attained the furthest point of blame, all of it."

Al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read (yaqturu) with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ta'. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ta'. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ta' with shadda, and all of these are dialects meaning constriction. Abu Hatim denied the use of the quadriliteral aqtara here, and said aqtara means became poor. From it comes ﴿And upon the straitened man according to his means﴾ [al-Baqara: 236]. He overlooked what al-Asma'i and others reported: from aqtara meaning constricted. Qiwam (the balance) is moderation between the two states. Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read (qiwaman) with a kasra. It was said: both are dialects with one meaning. It was also said: with the kasra, qiwam is that by which a thing is sustained; one says: "You are our qiwam," meaning that by which need is met, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It was said: (qiwaman) with a kasra means a limit, sufficiency and the basis of a state. And ﴿between that﴾ and (qiwaman) may be two predicates according to those who permit multiple predicates for kana; or (bayna) may be the predicate and (qiwaman) a emphatic circumstantial phrase; or (qiwaman) may be the predicate and (bayna dhalika) either an object of kana according to the view of those who hold that the defective kana governs the adverbial phrase, or a circumstantial phrase of (qiwaman), since if it were postponed it would be an attribute. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿bayna dhalika﴾ be the subject of (kana) and built because it is added to a built word, like His saying: ﴿and from the disgrace of that day﴾ [Hud: 66] in the reading of one who pronounces the mim with a fatha, with (qiwaman) as the predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Grammatically there is no harm in it, but the meaning is not strong, because what lies between extravagance and niggardliness is necessarily a balance, so there is no benefit in the predicate, which is the basis of the benefit.

He, may He be exalted, described them with the moderation that lies between excess and deficiency, and the Messenger (ﷺ) was addressed with the like in His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾ [al-Isra': 29], etc.

﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. Ibn Mas'ud asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to God while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." So God revealed its confirmation: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. It was said: Polytheists came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who had killed much and committed much adultery, and they said: "What you say and call to is indeed good; would you tell us that there is an expiation for what we have done?" Then it was revealed up to ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. It was also said: the occasion of revelation was the story of Wahshi in his Islam, in a long hadith.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He negated these great abominations from those described with those great qualities in religion, as a contrast with what the enemies of the believers, from Quraysh and others, were upon, as if it were said: "And those whom God has cleared and purified from what you are upon."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a removal of His believing servants from the attributes of the disbelievers in their worship of idols, their killing of souls by burying daughters alive, and other injustice, assassination and raids, and fornication which was permitted among them.

The explanation of the like of ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except with right﴾ [al-An'am: 151] has preceded in Surat al-An'am.

It was read (yulaqqa) with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the lam and the qaf with shadda. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Raja' read (yalqa) with an alif, as if he intended to delete the presumed damma on the alif and kept the alif.

Al-Athām in the language means punishment, and it is the recompense of sin. The poet said:

"May God recompense Ibn 'Urwa, since he became disobedient, and disobedience for him is athām."

That is: a prescribed punishment and a penalty, and Qatada and Ibn Zayd explained it thus. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Ibn Jubayr said: Athām is a valley in Hell bearing this name, which God made a punishment for the disbelievers. Abu Muslim said: al-athām is sin, and its meaning is (yalqa) the recompense of athām, so the name of the thing is applied to its recompense. Al-Hasan said: athām is one of the names of Hell. It was said: a well in it. It was said: a mountain. Ibn Mas'ud read: (yalqa ayyaman), plural of yawm, meaning hardships. One says: "a day of days" for a grievous day.

As for His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾, it appears that it refers to the whole of calling upon another god, killing a soul without right, and adultery, so the doubling is ordered upon the totality of these sins, and that doubling does not necessarily apply to each one of them. There is no doubt that the punishment of the disbelievers varies according to their crimes.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ in the passive with an alif, and (wa yakhlud) in the active. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Ibn Kathir likewise, except that they doubled the 'ayn and dropped the alif. Abu Ja'far also, and Shayba and Talha ibn Sulayman, read (nudaʻʻif) with a nun, damma, and a doubled kasra on the 'ayn, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Musarrif read (yudaʻif) with a ya' in the active, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Sulayman read (wa takhludu) with a ta' of address by way of iltifat, in the nominative, meaning: "and you, O disbeliever, will abide." Abu Haywa read (wa yukhalladu) in the passive, with a doubled lam, jussive. It was also reported from Abu 'Amr and on his authority likewise, with a single lam. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (yudaʻafu) and (wa yakhludu) with the nominative for both; likewise Ibn 'Amir and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim (yudaʻafu) and (wa yakhludu) in the passive, nominative, with a single lam. Al-A'mash with a damma on the ya' in the passive, doubled, nominative: the nominative is on resumption or circumstance, and the jussive is on substitution for (yalqa), as the poet said:

"Whenever you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firm wood and a blazing fire."

The pronoun in (fihi) refers to the punishment. The apparent view is that the repentance of a believing man who kills a soul without right is accepted, contrary to Ibn 'Abbas, and this was discussed in al-Nisa'. As for the changing of their evil deeds into good deeds, it means making their deeds in place of their former sins into obedience, and that will be the cause of God's mercy toward them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, and they refuted those who said it refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: The evil deed itself does not become a good deed, but the evil deed is erased by repentance, and the good deed is recorded along with repentance, while the disbeliever's deed is nullified and his evil deeds are established against him. Ibn al-Musayyab and Makhul interpreted that it is on the Day of Resurrection, and it has the sense of the generosity of pardon. In Muslim's book: God will, on the Day of Resurrection, change for whomever among the monotheists He wishes to forgive, his evil deeds into good deeds. They said: the evil deed is erased and a good deed is established in its place. Al-Qaffal and al-Qadi said: the punishment is changed into reward, mentioning both, and meaning what is deserved by each.

﴿Except one who repents﴾ is a connected exception from the genus, and it does not appear, because the excepted-from is judged to be one for whom ﴿the punishment will be doubled﴾, so the sense becomes: ﴿except one who repents and believes and does righteous deeds﴾, so the punishment is not doubled for him. The absence of doubling does not entail the absence of punishment other than the doubled punishment, so in my view it is better that it be a disconnected exception, meaning: but whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, ﴿those, God will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾, and when it is so, he does not suffer punishment at all. (Their evil deeds) is the second object, which originally should be restricted by a preposition, i.e., (bi-sayyi'atihim). (Good deeds) is the first object, which is the stated one, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We replaced them with two gardens, two gardens﴾ [Saba': 16]. A poet said:

"The sister of the one with two jars laughs at me: 'May God replace you with two colours: the blackness of a face and the whiteness of two eyes.'"

It appears that (whoever repents), meaning initiates repentance, will repent to God, meaning returns to His reward and His kindness. Ibn 'Atiyya said: (whoever repents) has truly grasped a firm matter, just as you say to one whose speech about a matter is praised: "Indeed you have spoken a word, O so-and-so," so likewise the verse means the praise of repentance, as if He said: he will find relief and great forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: Whoever abandons sins, regrets them and enters into righteous deeds, is by that a repenter to God, who knows the right of the repenters and does with them what they deserve; and God loves the repenting and loves the purified. It was said: whoever resolves on repentance will repent to God, so let him hasten to it and turn to God with it. It was said: (whoever repents) from his sins, he repents to Him who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evil deeds. It was said: (whoever repents) continues steadfast in repentance, so he is the true penitent before God.

﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾ returns to the mention of the attributes of the servants of the Merciful. The apparent meaning is that they do not testify to falsehood, or the testimony of falsehood; so said 'Ali and al-Baqir, and it is from testimony. It was said: the meaning is that they do not attend a gathering, from presence. Falsehood (al-zur) is idolatry and an idol, or lying, or musical instruments, or the festivals of the Christians, or a game that was in the Jahiliyya, or wailing, or gatherings in which the righteous are disparaged: these are sayings. Idolatry was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, singing by Mujahid, lying by Ibn Jurayj. In al-Kashshaf, from Qatada: gatherings of falsehood. From Ibn al-Hanafiyya: play and singing. From Mujahid: the festivals of the polytheists; and "idle talk" (laghw) is everything that should be cast aside and discarded. The meaning is: (and when they pass) by people of idle talk, (they pass by) turning away from them, honouring themselves against stopping over them or engaging with them; by His saying: ﴿And when they hear idle talk they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. End.

﴿with the signs of their Lord﴾: these are the Qur'an.

﴿لَمْ يَخِرُّوا عَلَيْها صُمًّا وعُمْيانًا﴾ The negation applies to the qualifier that follows, which is "deaf and blind," and not to the falling down (khurur) that the negation particle precedes. In the usage of the Arabs, the most common view is that the negation applies to the qualifier. The meaning is that when they are reminded of these verses, they bend over them eagerly to listen, and they turn toward the one who reminds them with attentive ears and watchful eyes. This is unlike the hypocrites and others like them, who, when reminded, are bent over the verses and turned toward the one who reminds them only outwardly, and they are "deaf and blind" in that they do not grasp them and do not perceive what is in them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rather, their falling down is in prostration and weeping, just as you say: "Zayd did not go out to war in fear," meaning that he went out only boldly and resolutely. The listener who is reminded is one whose ear is upright and whose affair is sound, so when he turns away, that is a khurur, which is a falling without order or arrangement. Although it resembles one who falls down in prostration, its basic sense is falling without order. End of quote. al-Suddi said: "They do not fall down" and "deaf and blind" describe the disbelievers, and it is an expression of their turning away and their exertion in that. He paired this with your saying: "So-and-so sat wishing," and "So-and-so stood weeping," while you did not intend to report sitting or standing, but these are preparatory phrases in speech and expression.

﴿قُرَّةَ أعْيُنٍ﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for joy and happiness, and it is derived from qurr, which means coolness. It is said: "The tears of joy are cool, and the tears of sorrow are hot." It is also said: "God cool your eye," and "God heat the eye of the enemy." Abu Tammam said:
As for the eyes of lovers, they were heated (with tears),
and as for the eyes of the gloaters, they were cooled.
It was also said that it is derived from qarar, meaning that the gaze rests on it and does not look at anything else. Abu 'Amr said: "The comfort of the eye is sleep," meaning security, because security does not come with fear. This was related by al-Qaffal. The comfort of the eyes, regarding those whose righteousness they mention, is seeing them obedient to God (p-517). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Hadrami. In the early period of Islam, a father would be guided while his son was a disbeliever, or a husband while his wife was a disbeliever, and the comfort of their eyes was in the faith of their beloved ones. Ibn 'Abbas said: The comfort of a child's eye is that you see him writing jurisprudence (fiqh). The apparent meaning is that they prayed for this so that they would be obeyed in this world and they would be gladdened by them. It was also said: They asked that God join those people with them in Paradise so that their joy would be complete. End of quote. This second view includes the first, which concerns this world, because that is the result of their faith in this world. It is clear that min here is for the inception of the end point (ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning: ﴿هَبْ لَنا﴾ grant us, from their side, what cools our eyes of obedience and righteousness. It is also permitted that min be for specification (bayan), as al-Zamakhshari said. He said: It is as if it were said: "Grant us ﴿قُرَّةَ أعْيُنٍ﴾ (comfort of the eyes)," and then the comfort was specified and explained by His saying: ﴿مِن أزْواجِنا وذُرِّيّاتِنا﴾ (from our spouses and our offspring). Its meaning is that God makes them, for them, a comfort of the eyes, from your saying: "I saw from you a lion," meaning: you are a lion. End of quote. We have previously noted that min which is for specifying the genus (bayan al-jins) must come before what it specifies, and then it comes with min of specification. This is according to the view of those who affirmed that it can be for specifying the genus. The correct view is that this meaning is not established for min.

Ibn 'Amir, the two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), and Hafs read ﴿وذُرِّيّاتِنا﴾ in the plural. The rest of the seven read it in the singular, and Talhah also read it in the singular. 'Abdullah, Abu al-Darda', and Abu Hurayrah read (qurrat) in the plural, while the majority read it in the singular. The word qurrah is indefinite to match the indefiniteness of a'yun (eyes), as if he said: "Grant us from them joy and happiness." The word a'yun comes in the form of the paucity plural (jam' qillah) rather than 'uyun, which is the form of the plurality plural (jam' kathrah), because what is meant is the eyes of the righteous, and they are few in comparison to the eyes of others. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, but it is not sound, because a'yun applies to ten and less of plurals, while the righteous do not have ten eyes; rather, their eyes are very many. Even if their eyes are few in comparison to the eyes of others, they are so many as to be uncountable. The word imaman is in the singular, either because the singular is sufficient in place of the plural, and it is made good by its being a rhyme-final (fasilah), and it indicates the genus without ambiguity; or because the meaning is "make each one of them an imam"; or it may be the plural of amm, like hall and hilal; or because they were united and their word was agreed upon. They said: "Make us one imam," they asked God that they would be exemplars in religion, and they did not seek leadership. This was said by al-Nakha'i. It was also said: the verse contains what indicates that leadership in religion must be sought. It was revealed concerning the ten who were given glad tidings of Paradise.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ (those) is a reference to those described with these ten qualities. ﴿الغُرْفَةَ﴾ (the chamber) is a definite noun with the article al, so it is general, meaning the chambers, as in His saying: ﴿وهم في الغُرُفاتِ آمِنُونَ﴾ (and they will be secure in the upper chambers) [Saba' 34:37], and they are the lofty places. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are houses of emerald, pearl, and ruby. It was said that al-Ghurfah is one of the names of Paradise. It was said: the seventh heaven is a ghurfah. It was said: it is the highest of the dwellings of Paradise. It was said: what is meant is elevation in ranks. The preposition ba' in ﴿بِما صَبَرُوا﴾ (for what they endured) indicates cause. It was also said that it indicates substitution (badal), meaning in place of their patience, as in the saying: "Would that I had for them a people when they ride," meaning: would that I had in their place a people. He did not mention the object of patience specifically, so that it would include all its objects. al-Hasan, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, the two Harams, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr read ﴿ويُلَقَّوْنَ﴾ (and they will be met) with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the lam, and a shaddah on the qaf. Talhah, Muhammad al-Yamani, and the rest of the seven read it with a fathah on the ya', a sukun on the lam, and a light qaf. The tahiyyah is a prayer for long life, and the salam is a prayer for safety, meaning: the angels greet them, or some of them greet others. It was also said: they will be greeted with gifts, so that the benefits and honor are combined for them.

﴿حَسُنَتْ مُسْتَقَرًّا ومُقامًا﴾ (how good as a resting place and a dwelling) is a counterpart to His saying about Hell: ﴿ساءَتْ مُسْتَقَرًّا ومُقامًا﴾ (how evil as a resting place and a dwelling) [al-Furqan 25:66].

When He described His servants, the worshippers, and enumerated the righteous deeds they have, He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to declare plainly to people that they have no weight with their Lord except worship and supplication. In His saying: ﴿لَوْلا دُعاؤُكُمْ﴾ (were it not for your supplication), the word dua' means worship. The apparent meaning is that ma is a negation, meaning: "My Lord does not weigh you at all, were it not for your supplication." It is also permitted that it be interrogative with the meaning of negation, meaning: "What weight does He give you?" The word du'a'ukum is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its subject, meaning: were it not for your worship of Him, that is, were it not for your supplication and humbling yourselves to Him, or: He would not care about your punishment, were it not for your calling upon idols as gods. It was also said that it is added to its object, meaning: were it not for His calling you to His obedience. What appears to be the case is that His saying ﴿قُلْ ما يَعْبَأُ بِكُمْ﴾ (Say: He does not weigh you at all) is an address to the Quraysh disbelievers who said (p-518): "We will prostrate to what you command us." Meaning: My Lord does not concern Himself with you, were it not for your humbling yourselves to Him and your seeking His aid in hardships.

﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبْتُمْ﴾ (then you have denied) what the Messenger ﷺ brought, so you deserve punishment. ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ (then it will be) the punishment, which is what your denial produced. He gave them room in its arrival with the expression ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ لِزامًا﴾ (then it will be inevitable), meaning: it will be lasting for them, and they will not be free of it. 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr read: "The disbelievers have denied," and this is understood to be an explanation, not Qur'an. Most of them hold that al-Lizam here is the Day of Badr. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy. It was also said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. It was also said: it is death, but it is not to be understood as ordinary death, rather it is killing at Badr. It was said that the implied meaning is: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ it, meaning the punishment, and this was made explicit by the one who read: "Then the punishment will be inevitable." The sound view is that the subject of kana is left unspoken after it is known that it is something threatened, for the sake of vagueness and to encompass what the description cannot contain. From Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ it, meaning the denial, (lizaman), meaning inevitable for you, and you will not be granted repentance. This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi. Al-Zamakhshari said: The address is to people in general, among whom are believing worshippers and denying sinners, so they are addressed with what is found in their kind of worship and denial: ﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبْتُمْ﴾ (then you have denied). He says: If I have informed you that My judgment is that I do not reckon anything except their worship, then by your denial you have opposed My judgment, so the effect of your denial will surely cling to you until it hurls you into the Fire. A parallel in speech is when a king says to one who disobeyed him: "It is my custom to be kind to whoever obeys me and follows my command. You have disobeyed, so you will see what I will bring upon you because of your disobedience." Ibn Juraij read ﴿فَسَوْفَ تَكُونُ﴾ with the feminine ta', meaning: then the consequence will be. The majority read (lizaman) with a kasrah on the lam. al-Minhal, Aban ibn Tha'lab, and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fathah, as a verbal noun. It is said: lazima yalzamu luzuman and lizaman, like thabata thubutan and thabatan. Abu 'Ubaydah cited, for the kasrah on the lam, the verse of Sakhr al-Ghayy:
So if they escape the death of one land,
they will have met their deaths, inevitably.
Ibn Khalawayh related from Abu al-Sammal that he read "lazama" on the pattern of "hadhama," taking it as a verbal noun deviated from al-lazamah, like fujjar deviated from al-fajarah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verse 67–77 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They are neither extravagant nor niggardly﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jili said: Spending in what is not obedience to God is extravagance (israf), and withholding from obedience is niggardliness (iqtar). The same meaning was given by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. A man heard another man say: "There is no good in extravagance," so he said: "There is no extravagance in good." 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba said: Extravagance is that you spend the property of another. Al-Nakha'i said: It is the one who does not let anyone go hungry or naked, and does not spend an outlay which people say is extravagant. Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: They are those who do not wear clothes for beauty and do not eat food for pleasure. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz when he married him to his daughter Fatima: "What is your expenditure?" 'Umar said to him: "The good deed between the two evil ones," and then he recited the verse. Extravagance (israf) is exceeding the limit in spending, and qatr (niggardliness) is constriction, which is the opposite of extravagance. It is reported from Anas in the Sunan of Ibn Majah that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, among extravagance is that you eat whatever you desire." A poet said:

"Do not go to excess in any matter, but moderate: both extremes of the affairs are blameworthy."

Another said:

"When a man gives his soul whatever it desires, and does not restrain it, it reaches out to every falsehood.
And it drives him toward sin and shame by means of the sweetness of the fleeting thing that calls him to it."

Hatim said:

"If you have given your belly its desire, and your private part too, then you have attained the furthest point of blame, all of it."

Al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read (yaqturu) with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ta'. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ta'. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ta' with shadda, and all of these are dialects meaning constriction. Abu Hatim denied the use of the quadriliteral aqtara here, and said aqtara means became poor. From it comes ﴿And upon the straitened man according to his means﴾ [al-Baqara: 236]. He overlooked what al-Asma'i and others reported: from aqtara meaning constricted. Qiwam (the balance) is moderation between the two states. Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read (qiwaman) with a kasra. It was said: both are dialects with one meaning. It was also said: with the kasra, qiwam is that by which a thing is sustained; one says: "You are our qiwam," meaning that by which need is met, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It was said: (qiwaman) with a kasra means a limit, sufficiency and the basis of a state. And ﴿between that﴾ and (qiwaman) may be two predicates according to those who permit multiple predicates for kana; or (bayna) may be the predicate and (qiwaman) a emphatic circumstantial phrase; or (qiwaman) may be the predicate and (bayna dhalika) either an object of kana according to the view of those who hold that the defective kana governs the adverbial phrase, or a circumstantial phrase of (qiwaman), since if it were postponed it would be an attribute. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿bayna dhalika﴾ be the subject of (kana) and built because it is added to a built word, like His saying: ﴿and from the disgrace of that day﴾ [Hud: 66] in the reading of one who pronounces the mim with a fatha, with (qiwaman) as the predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Grammatically there is no harm in it, but the meaning is not strong, because what lies between extravagance and niggardliness is necessarily a balance, so there is no benefit in the predicate, which is the basis of the benefit.

He, may He be exalted, described them with the moderation that lies between excess and deficiency, and the Messenger (ﷺ) was addressed with the like in His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾ [al-Isra': 29], etc.

﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. Ibn Mas'ud asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to God while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." So God revealed its confirmation: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. It was said: Polytheists came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who had killed much and committed much adultery, and they said: "What you say and call to is indeed good; would you tell us that there is an expiation for what we have done?" Then it was revealed up to ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. It was also said: the occasion of revelation was the story of Wahshi in his Islam, in a long hadith.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He negated these great abominations from those described with those great qualities in religion, as a contrast with what the enemies of the believers, from Quraysh and others, were upon, as if it were said: "And those whom God has cleared and purified from what you are upon."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a removal of His believing servants from the attributes of the disbelievers in their worship of idols, their killing of souls by burying daughters alive, and other injustice, assassination and raids, and fornication which was permitted among them.

The explanation of the like of ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except with right﴾ [al-An'am: 151] has preceded in Surat al-An'am.

It was read (yulaqqa) with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the lam and the qaf with shadda. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Raja' read (yalqa) with an alif, as if he intended to delete the presumed damma on the alif and kept the alif.

Al-Athām in the language means punishment, and it is the recompense of sin. The poet said:

"May God recompense Ibn 'Urwa, since he became disobedient, and disobedience for him is athām."

That is: a prescribed punishment and a penalty, and Qatada and Ibn Zayd explained it thus. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Ibn Jubayr said: Athām is a valley in Hell bearing this name, which God made a punishment for the disbelievers. Abu Muslim said: al-athām is sin, and its meaning is (yalqa) the recompense of athām, so the name of the thing is applied to its recompense. Al-Hasan said: athām is one of the names of Hell. It was said: a well in it. It was said: a mountain. Ibn Mas'ud read: (yalqa ayyaman), plural of yawm, meaning hardships. One says: "a day of days" for a grievous day.

As for His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾, it appears that it refers to the whole of calling upon another god, killing a soul without right, and adultery, so the doubling is ordered upon the totality of these sins, and that doubling does not necessarily apply to each one of them. There is no doubt that the punishment of the disbelievers varies according to their crimes.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ in the passive with an alif, and (wa yakhlud) in the active. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Ibn Kathir likewise, except that they doubled the 'ayn and dropped the alif. Abu Ja'far also, and Shayba and Talha ibn Sulayman, read (nudaʻʻif) with a nun, damma, and a doubled kasra on the 'ayn, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Musarrif read (yudaʻif) with a ya' in the active, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Sulayman read (wa takhludu) with a ta' of address by way of iltifat, in the nominative, meaning: "and you, O disbeliever, will abide." Abu Haywa read (wa yukhalladu) in the passive, with a doubled lam, jussive. It was also reported from Abu 'Amr and on his authority likewise, with a single lam. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (yudaʻafu) and (wa yakhludu) with the nominative for both; likewise Ibn 'Amir and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim (yudaʻafu) and (wa yakhludu) in the passive, nominative, with a single lam. Al-A'mash with a damma on the ya' in the passive, doubled, nominative: the nominative is on resumption or circumstance, and the jussive is on substitution for (yalqa), as the poet said:

"Whenever you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firm wood and a blazing fire."

The pronoun in (fihi) refers to the punishment. The apparent view is that the repentance of a believing man who kills a soul without right is accepted, contrary to Ibn 'Abbas, and this was discussed in al-Nisa'. As for the changing of their evil deeds into good deeds, it means making their deeds in place of their former sins into obedience, and that will be the cause of God's mercy toward them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, and they refuted those who said it refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: The evil deed itself does not become a good deed, but the evil deed is erased by repentance, and the good deed is recorded along with repentance, while the disbeliever's deed is nullified and his evil deeds are established against him. Ibn al-Musayyab and Makhul interpreted that it is on the Day of Resurrection, and it has the sense of the generosity of pardon. In Muslim's book: God will, on the Day of Resurrection, change for whomever among the monotheists He wishes to forgive, his evil deeds into good deeds. They said: the evil deed is erased and a good deed is established in its place. Al-Qaffal and al-Qadi said: the punishment is changed into reward, mentioning both, and meaning what is deserved by each.

﴿Except one who repents﴾ is a connected exception from the genus, and it does not appear, because the excepted-from is judged to be one for whom ﴿the punishment will be doubled﴾, so the sense becomes: ﴿except one who repents and believes and does righteous deeds﴾, so the punishment is not doubled for him. The absence of doubling does not entail the absence of punishment other than the doubled punishment, so in my view it is better that it be a disconnected exception, meaning: but whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, ﴿those, God will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾, and when it is so, he does not suffer punishment at all. (Their evil deeds) is the second object, which originally should be restricted by a preposition, i.e., (bi-sayyi'atihim). (Good deeds) is the first object, which is the stated one, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We replaced them with two gardens, two gardens﴾ [Saba': 16]. A poet said:

"The sister of the one with two jars laughs at me: 'May God replace you with two colours: the blackness of a face and the whiteness of two eyes.'"

It appears that (whoever repents), meaning initiates repentance, will repent to God, meaning returns to His reward and His kindness. Ibn 'Atiyya said: (whoever repents) has truly grasped a firm matter, just as you say to one whose speech about a matter is praised: "Indeed you have spoken a word, O so-and-so," so likewise the verse means the praise of repentance, as if He said: he will find relief and great forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: Whoever abandons sins, regrets them and enters into righteous deeds, is by that a repenter to God, who knows the right of the repenters and does with them what they deserve; and God loves the repenting and loves the purified. It was said: whoever resolves on repentance will repent to God, so let him hasten to it and turn to God with it. It was said: (whoever repents) from his sins, he repents to Him who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evil deeds. It was said: (whoever repents) continues steadfast in repentance, so he is the true penitent before God.

﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾ returns to the mention of the attributes of the servants of the Merciful. The apparent meaning is that they do not testify to falsehood, or the testimony of falsehood; so said 'Ali and al-Baqir, and it is from testimony. It was said: the meaning is that they do not attend a gathering, from presence. Falsehood (al-zur) is idolatry and an idol, or lying, or musical instruments, or the festivals of the Christians, or a game that was in the Jahiliyya, or wailing, or gatherings in which the righteous are disparaged: these are sayings. Idolatry was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, singing by Mujahid, lying by Ibn Jurayj. In al-Kashshaf, from Qatada: gatherings of falsehood. From Ibn al-Hanafiyya: play and singing. From Mujahid: the festivals of the polytheists; and "idle talk" (laghw) is everything that should be cast aside and discarded. The meaning is: (and when they pass) by people of idle talk, (they pass by) turning away from them, honouring themselves against stopping over them or engaging with them; by His saying: ﴿And when they hear idle talk they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. End.

﴿with the signs of their Lord﴾: these are the Qur'an.

﴿لَمْ يَخِرُّوا عَلَيْها صُمًّا وعُمْيانًا﴾ The negation applies to the qualifier that follows, which is "deaf and blind," and not to the falling down (khurur) that the negation particle precedes. In the usage of the Arabs, the most common view is that the negation applies to the qualifier. The meaning is that when they are reminded of these verses, they bend over them eagerly to listen, and they turn toward the one who reminds them with attentive ears and watchful eyes. This is unlike the hypocrites and others like them, who, when reminded, are bent over the verses and turned toward the one who reminds them only outwardly, and they are "deaf and blind" in that they do not grasp them and do not perceive what is in them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rather, their falling down is in prostration and weeping, just as you say: "Zayd did not go out to war in fear," meaning that he went out only boldly and resolutely. The listener who is reminded is one whose ear is upright and whose affair is sound, so when he turns away, that is a khurur, which is a falling without order or arrangement. Although it resembles one who falls down in prostration, its basic sense is falling without order. End of quote. al-Suddi said: "They do not fall down" and "deaf and blind" describe the disbelievers, and it is an expression of their turning away and their exertion in that. He paired this with your saying: "So-and-so sat wishing," and "So-and-so stood weeping," while you did not intend to report sitting or standing, but these are preparatory phrases in speech and expression.

﴿قُرَّةَ أعْيُنٍ﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for joy and happiness, and it is derived from qurr, which means coolness. It is said: "The tears of joy are cool, and the tears of sorrow are hot." It is also said: "God cool your eye," and "God heat the eye of the enemy." Abu Tammam said:
As for the eyes of lovers, they were heated (with tears),
and as for the eyes of the gloaters, they were cooled.
It was also said that it is derived from qarar, meaning that the gaze rests on it and does not look at anything else. Abu 'Amr said: "The comfort of the eye is sleep," meaning security, because security does not come with fear. This was related by al-Qaffal. The comfort of the eyes, regarding those whose righteousness they mention, is seeing them obedient to God (p-517). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Hadrami. In the early period of Islam, a father would be guided while his son was a disbeliever, or a husband while his wife was a disbeliever, and the comfort of their eyes was in the faith of their beloved ones. Ibn 'Abbas said: The comfort of a child's eye is that you see him writing jurisprudence (fiqh). The apparent meaning is that they prayed for this so that they would be obeyed in this world and they would be gladdened by them. It was also said: They asked that God join those people with them in Paradise so that their joy would be complete. End of quote. This second view includes the first, which concerns this world, because that is the result of their faith in this world. It is clear that min here is for the inception of the end point (ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning: ﴿هَبْ لَنا﴾ grant us, from their side, what cools our eyes of obedience and righteousness. It is also permitted that min be for specification (bayan), as al-Zamakhshari said. He said: It is as if it were said: "Grant us ﴿قُرَّةَ أعْيُنٍ﴾ (comfort of the eyes)," and then the comfort was specified and explained by His saying: ﴿مِن أزْواجِنا وذُرِّيّاتِنا﴾ (from our spouses and our offspring). Its meaning is that God makes them, for them, a comfort of the eyes, from your saying: "I saw from you a lion," meaning: you are a lion. End of quote. We have previously noted that min which is for specifying the genus (bayan al-jins) must come before what it specifies, and then it comes with min of specification. This is according to the view of those who affirmed that it can be for specifying the genus. The correct view is that this meaning is not established for min.

Ibn 'Amir, the two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), and Hafs read ﴿وذُرِّيّاتِنا﴾ in the plural. The rest of the seven read it in the singular, and Talhah also read it in the singular. 'Abdullah, Abu al-Darda', and Abu Hurayrah read (qurrat) in the plural, while the majority read it in the singular. The word qurrah is indefinite to match the indefiniteness of a'yun (eyes), as if he said: "Grant us from them joy and happiness." The word a'yun comes in the form of the paucity plural (jam' qillah) rather than 'uyun, which is the form of the plurality plural (jam' kathrah), because what is meant is the eyes of the righteous, and they are few in comparison to the eyes of others. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, but it is not sound, because a'yun applies to ten and less of plurals, while the righteous do not have ten eyes; rather, their eyes are very many. Even if their eyes are few in comparison to the eyes of others, they are so many as to be uncountable. The word imaman is in the singular, either because the singular is sufficient in place of the plural, and it is made good by its being a rhyme-final (fasilah), and it indicates the genus without ambiguity; or because the meaning is "make each one of them an imam"; or it may be the plural of amm, like hall and hilal; or because they were united and their word was agreed upon. They said: "Make us one imam," they asked God that they would be exemplars in religion, and they did not seek leadership. This was said by al-Nakha'i. It was also said: the verse contains what indicates that leadership in religion must be sought. It was revealed concerning the ten who were given glad tidings of Paradise.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ (those) is a reference to those described with these ten qualities. ﴿الغُرْفَةَ﴾ (the chamber) is a definite noun with the article al, so it is general, meaning the chambers, as in His saying: ﴿وهم في الغُرُفاتِ آمِنُونَ﴾ (and they will be secure in the upper chambers) [Saba' 34:37], and they are the lofty places. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are houses of emerald, pearl, and ruby. It was said that al-Ghurfah is one of the names of Paradise. It was said: the seventh heaven is a ghurfah. It was said: it is the highest of the dwellings of Paradise. It was said: what is meant is elevation in ranks. The preposition ba' in ﴿بِما صَبَرُوا﴾ (for what they endured) indicates cause. It was also said that it indicates substitution (badal), meaning in place of their patience, as in the saying: "Would that I had for them a people when they ride," meaning: would that I had in their place a people. He did not mention the object of patience specifically, so that it would include all its objects. al-Hasan, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, the two Harams, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr read ﴿ويُلَقَّوْنَ﴾ (and they will be met) with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the lam, and a shaddah on the qaf. Talhah, Muhammad al-Yamani, and the rest of the seven read it with a fathah on the ya', a sukun on the lam, and a light qaf. The tahiyyah is a prayer for long life, and the salam is a prayer for safety, meaning: the angels greet them, or some of them greet others. It was also said: they will be greeted with gifts, so that the benefits and honor are combined for them.

﴿حَسُنَتْ مُسْتَقَرًّا ومُقامًا﴾ (how good as a resting place and a dwelling) is a counterpart to His saying about Hell: ﴿ساءَتْ مُسْتَقَرًّا ومُقامًا﴾ (how evil as a resting place and a dwelling) [al-Furqan 25:66].

When He described His servants, the worshippers, and enumerated the righteous deeds they have, He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to declare plainly to people that they have no weight with their Lord except worship and supplication. In His saying: ﴿لَوْلا دُعاؤُكُمْ﴾ (were it not for your supplication), the word dua' means worship. The apparent meaning is that ma is a negation, meaning: "My Lord does not weigh you at all, were it not for your supplication." It is also permitted that it be interrogative with the meaning of negation, meaning: "What weight does He give you?" The word du'a'ukum is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its subject, meaning: were it not for your worship of Him, that is, were it not for your supplication and humbling yourselves to Him, or: He would not care about your punishment, were it not for your calling upon idols as gods. It was also said that it is added to its object, meaning: were it not for His calling you to His obedience. What appears to be the case is that His saying ﴿قُلْ ما يَعْبَأُ بِكُمْ﴾ (Say: He does not weigh you at all) is an address to the Quraysh disbelievers who said (p-518): "We will prostrate to what you command us." Meaning: My Lord does not concern Himself with you, were it not for your humbling yourselves to Him and your seeking His aid in hardships.

﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبْتُمْ﴾ (then you have denied) what the Messenger ﷺ brought, so you deserve punishment. ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ (then it will be) the punishment, which is what your denial produced. He gave them room in its arrival with the expression ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ لِزامًا﴾ (then it will be inevitable), meaning: it will be lasting for them, and they will not be free of it. 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr read: "The disbelievers have denied," and this is understood to be an explanation, not Qur'an. Most of them hold that al-Lizam here is the Day of Badr. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy. It was also said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. It was also said: it is death, but it is not to be understood as ordinary death, rather it is killing at Badr. It was said that the implied meaning is: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ it, meaning the punishment, and this was made explicit by the one who read: "Then the punishment will be inevitable." The sound view is that the subject of kana is left unspoken after it is known that it is something threatened, for the sake of vagueness and to encompass what the description cannot contain. From Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ it, meaning the denial, (lizaman), meaning inevitable for you, and you will not be granted repentance. This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi. Al-Zamakhshari said: The address is to people in general, among whom are believing worshippers and denying sinners, so they are addressed with what is found in their kind of worship and denial: ﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبْتُمْ﴾ (then you have denied). He says: If I have informed you that My judgment is that I do not reckon anything except their worship, then by your denial you have opposed My judgment, so the effect of your denial will surely cling to you until it hurls you into the Fire. A parallel in speech is when a king says to one who disobeyed him: "It is my custom to be kind to whoever obeys me and follows my command. You have disobeyed, so you will see what I will bring upon you because of your disobedience." Ibn Juraij read ﴿فَسَوْفَ تَكُونُ﴾ with the feminine ta', meaning: then the consequence will be. The majority read (lizaman) with a kasrah on the lam. al-Minhal, Aban ibn Tha'lab, and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fathah, as a verbal noun. It is said: lazima yalzamu luzuman and lizaman, like thabata thubutan and thabatan. Abu 'Ubaydah cited, for the kasrah on the lam, the verse of Sakhr al-Ghayy:
So if they escape the death of one land,
they will have met their deaths, inevitably.
Ibn Khalawayh related from Abu al-Sammal that he read "lazama" on the pattern of "hadhama," taking it as a verbal noun deviated from al-lazamah, like fujjar deviated from al-fajarah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verse 67–77 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They are neither extravagant nor niggardly﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jili said: Spending in what is not obedience to God is extravagance (israf), and withholding from obedience is niggardliness (iqtar). The same meaning was given by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. A man heard another man say: "There is no good in extravagance," so he said: "There is no extravagance in good." 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba said: Extravagance is that you spend the property of another. Al-Nakha'i said: It is the one who does not let anyone go hungry or naked, and does not spend an outlay which people say is extravagant. Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: They are those who do not wear clothes for beauty and do not eat food for pleasure. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz when he married him to his daughter Fatima: "What is your expenditure?" 'Umar said to him: "The good deed between the two evil ones," and then he recited the verse. Extravagance (israf) is exceeding the limit in spending, and qatr (niggardliness) is constriction, which is the opposite of extravagance. It is reported from Anas in the Sunan of Ibn Majah that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, among extravagance is that you eat whatever you desire." A poet said:

"Do not go to excess in any matter, but moderate: both extremes of the affairs are blameworthy."

Another said:

"When a man gives his soul whatever it desires, and does not restrain it, it reaches out to every falsehood.
And it drives him toward sin and shame by means of the sweetness of the fleeting thing that calls him to it."

Hatim said:

"If you have given your belly its desire, and your private part too, then you have attained the furthest point of blame, all of it."

Al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read (yaqturu) with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ta'. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ta'. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ta' with shadda, and all of these are dialects meaning constriction. Abu Hatim denied the use of the quadriliteral aqtara here, and said aqtara means became poor. From it comes ﴿And upon the straitened man according to his means﴾ [al-Baqara: 236]. He overlooked what al-Asma'i and others reported: from aqtara meaning constricted. Qiwam (the balance) is moderation between the two states. Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read (qiwaman) with a kasra. It was said: both are dialects with one meaning. It was also said: with the kasra, qiwam is that by which a thing is sustained; one says: "You are our qiwam," meaning that by which need is met, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It was said: (qiwaman) with a kasra means a limit, sufficiency and the basis of a state. And ﴿between that﴾ and (qiwaman) may be two predicates according to those who permit multiple predicates for kana; or (bayna) may be the predicate and (qiwaman) a emphatic circumstantial phrase; or (qiwaman) may be the predicate and (bayna dhalika) either an object of kana according to the view of those who hold that the defective kana governs the adverbial phrase, or a circumstantial phrase of (qiwaman), since if it were postponed it would be an attribute. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿bayna dhalika﴾ be the subject of (kana) and built because it is added to a built word, like His saying: ﴿and from the disgrace of that day﴾ [Hud: 66] in the reading of one who pronounces the mim with a fatha, with (qiwaman) as the predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Grammatically there is no harm in it, but the meaning is not strong, because what lies between extravagance and niggardliness is necessarily a balance, so there is no benefit in the predicate, which is the basis of the benefit.

He, may He be exalted, described them with the moderation that lies between excess and deficiency, and the Messenger (ﷺ) was addressed with the like in His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾ [al-Isra': 29], etc.

﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. Ibn Mas'ud asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to God while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." So God revealed its confirmation: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. It was said: Polytheists came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who had killed much and committed much adultery, and they said: "What you say and call to is indeed good; would you tell us that there is an expiation for what we have done?" Then it was revealed up to ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. It was also said: the occasion of revelation was the story of Wahshi in his Islam, in a long hadith.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He negated these great abominations from those described with those great qualities in religion, as a contrast with what the enemies of the believers, from Quraysh and others, were upon, as if it were said: "And those whom God has cleared and purified from what you are upon."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a removal of His believing servants from the attributes of the disbelievers in their worship of idols, their killing of souls by burying daughters alive, and other injustice, assassination and raids, and fornication which was permitted among them.

The explanation of the like of ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except with right﴾ [al-An'am: 151] has preceded in Surat al-An'am.

It was read (yulaqqa) with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the lam and the qaf with shadda. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Raja' read (yalqa) with an alif, as if he intended to delete the presumed damma on the alif and kept the alif.

Al-Athām in the language means punishment, and it is the recompense of sin. The poet said:

"May God recompense Ibn 'Urwa, since he became disobedient, and disobedience for him is athām."

That is: a prescribed punishment and a penalty, and Qatada and Ibn Zayd explained it thus. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Ibn Jubayr said: Athām is a valley in Hell bearing this name, which God made a punishment for the disbelievers. Abu Muslim said: al-athām is sin, and its meaning is (yalqa) the recompense of athām, so the name of the thing is applied to its recompense. Al-Hasan said: athām is one of the names of Hell. It was said: a well in it. It was said: a mountain. Ibn Mas'ud read: (yalqa ayyaman), plural of yawm, meaning hardships. One says: "a day of days" for a grievous day.

As for His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾, it appears that it refers to the whole of calling upon another god, killing a soul without right, and adultery, so the doubling is ordered upon the totality of these sins, and that doubling does not necessarily apply to each one of them. There is no doubt that the punishment of the disbelievers varies according to their crimes.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ in the passive with an alif, and (wa yakhlud) in the active. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Ibn Kathir likewise, except that they doubled the 'ayn and dropped the alif. Abu Ja'far also, and Shayba and Talha ibn Sulayman, read (nudaʻʻif) with a nun, damma, and a doubled kasra on the 'ayn, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Musarrif read (yudaʻif) with a ya' in the active, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Sulayman read (wa takhludu) with a ta' of address by way of iltifat, in the nominative, meaning: "and you, O disbeliever, will abide." Abu Haywa read (wa yukhalladu) in the passive, with a doubled lam, jussive. It was also reported from Abu 'Amr and on his authority likewise, with a single lam. Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (yudaʻafu) and (wa yakhludu) with the nominative for both; likewise Ibn 'Amir and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim (yudaʻafu) and (wa yakhludu) in the passive, nominative, with a single lam. Al-A'mash with a damma on the ya' in the passive, doubled, nominative: the nominative is on resumption or circumstance, and the jussive is on substitution for (yalqa), as the poet said:

"Whenever you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firm wood and a blazing fire."

The pronoun in (fihi) refers to the punishment. The apparent view is that the repentance of a believing man who kills a soul without right is accepted, contrary to Ibn 'Abbas, and this was discussed in al-Nisa'. As for the changing of their evil deeds into good deeds, it means making their deeds in place of their former sins into obedience, and that will be the cause of God's mercy toward them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, and they refuted those who said it refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: The evil deed itself does not become a good deed, but the evil deed is erased by repentance, and the good deed is recorded along with repentance, while the disbeliever's deed is nullified and his evil deeds are established against him. Ibn al-Musayyab and Makhul interpreted that it is on the Day of Resurrection, and it has the sense of the generosity of pardon. In Muslim's book: God will, on the Day of Resurrection, change for whomever among the monotheists He wishes to forgive, his evil deeds into good deeds. They said: the evil deed is erased and a good deed is established in its place. Al-Qaffal and al-Qadi said: the punishment is changed into reward, mentioning both, and meaning what is deserved by each.

﴿Except one who repents﴾ is a connected exception from the genus, and it does not appear, because the excepted-from is judged to be one for whom ﴿the punishment will be doubled﴾, so the sense becomes: ﴿except one who repents and believes and does righteous deeds﴾, so the punishment is not doubled for him. The absence of doubling does not entail the absence of punishment other than the doubled punishment, so in my view it is better that it be a disconnected exception, meaning: but whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, ﴿those, God will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾, and when it is so, he does not suffer punishment at all. (Their evil deeds) is the second object, which originally should be restricted by a preposition, i.e., (bi-sayyi'atihim). (Good deeds) is the first object, which is the stated one, as He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We replaced them with two gardens, two gardens﴾ [Saba': 16]. A poet said:

"The sister of the one with two jars laughs at me: 'May God replace you with two colours: the blackness of a face and the whiteness of two eyes.'"

It appears that (whoever repents), meaning initiates repentance, will repent to God, meaning returns to His reward and His kindness. Ibn 'Atiyya said: (whoever repents) has truly grasped a firm matter, just as you say to one whose speech about a matter is praised: "Indeed you have spoken a word, O so-and-so," so likewise the verse means the praise of repentance, as if He said: he will find relief and great forgiveness. Al-Zamakhshari said: Whoever abandons sins, regrets them and enters into righteous deeds, is by that a repenter to God, who knows the right of the repenters and does with them what they deserve; and God loves the repenting and loves the purified. It was said: whoever resolves on repentance will repent to God, so let him hasten to it and turn to God with it. It was said: (whoever repents) from his sins, he repents to Him who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evil deeds. It was said: (whoever repents) continues steadfast in repentance, so he is the true penitent before God.

﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾ returns to the mention of the attributes of the servants of the Merciful. The apparent meaning is that they do not testify to falsehood, or the testimony of falsehood; so said 'Ali and al-Baqir, and it is from testimony. It was said: the meaning is that they do not attend a gathering, from presence. Falsehood (al-zur) is idolatry and an idol, or lying, or musical instruments, or the festivals of the Christians, or a game that was in the Jahiliyya, or wailing, or gatherings in which the righteous are disparaged: these are sayings. Idolatry was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, singing by Mujahid, lying by Ibn Jurayj. In al-Kashshaf, from Qatada: gatherings of falsehood. From Ibn al-Hanafiyya: play and singing. From Mujahid: the festivals of the polytheists; and "idle talk" (laghw) is everything that should be cast aside and discarded. The meaning is: (and when they pass) by people of idle talk, (they pass by) turning away from them, honouring themselves against stopping over them or engaging with them; by His saying: ﴿And when they hear idle talk they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. End.

﴿with the signs of their Lord﴾: these are the Qur'an.

﴿لَمْ يَخِرُّوا عَلَيْها صُمًّا وعُمْيانًا﴾ The negation applies to the qualifier that follows, which is "deaf and blind," and not to the falling down (khurur) that the negation particle precedes. In the usage of the Arabs, the most common view is that the negation applies to the qualifier. The meaning is that when they are reminded of these verses, they bend over them eagerly to listen, and they turn toward the one who reminds them with attentive ears and watchful eyes. This is unlike the hypocrites and others like them, who, when reminded, are bent over the verses and turned toward the one who reminds them only outwardly, and they are "deaf and blind" in that they do not grasp them and do not perceive what is in them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Rather, their falling down is in prostration and weeping, just as you say: "Zayd did not go out to war in fear," meaning that he went out only boldly and resolutely. The listener who is reminded is one whose ear is upright and whose affair is sound, so when he turns away, that is a khurur, which is a falling without order or arrangement. Although it resembles one who falls down in prostration, its basic sense is falling without order. End of quote. al-Suddi said: "They do not fall down" and "deaf and blind" describe the disbelievers, and it is an expression of their turning away and their exertion in that. He paired this with your saying: "So-and-so sat wishing," and "So-and-so stood weeping," while you did not intend to report sitting or standing, but these are preparatory phrases in speech and expression.

﴿قُرَّةَ أعْيُنٍ﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for joy and happiness, and it is derived from qurr, which means coolness. It is said: "The tears of joy are cool, and the tears of sorrow are hot." It is also said: "God cool your eye," and "God heat the eye of the enemy." Abu Tammam said:
As for the eyes of lovers, they were heated (with tears),
and as for the eyes of the gloaters, they were cooled.
It was also said that it is derived from qarar, meaning that the gaze rests on it and does not look at anything else. Abu 'Amr said: "The comfort of the eye is sleep," meaning security, because security does not come with fear. This was related by al-Qaffal. The comfort of the eyes, regarding those whose righteousness they mention, is seeing them obedient to God (p-517). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Hadrami. In the early period of Islam, a father would be guided while his son was a disbeliever, or a husband while his wife was a disbeliever, and the comfort of their eyes was in the faith of their beloved ones. Ibn 'Abbas said: The comfort of a child's eye is that you see him writing jurisprudence (fiqh). The apparent meaning is that they prayed for this so that they would be obeyed in this world and they would be gladdened by them. It was also said: They asked that God join those people with them in Paradise so that their joy would be complete. End of quote. This second view includes the first, which concerns this world, because that is the result of their faith in this world. It is clear that min here is for the inception of the end point (ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning: ﴿هَبْ لَنا﴾ grant us, from their side, what cools our eyes of obedience and righteousness. It is also permitted that min be for specification (bayan), as al-Zamakhshari said. He said: It is as if it were said: "Grant us ﴿قُرَّةَ أعْيُنٍ﴾ (comfort of the eyes)," and then the comfort was specified and explained by His saying: ﴿مِن أزْواجِنا وذُرِّيّاتِنا﴾ (from our spouses and our offspring). Its meaning is that God makes them, for them, a comfort of the eyes, from your saying: "I saw from you a lion," meaning: you are a lion. End of quote. We have previously noted that min which is for specifying the genus (bayan al-jins) must come before what it specifies, and then it comes with min of specification. This is according to the view of those who affirmed that it can be for specifying the genus. The correct view is that this meaning is not established for min.

Ibn 'Amir, the two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), and Hafs read ﴿وذُرِّيّاتِنا﴾ in the plural. The rest of the seven read it in the singular, and Talhah also read it in the singular. 'Abdullah, Abu al-Darda', and Abu Hurayrah read (qurrat) in the plural, while the majority read it in the singular. The word qurrah is indefinite to match the indefiniteness of a'yun (eyes), as if he said: "Grant us from them joy and happiness." The word a'yun comes in the form of the paucity plural (jam' qillah) rather than 'uyun, which is the form of the plurality plural (jam' kathrah), because what is meant is the eyes of the righteous, and they are few in comparison to the eyes of others. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, but it is not sound, because a'yun applies to ten and less of plurals, while the righteous do not have ten eyes; rather, their eyes are very many. Even if their eyes are few in comparison to the eyes of others, they are so many as to be uncountable. The word imaman is in the singular, either because the singular is sufficient in place of the plural, and it is made good by its being a rhyme-final (fasilah), and it indicates the genus without ambiguity; or because the meaning is "make each one of them an imam"; or it may be the plural of amm, like hall and hilal; or because they were united and their word was agreed upon. They said: "Make us one imam," they asked God that they would be exemplars in religion, and they did not seek leadership. This was said by al-Nakha'i. It was also said: the verse contains what indicates that leadership in religion must be sought. It was revealed concerning the ten who were given glad tidings of Paradise.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ (those) is a reference to those described with these ten qualities. ﴿الغُرْفَةَ﴾ (the chamber) is a definite noun with the article al, so it is general, meaning the chambers, as in His saying: ﴿وهم في الغُرُفاتِ آمِنُونَ﴾ (and they will be secure in the upper chambers) [Saba' 34:37], and they are the lofty places. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are houses of emerald, pearl, and ruby. It was said that al-Ghurfah is one of the names of Paradise. It was said: the seventh heaven is a ghurfah. It was said: it is the highest of the dwellings of Paradise. It was said: what is meant is elevation in ranks. The preposition ba' in ﴿بِما صَبَرُوا﴾ (for what they endured) indicates cause. It was also said that it indicates substitution (badal), meaning in place of their patience, as in the saying: "Would that I had for them a people when they ride," meaning: would that I had in their place a people. He did not mention the object of patience specifically, so that it would include all its objects. al-Hasan, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far, the two Harams, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr read ﴿ويُلَقَّوْنَ﴾ (and they will be met) with a dammah on the ya', a fathah on the lam, and a shaddah on the qaf. Talhah, Muhammad al-Yamani, and the rest of the seven read it with a fathah on the ya', a sukun on the lam, and a light qaf. The tahiyyah is a prayer for long life, and the salam is a prayer for safety, meaning: the angels greet them, or some of them greet others. It was also said: they will be greeted with gifts, so that the benefits and honor are combined for them.

﴿حَسُنَتْ مُسْتَقَرًّا ومُقامًا﴾ (how good as a resting place and a dwelling) is a counterpart to His saying about Hell: ﴿ساءَتْ مُسْتَقَرًّا ومُقامًا﴾ (how evil as a resting place and a dwelling) [al-Furqan 25:66].

When He described His servants, the worshippers, and enumerated the righteous deeds they have, He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to declare plainly to people that they have no weight with their Lord except worship and supplication. In His saying: ﴿لَوْلا دُعاؤُكُمْ﴾ (were it not for your supplication), the word dua' means worship. The apparent meaning is that ma is a negation, meaning: "My Lord does not weigh you at all, were it not for your supplication." It is also permitted that it be interrogative with the meaning of negation, meaning: "What weight does He give you?" The word du'a'ukum is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its subject, meaning: were it not for your worship of Him, that is, were it not for your supplication and humbling yourselves to Him, or: He would not care about your punishment, were it not for your calling upon idols as gods. It was also said that it is added to its object, meaning: were it not for His calling you to His obedience. What appears to be the case is that His saying ﴿قُلْ ما يَعْبَأُ بِكُمْ﴾ (Say: He does not weigh you at all) is an address to the Quraysh disbelievers who said (p-518): "We will prostrate to what you command us." Meaning: My Lord does not concern Himself with you, were it not for your humbling yourselves to Him and your seeking His aid in hardships.

﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبْتُمْ﴾ (then you have denied) what the Messenger ﷺ brought, so you deserve punishment. ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ (then it will be) the punishment, which is what your denial produced. He gave them room in its arrival with the expression ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ لِزامًا﴾ (then it will be inevitable), meaning: it will be lasting for them, and they will not be free of it. 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr read: "The disbelievers have denied," and this is understood to be an explanation, not Qur'an. Most of them hold that al-Lizam here is the Day of Badr. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy. It was also said: it is the punishment of the Hereafter. It was also said: it is death, but it is not to be understood as ordinary death, rather it is killing at Badr. It was said that the implied meaning is: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ it, meaning the punishment, and this was made explicit by the one who read: "Then the punishment will be inevitable." The sound view is that the subject of kana is left unspoken after it is known that it is something threatened, for the sake of vagueness and to encompass what the description cannot contain. From Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَكُونُ﴾ it, meaning the denial, (lizaman), meaning inevitable for you, and you will not be granted repentance. This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi. Al-Zamakhshari said: The address is to people in general, among whom are believing worshippers and denying sinners, so they are addressed with what is found in their kind of worship and denial: ﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبْتُمْ﴾ (then you have denied). He says: If I have informed you that My judgment is that I do not reckon anything except their worship, then by your denial you have opposed My judgment, so the effect of your denial will surely cling to you until it hurls you into the Fire. A parallel in speech is when a king says to one who disobeyed him: "It is my custom to be kind to whoever obeys me and follows my command. You have disobeyed, so you will see what I will bring upon you because of your disobedience." Ibn Juraij read ﴿فَسَوْفَ تَكُونُ﴾ with the feminine ta', meaning: then the consequence will be. The majority read (lizaman) with a kasrah on the lam. al-Minhal, Aban ibn Tha'lab, and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fathah, as a verbal noun. It is said: lazima yalzamu luzuman and lizaman, like thabata thubutan and thabatan. Abu 'Ubaydah cited, for the kasrah on the lam, the verse of Sakhr al-Ghayy:
So if they escape the death of one land,
they will have met their deaths, inevitably.
Ibn Khalawayh related from Abu al-Sammal that he read "lazama" on the pattern of "hadhama," taking it as a verbal noun deviated from al-lazamah, like fujjar deviated from al-fajarah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 25, verse 67–77 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They are neither extravagant nor niggardly﴾. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jili said: Spending in what is not obedience to God is extravagance (israf), and withholding from obedience is niggardliness (iqtar). The same meaning was given by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. A man heard another man say: "There is no good in extravagance," so he said: "There is no extravagance in good." 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba said: Extravagance is that you spend the property of another. Al-Nakha'i said: It is the one who does not let anyone go hungry or naked, and does not spend an outlay which people say is extravagant. Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: They are those who do not wear clothes for beauty and do not eat food for pleasure. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz when he married him to his daughter Fatima: "What is your expenditure?" 'Umar said to him: "The good deed between the two evil ones," and then he recited the verse. Extravagance (israf) is exceeding the limit in spending, and qatr (niggardliness) is constriction, which is the opposite of extravagance. It is reported from Anas in the Sunan of Ibn Majah that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, among extravagance is that you eat whatever you desire." A poet said:

"Do not go to excess in any matter, but moderate: both extremes of the affairs are blameworthy."

Another said:

"When a man gives his soul whatever it desires, and does not restrain it, it reaches out to every falsehood.
And it drives him toward sin and shame by means of the sweetness of the fleeting thing that calls him to it."

Hatim said:

"If you have given your belly its desire, and your private part too, then you have attained the furthest point of blame, all of it."

Al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read (yaqturu) with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the ta'. Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ta'. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ta' with shadda, and all of these are dialects meaning constriction. Abu Hatim denied the use of the quadriliteral aqtara here, and said aqtara means became poor. From it comes ﴿And upon the straitened man according to his means﴾ [al-Baqara: 236]. He overlooked what al-Asma'i and others reported: from aqtara meaning constricted. Qiwam (the balance) is moderation between the two states. Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read (qiwaman) with a kasra. It was said: both are dialects with one meaning. It was also said: with the kasra, qiwam is that by which a thing is sustained; one says: "You are our qiwam," meaning that by which need is met, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. It was said: (qiwaman) with a kasra means a limit, sufficiency and the basis of a state. And ﴿between that﴾ and (qiwaman) may be two predicates according to those who permit multiple predicates for kana; or (bayna) may be the predicate and (qiwaman) a emphatic circumstantial phrase; or (qiwaman) may be the predicate and (bayna dhalika) either an object of kana according to the view of those who hold that the defective kana governs the adverbial phrase, or a circumstantial phrase of (qiwaman), since if it were postponed it would be an attribute. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿bayna dhalika﴾ be the subject of (kana) and built because it is added to a built word, like His saying: ﴿and from the disgrace of that day﴾ [Hud: 66] in the reading of one who pronounces the mim with a fatha, with (qiwaman) as the predicate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Grammatically there is no harm in it, but the meaning is not strong, because what lies between extravagance and niggardliness is necessarily a balance, so there is no benefit in the predicate, which is the basis of the benefit.

He, may He be exalted, described them with the moderation that lies between excess and deficiency, and the Messenger (ﷺ) was addressed with the like in His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand shackled to your neck﴾ [al-Isra': 29], etc.

﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. Ibn Mas'ud asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to God while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." So God revealed its confirmation: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god with God﴾, etc. It was said: Polytheists came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who had killed much and committed much adultery, and they said: "What you say and call to is indeed good; would you tell us that there is an expiation for what we have done?" Then it was revealed up to ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. It was also said: the occasion of revelation was the story of Wahshi in his Islam, in a long hadith.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He negated these great abominations from those described with those great qualities in religion, as a contrast with what the enemies of the believers, from Quraysh and others, were upon, as if it were said: "And those whom God has cleared and purified from what you are upon."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a removal of His believing servants from the attributes of the disbelievers in their worship of idols, their killing of souls by burying daughters alive, and other injustice, assassination and raids, and fornication which was permitted among them.

The explanation of the like of ﴿and do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except with right﴾ [al-An'am: 151] has preceded in Surat al-An'am.

It was read (yulaqqa) with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the lam and the qaf with shadda. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Raja' read (yalqa) with an alif, as if he intended to delete the presumed damma on the alif and kept the alif.

Al-Athām in the language means punishment, and it is the recompense of sin. The poet said:

"May God recompense Ibn 'Urwa, since he became disobedient, and disobedience for him is athām."

That is: a prescribed punishment and a penalty, and Qatada and Ibn Zayd explained it thus. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Ibn Jubayr said: Athām is a valley in Hell bearing this name, which God made a punishment for the disbelievers. Abu Muslim said: al-athām is sin, and its meaning is (yalqa) the recompense of athām, so the name of the thing is applied to its recompense. Al-Hasan said: athām is one of the names of Hell. It was said: a well in it. It was said: a mountain. Ibn Mas'ud read: (yalqa ayyaman), plural of yawm, meaning hardships. One says: "a day of days" for a grievous day.

As for His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾, it appears that it refers to the whole of calling upon another god, killing a soul without right, and adultery, so the doubling is ordered upon the totality of these sins, and that doubling does not necessarily apply to each one of them. There is no doubt that the punishment of the disbelievers varies according to their crimes.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ in the passive with an alif, and (wa yakhlud) in the active. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Ibn Kathir likewise, except that they doubled the 'ayn and dropped the alif. Abu Ja'far also, and Shayba and Talha ibn Sulayman, read (nudaʻʻif) with a nun, damma, and a doubled kasra on the 'ayn, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Musarrif read (yudaʻif) with a ya' in the active, (al-'adhab) in the accusative. Talha ibn Sulayman read (wa takhludu) with a ta' of address by way of iltifat, in the nominative, meaning: "and you, O disbeliever, will abide." Abu Haywa read (wa yukhalladu) in the passive, with a doubled lam, jussive. It was also reported from Abu 'Amr and on his authority likewise, with a single lam.
